one_line: Early-training label-assignment entropy predicts final detection AP better than early loss value.
problem: Model selection and hyperparameter search for detectors is expensive because early loss curves are poor predictors of final AP.
core_hypothesis: The ambiguity of the assignment problem (entropy over near-equal-cost anchor/query-to-GT assignments measured in the first few epochs) captures how well the detector's supervision is structured, and is a stronger early predictor of final AP than the raw training loss at the same step.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of runs varying assignment hyperparameters and learning rates on the same data, rank correlation between epoch-2 assignment entropy and final AP will be substantially higher than rank correlation between epoch-2 total loss and final AP.
why_important: A reliable early predictor would cut hyperparameter search cost for detection training by allowing early termination of doomed runs.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: early-stopping predictors are usually loss- or gradient-based; using the assignment problem's solution entropy as the predictive signal for detection specifically has not, to my knowledge, been isolated and tested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 20-30 small detector runs with varied assignment settings and LRs on a standard COCO-style dataset subset; log assignment entropy and loss at epoch 2; compare Spearman correlation of each signal with final AP.
main_risk: Assignment entropy may just proxy for learning rate or loss scale, adding no independent predictive power once those are controlled.
community_default_belief: Early training loss (or proxy tasks) is the standard cheap signal for run selection; assignment internals are treated as an implementation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Detection loss conflates classification and regression terms whose scales shift as assignment changes, so loss can look healthy while supervision is incoherently routed; the assignment distribution measures supervision coherence directly.
fastest_falsification: Reuse existing training logs if assignment costs were checkpointed; otherwise a grid of short runs on a small dataset subset suffices (single-GPU scale).

one_line: One-to-one matching instability disproportionately harms small objects, explaining part of the small-object gap in end-to-end detectors.
problem: End-to-end set-prediction detectors are known to lag on small objects, but the mechanism is usually attributed to feature resolution rather than optimization.
core_hypothesis: The identity of the query matched to a given GT box flips between consecutive epochs far more often for small objects, and this matching churn (not feature resolution alone) accounts for a measurable share of the small-object AP deficit.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-GT matching-flip rate will be significantly higher for small objects than large ones, and stabilizing matches for small objects only (e.g., by temporal assignment smoothing restricted to small GTs) will improve small-object AP without touching feature resolution.
why_important: If churn is causal, cheap assignment-stabilization fixes could close part of a widely lamented gap without expensive high-resolution features.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: matching instability has been discussed generally, but a size-stratified causal analysis attributing the small-object gap specifically to churn appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a one-to-one-matching detector to log matched-query identity per GT per epoch; stratify flip rate by GT size; then run an intervention that smooths assignment only for small GTs and measure size-stratified AP change.
main_risk: Flip rate and object size may both be driven by a confound (low IoU candidates for small boxes), making the intervention ineffective.
community_default_belief: Small-object weakness in set-prediction detectors is primarily a feature-resolution problem solved by higher-resolution attention or multi-scale features.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Small boxes have flatter matching-cost landscapes (many queries with similar cost), so bipartite matching is near-degenerate for them; optimization noise then scatters supervision across queries, which resolution improvements do not fix.
fastest_falsification: The logging-only part (flip rate vs size) requires one instrumented training run; if flip rates show no size dependence the hypothesis dies immediately.

one_line: Dynamic-k assignment works mainly by enacting an implicit size-based curriculum, reproducible with a fixed size-conditioned k schedule.
problem: Adaptive assignment schemes are effective but poorly understood, making them hard to tune or simplify.
core_hypothesis: The benefit of dynamic top-k positive selection comes mostly from allocating more positives to large/easy objects early and fewer to small/hard ones, i.e., an implicit curriculum indexable by object size; a static k-vs-size schedule distilled from one run reproduces most of the gain.
falsifiable_prediction: A fixed lookup table mapping GT size band to k (fit once from a dynamic-k run's statistics) will recover the majority of dynamic-k's AP improvement over fixed global k, across at least two detector families.
why_important: Replacing adaptive machinery with a static schedule simplifies implementations and reveals what the adaptivity actually buys.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: ablations of dynamic-k exist, but a distillation-to-static-schedule test that isolates the size-curriculum explanation appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with dynamic-k, record per-size-band average k over training; freeze that schedule as a function of size (and optionally epoch); retrain from scratch with the frozen schedule; compare AP to dynamic-k and fixed-k baselines.
main_risk: Dynamic-k's benefit may depend on per-image scene statistics (density, overlap) that a size-only schedule cannot capture.
community_default_belief: Adaptivity per-instance and per-iteration is intrinsic to why dynamic assignment works.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most of the variance in chosen k may be explained by object size alone, in which case per-instance adaptivity is mostly noise around a size-determined mean.
fastest_falsification: Variance decomposition of logged k values (size vs residual) from a single instrumented run: if size explains little variance, the hypothesis is dead before any retraining.

one_line: Center-biased positive sampling causes systematic under-detection of occluded objects whose visible region is off-center.
problem: Occluded-object recall remains poor and is usually attributed to appearance corruption rather than supervision placement.
core_hypothesis: Assignment schemes that favor locations near the GT box center systematically place positives on occluder pixels when the visible fragment is off-center, teaching the model to fire on the wrong evidence; re-centering positives on the visible-region centroid improves occluded recall.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall for occluded objects will correlate negatively with the distance between box center and visible-region centroid; shifting positive sampling toward the visible centroid (using amodal/modal mask info where available, or a saliency proxy) will improve occluded-object recall with negligible change on unoccluded objects.
why_important: Occlusion is the dominant failure mode in crowded and safety-critical scenes; a supervision-placement fix is far cheaper than occlusion-specific architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: center-prior sampling is standard and its interaction with occlusion geometry, to my knowledge, has not been isolated as a causal recall factor.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with visibility annotations, bin occluded GTs by center-to-visible-centroid offset and measure recall per bin for a standard detector; then retrain with visible-centroid-shifted positive sampling and compare the binned recall curves.
main_risk: Visible-region centroids may be unavailable or noisy at scale, and the saliency proxy may introduce its own bias.
community_default_belief: Occlusion failures stem from corrupted appearance features; sampling location within the GT box is a minor detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The model may have adequate features for the visible fragment but never receives positive gradient there, because the center prior consistently supervises occluder pixels instead.
fastest_falsification: The correlational part needs only inference plus visibility annotations on an existing checkpoint - no training.

one_line: Assignment conflicts at object boundaries are the dominant source of classification label noise in dense detectors, and masking them beats focal-loss tuning for calibration.
problem: Dense detectors are badly calibrated, and the standard remedy (focal-loss variants and post-hoc scaling) treats symptoms rather than sources of label noise.
core_hypothesis: Feature locations plausibly assignable to two different GT objects (or to a GT and background) receive effectively contradictory classification targets across iterations and images; excluding these conflicted locations from the classification loss removes more miscalibration than tuning the focusing parameter.
falsifiable_prediction: Masking classification loss at locations where the top-2 assignment costs are within a small margin will improve detection calibration error more than a sweep over focal-loss hyperparameters, at equal or better AP.
why_important: Calibrated detection scores are prerequisites for downstream decision systems; identifying the noise source enables principled fixes.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: ambiguity-aware assignment exists, but framing boundary conflicts as the primary calibration noise source and testing mask-vs-focal head-to-head appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a dense one-stage detector with (a) baseline, (b) focal sweep, (c) conflict-masked classification loss; compare expected calibration error of detection scores and AP on held-out data.
main_risk: Masking may starve the model of hard-negative supervision precisely where discrimination is most needed, hurting AP.
community_default_belief: Detection miscalibration is an inherent side effect of extreme foreground-background imbalance, best handled by focal-style reweighting or post-hoc calibration.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Imbalance explains overconfidence in background, but not the specific miscalibration near object boundaries; if conflicted targets are the driver, reweighting cannot fix what masking can.
fastest_falsification: A single pair of short training runs (masked vs baseline) on a small dataset with calibration measurement suffices for a first signal.

one_line: Soft/quality-weighted classification targets help mainly by down-weighting misassigned positives, not by providing graded supervision.
problem: Quality-aware soft targets are widely adopted in detection heads, but which of their effects matters is unknown, leading to cargo-cult adoption.
core_hypothesis: The gain from IoU-weighted soft classification targets is dominated by the suppression of low-quality (likely misassigned) positives; a hard binary mask at a quality threshold captures most of the benefit, and the graded values above threshold contribute little.
falsifiable_prediction: Replacing soft targets with a hard quality-threshold mask (binary keep/drop of positives) will retain the large majority of the AP gain over vanilla hard targets, while randomizing the graded values above threshold will barely hurt.
why_important: Understanding the active ingredient simplifies heads and guides where further gains can come from (better assignment vs better target shaping).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: soft-target ablations usually compare formulations against each other; the specific decomposition into mask-effect vs gradation-effect appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three matched runs: soft targets, thresholded hard mask, and above-threshold-value-shuffled soft targets; compare AP and per-quality-band error rates.
main_risk: The right threshold may vary by dataset/architecture, making the hard-mask variant look artificially weak if not tuned.
community_default_belief: Graded quality supervision teaches the head to rank predictions by localization quality, which is the core benefit.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The ranking signal may be redundant with what the regression branch already induces; the decisive effect may be simply removing gradient from wrong positives.
fastest_falsification: The value-shuffle control alone (one run) is highly diagnostic: if shuffling graded values above threshold doesn't hurt, gradation is not the ingredient.

one_line: Assignment churn creates measurable gradient interference between classification and regression, and EMA-smoothed assignment reduces it.
problem: Detection training is slower and noisier than classification at matched scale, and the sources of gradient noise specific to detection are not well decomposed.
core_hypothesis: When a location flips between positive and negative across iterations, its classification and regression gradients alternate in direction, producing negative cosine similarity between successive per-location gradients; smoothing the assignment decision with an EMA over iterations reduces this interference and speeds convergence.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-location gradient cosine similarity across nearby iterations will be systematically lower at churn-prone locations; EMA-smoothed assignment will raise it and reach baseline final AP in measurably fewer iterations.
why_important: A general convergence-speed lever for all assignment-based detectors would reduce training cost across the field.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: gradient-interference analyses exist for multi-task learning, but applying them to assignment churn within a single detection task appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument per-location gradients in a short training run, correlate interference with churn; implement assignment EMA and compare iterations-to-target-AP against baseline on a small dataset.
main_risk: Assignment EMA may lag ground-truth-appropriate assignments as features improve, capping final AP below baseline.
community_default_belief: Assignment noise is an unavoidable and largely harmless part of detector training; convergence speed is addressed via LR schedules and pretraining.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If interference is concentrated and structured (not white noise), it is exactly the kind of noise that smoothing can remove without biasing the solution.
fastest_falsification: The instrumentation-only phase (correlating churn with gradient cosine) needs a single short run and no new method.

consolidation.mutation_note: The churn-to-gradient-interference measurement is the strong falsifiable core; EMA-smoothed assignment is a bolt-on fix. Mutate: lead with the instrumentation-only interference measurement and demote the EMA intervention to one validation arm.

one_line: One-to-many assignment's crowded-scene advantage is explained by positive-gradient mass, not by duplicate-hypothesis diversity.
problem: It is unclear why one-to-many assignment outperforms one-to-one in crowded scenes, which blocks principled hybrid designs.
core_hypothesis: The crowded-scene gap between one-to-many and one-to-one assignment is mostly a gradient-quantity effect: one-to-many delivers more positive gradient mass per GT; equalizing positive gradient mass (by loss reweighting in the one-to-one detector) eliminates most of the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Scaling per-positive loss weights in a one-to-one detector to match the total positive gradient mass of a one-to-many counterpart will recover the majority of the crowded-scene AP difference, without adding extra positives.
why_important: If true, hybrid assignment schemes chasing 'hypothesis diversity' are misdirected; simple reweighting achieves the same at zero architectural cost.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: comparisons of assignment families abound, but a gradient-mass-matched controlled comparison appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a crowded-scene detection dataset, train one-to-one baseline, one-to-many baseline, and gradient-mass-matched one-to-one; compare AP stratified by scene density.
main_risk: Loss reweighting may destabilize matching (higher effective LR on positives), conflating the comparison.
community_default_belief: One-to-many helps because multiple anchors/queries per GT provide redundancy and better coverage of crowded layouts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Redundant positives mostly deliver near-identical gradients through shared features, so their effect may reduce to a scalar on gradient magnitude rather than genuine diversity.
fastest_falsification: Density-stratified evaluation of the gradient-mass-matched run against both baselines; a single training run beyond the baselines.

one_line: A brief deliberately-randomized assignment phase early in training reduces easy-object-first bias and improves rare-class AP.
problem: Cost-based assignment early in training routes positives to whatever the randomly initialized model already scores well, potentially locking in a bias toward easy/frequent objects.
core_hypothesis: Because early assignment costs reflect initialization noise plus easy-object signals, cost-based assignment amplifies an easy-object-first curriculum; substituting uniformly random (but geometrically valid) positive selection for the first phase of training acts as exploration and yields better rare-class and hard-object AP at equal final compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Runs with a short random-assignment warm phase will show higher rare-class AP and lower per-class AP variance than cost-based-from-scratch runs, with overall AP no worse.
why_important: A zero-cost schedule change that mitigates class-difficulty bias would benefit long-tail detection broadly.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: warmup tricks for assignment exist (e.g., fixed geometric rules early), but deliberate randomization framed and evaluated as exploration against difficulty bias appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Matched runs on a long-tail detection dataset: baseline vs random-assignment for the first N iterations (sweep N over 2-3 values); compare rare-class AP and per-class AP spread.
main_risk: Random positives may slow early representation learning enough that the model never catches up within the budget.
community_default_belief: Assignment should always route supervision to the lowest-cost candidates; randomness in assignment is pure noise to be minimized.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Lowest-cost routing at initialization optimizes against a meaningless cost landscape and can entrench arbitrary early preferences, the same argument that motivates exploration in RL.
fastest_falsification: Two short runs on a small long-tail subset; if rare-class AP is not improved at any warm-phase length, the idea is falsified.

consolidation.mutation_note: Payload as written is a training-schedule trick. Mutate: reframe around the falsifiable curriculum claim (cost-based assignment enacts an easy-object-first ordering that suppresses rare-class AP), with the randomized phase as one intervention arm among controls.

one_line: Where box-voting helps is predictable from per-class annotation box variance: suppressed duplicates carry complementary localization information exactly when labels are noisy.
problem: Box voting / weighted NMS helps inconsistently across classes and datasets, and practitioners cannot predict when to enable it.
core_hypothesis: Duplicates suppressed by NMS are approximately independent draws around the true box whose spread tracks annotation ambiguity; therefore averaging them helps most for classes whose ground-truth boxes have high annotator variance, and per-class annotation variance predicts per-class box-voting gain.
falsifiable_prediction: Across classes, the AP75 gain from box voting will correlate positively with an annotation-variance proxy (e.g., disagreement between independent re-annotations on a small audit set, or duplicate-GT spread where available).
why_important: Turns an unreliable trick into a predictable tool and exposes annotation noise as the controlling variable for localization ensembling.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: box voting is old, but linking its per-class efficacy to measured annotation variance appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a small stratified sample of boxes with multiple annotators to estimate per-class box variance; measure per-class box-voting AP gain for an existing checkpoint; test the correlation.
main_risk: Per-class gains from box voting may be too noisy at feasible audit sizes to establish or refute a correlation.
community_default_belief: Box voting is a generic test-time trick whose benefit depends on the detector, not on properties of the labels.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If model box error were the driver, voting gains would track model quality; but voting averages model noise that mirrors label noise, so label variance may be the real moderator.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only per-class gain measurement plus a modest re-annotation audit; no training needed.

one_line: A per-image NMS threshold set from the pre-NMS prediction density recovers most crowd-scene AP lost to a fixed global threshold.
problem: A single NMS IoU threshold must trade off duplicate removal in sparse scenes against recall in crowded scenes, and is usually tuned to the dataset average.
core_hypothesis: The NMS threshold functions as a prior over scene density; the pre-NMS score-weighted prediction density is a sufficient statistic to set that prior per image, and doing so recovers the bulk of the AP lost in dense scenes without any retraining or crowd-specific machinery.
falsifiable_prediction: Density-adaptive NMS (threshold as a monotone function of pre-NMS local density, function fit on a held-out split) will improve AP on the densest decile of images by a clearly larger margin than any fixed threshold can, while leaving sparse-scene AP unchanged.
why_important: Crowded scenes dominate practical failure cases (retail, traffic, events); a training-free fix is immediately deployable.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: adaptive NMS ideas exist that predict density from features; using the detector's own pre-NMS output density as the control signal, with no learned component, appears not to have been isolated as sufficient.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For an existing checkpoint, fit the density-to-threshold map on validation images; evaluate density-stratified AP against the best fixed threshold on a disjoint test split.
main_risk: Pre-NMS density confounds true object density with model uncertainty; in high-FP regimes the adaptive rule could raise thresholds exactly when it should not.
community_default_belief: Solving crowded-scene suppression requires learned or feature-conditioned NMS variants or end-to-end set prediction.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The detector's raw output already encodes local density; the information may not need to be learned, only routed into the threshold.
fastest_falsification: Entirely inference-time; a day of compute on an existing checkpoint and dataset with density stratification.

consolidation.solo_drop_note: Density-adaptive NMS thresholding for crowded scenes is an established engineering direction; the 'pre-NMS density as sufficient statistic' reframing does not clear the novelty burden, and the payload is a threshold-scheduling tweak. Classic threshold+X permutation.

one_line: Score-localization miscorrelation has two distinct modes originating in different training phases, separable by checkpoint interpolation.
problem: The imperfect correlation between confidence and localization quality is treated as a single phenomenon, limiting targeted fixes.
core_hypothesis: Well-localized-but-low-score errors arise early (classification lags localization for hard positives) while poorly-localized-but-high-score errors arise late (classification overfits before regression saturates); interpolating between early and late checkpoints trades the two modes against each other in a predictable way.
falsifiable_prediction: The ratio of the two miscorrelation modes will shift monotonically along a checkpoint-interpolation path, and a mid-path interpolate will have better score-IoU correlation than either endpoint.
why_important: Decomposing the miscorrelation guides whether to fix scoring via training schedules, checkpoint averaging, or post-hoc rescoring.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: score-IoU miscorrelation is well known, but its decomposition into phase-attributable modes via weight interpolation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Save checkpoints across training; classify score-IoU outliers into the two modes at each checkpoint; evaluate mode ratios and score-IoU correlation along linear weight interpolations between early and late checkpoints.
main_risk: Weight interpolation between distant detection checkpoints may produce broken models (loss barriers), invalidating the path analysis.
community_default_belief: Score-IoU miscorrelation is a static head-design deficiency, addressed by IoU-aware scoring heads.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the two error modes evolve oppositely over training, no static head fix is optimal; the phenomenon is partly a checkpoint-selection artifact.
fastest_falsification: Requires only saved checkpoints from one training run plus inference; mode classification is automatic from (score, IoU) pairs.

one_line: Duplicate suppression in NMS-free detectors is modular: a small set of decoder components implements it and can be ablated to restore duplicates.
problem: How end-to-end detectors suppress duplicates internally is unknown, which blocks both diagnosis (when suppression fails) and reuse (porting suppression to other models).
core_hypothesis: Duplicate suppression is implemented by a sparse, identifiable subcircuit (specific self-attention heads / decoder layers that mediate query-to-query inhibition) rather than being distributed; ablating that subcircuit selectively restores duplicate predictions while leaving single-object accuracy largely intact.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating a small fraction of decoder self-attention heads (selected by a query-inhibition attribution score) will multiply the duplicate rate several-fold while changing single-object AP only marginally; ablating random heads of equal count will not.
why_important: A localized suppression circuit could be monitored, strengthened for crowded scenes, or deliberately relaxed for high-recall applications, at inference time.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: analyses note that query self-attention matters for suppression, but a causal, sparse-circuit-level localization with selective restoration of duplicates appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score each decoder head by how much its removal increases duplicates-per-GT on a validation set; ablate top-scored heads vs random heads; measure duplicate rate and AP.
main_risk: Suppression may be redundant across layers (removing one path activates another), masking modularity.
community_default_belief: End-to-end suppression emerges holistically from bipartite-matching training and cannot be localized to components.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Networks trained with a single sharp constraint often satisfy it with specialized components; suppression is exactly such a constraint and query self-attention is its natural home.
fastest_falsification: Head-ablation sweeps are inference-only on a public end-to-end detector checkpoint.

one_line: The score gap between a top box and its best suppressed duplicate predicts localization error better than the top score itself.
problem: Confidence scores are weak predictors of localization quality, yet the information discarded by NMS is never used for uncertainty estimation.
core_hypothesis: The suppressed runner-up box encodes the model's alternative hypothesis; a small score gap with high spatial disagreement indicates genuine localization ambiguity, so gap-and-disagreement statistics of suppressed duplicates outperform the raw score as a per-detection localization-error predictor.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking detections by a duplicate-gap statistic will yield a strictly better error-retention curve (localization error vs coverage) than ranking by score, on multiple detector families without retraining.
why_important: Free, training-less uncertainty from information every detector already computes and throws away; useful for active learning and safety filtering.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: NMS-retained candidates have been used for ensembling boxes, but using the top-vs-duplicate score gap explicitly as a calibrated localization-uncertainty signal appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For existing checkpoints, record top box, best suppressed duplicate, score gap, and IoU between them; compare AUROC for predicting large localization error against score-only and box-variance baselines.
main_risk: In one-to-one detectors duplicates are trained away, so the signal may exist only for one-to-many models, limiting generality.
community_default_belief: Post-NMS, suppressed boxes are redundant noise; per-detection uncertainty requires dedicated heads or MC sampling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Suppressed duplicates are produced by different anchors/queries viewing different evidence, making them a cheap implicit ensemble the score alone cannot summarize.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only evaluation on public checkpoints; a null result across two families falsifies cheaply.

one_line: Cross-class NMS suppression errors grow superlinearly with vocabulary size, becoming a first-order cost in large-vocabulary detection.
problem: Large-vocabulary detectors are evaluated end-to-end, so losses specific to inter-class suppression (a correct box of class A killed by an overlapping high-score class B box) are never isolated.
core_hypothesis: As vocabulary grows, near-synonym and part-whole class pairs proliferate faster than linearly, so class-agnostic or cross-class suppression destroys a superlinearly growing fraction of correct detections; the loss is measurable by vocabulary-subset ablation on a fixed model.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating the same detector restricted to nested vocabulary subsets will show per-class recall for a fixed class set decreasing as vocabulary grows, with the decrease concentrated in classes having high-overlap sibling classes, and the aggregate loss growing faster than linear in vocabulary size.
why_important: Quantifies a hidden tax on open-vocabulary and large-taxonomy detection, motivating suppression schemes that reason over class relations.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: class-aware vs class-agnostic NMS comparisons exist, but a scaling analysis of suppression error versus vocabulary size on fixed models appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a trained large-vocabulary detector; evaluate a fixed 50-class subset's recall while activating increasingly large superset vocabularies at inference; attribute recall changes to suppression events via logging.
main_risk: Score competition in the classifier (softmax mass splitting) may confound suppression effects; needs careful attribution of each lost detection.
community_default_belief: Vocabulary size mainly stresses the classifier; the suppression stage is class-count-agnostic plumbing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Suppression operates on overlapping boxes regardless of semantics, and semantic proximity grows with taxonomy density, so the plumbing becomes semantics-sensitive precisely at scale.
fastest_falsification: Pure inference with vocabulary masking and suppression-event logging on an existing checkpoint.

one_line: Learned-NMS gains are mostly context-aware rescoring, not better suppression ordering; rescoring alone captures the benefit.
problem: Learned duplicate-removal modules improve AP, but conflate two mechanisms (changing scores vs changing which boxes suppress which), so the field cannot tell what to build next.
core_hypothesis: The dominant effect of learned suppression modules is that they rescore boxes using scene context; if their learned scores are used only to reorder/reweight standard greedy NMS (keeping classic suppression logic), most of the AP gain survives.
falsifiable_prediction: A hybrid using learned scores with vanilla greedy NMS will recover the majority of the learned module's AP gain over baseline NMS, and the residual attributable to learned suppression topology will be small.
why_important: Directs research effort toward context rescoring (cheap, modular) rather than replacing suppression logic (complex, latency-heavy).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: papers report end-to-end gains of learned NMS; a decomposition isolating rescoring from suppression-structure contributions appears unpublished to my knowledge.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or obtain a learned suppression module; evaluate (a) full module, (b) its scores + greedy NMS, (c) original scores + greedy NMS; compare AP deltas.
main_risk: Learned modules may produce scores meaningful only within their own suppression procedure, making the hybrid unfairly weak.
community_default_belief: Learned NMS works because it learns which boxes should suppress which, i.e., relational suppression structure.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most duplicate structure is captured by simple overlap geometry already; the learnable headroom is in scores conditioned on context, which greedy NMS can consume directly.
fastest_falsification: If an off-the-shelf learned-suppression checkpoint is available, the decomposition is inference-only; otherwise one small training run.

one_line: Orientation-normalized overlap in NMS fixes a systematic suppression bias against elongated objects with zero retraining.
problem: Elongated objects (axis-aligned boxes with extreme aspect ratio) suffer both duplicate leakage along their long axis and wrongful suppression across their short axis under standard IoU-based NMS.
core_hypothesis: Because IoU between shifted copies of an elongated box decays slowly along the principal axis and quickly across it, a single IoU threshold cannot serve both axes; normalizing the overlap measure by box shape (e.g., per-axis intersection ratios) removes a shape-conditioned suppression bias measurable on existing detectors.
falsifiable_prediction: Shape-normalized NMS will improve AP on the high-eccentricity decile of objects while leaving near-square objects unchanged, on multiple existing checkpoints without retraining.
why_important: Elongated objects (vehicles from the side, tools, furniture, text regions) are common; a drop-in post-processing fix has immediate practical value.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: many IoU variants exist for losses and rotated boxes, but a shape-normalized overlap used specifically in axis-aligned NMS, motivated by axis-anisotropic IoU decay, appears not isolated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement per-axis-normalized overlap in NMS; evaluate eccentricity-stratified AP for two public checkpoints against tuned standard NMS.
main_risk: Duplicate structure along elongated objects may reflect genuine multi-instance ambiguity (e.g., parked car rows) where aggressive axis handling harms recall.
community_default_belief: NMS with a tuned IoU threshold is shape-neutral enough; shape issues belong to the loss/assignment stage.
why_that_may_be_wrong: IoU's geometry is provably anisotropic under translation for non-square boxes, so a scalar threshold necessarily encodes a shape prior; the bias is in the operator, not the training.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only stratified evaluation; falsified if eccentric-object AP does not improve on any checkpoint.

consolidation.mutation_note: The shape-conditioned suppression-bias measurement is crisp and inference-only, but the per-axis-normalized-overlap fix lands in a crowded NMS-variant space. Mutate: measurement-first framing; any fix claim requires a prior-art sweep of shape-aware NMS variants.

one_line: Rising pre-NMS duplicate rate is a leading indicator of detector overfitting, preceding validation AP decline.
problem: Detecting the onset of overfitting in detectors currently requires held-out AP evaluation, which is expensive to run frequently.
core_hypothesis: As a detector begins to overfit, its predictions become sharper but less consistent across nearby locations/queries, manifesting first as an increase in confident duplicates per GT on training-distribution data; this duplicate-rate inflection precedes the validation AP peak by a measurable margin.
falsifiable_prediction: In standard training runs, the minimum of the pre-NMS duplicates-per-GT curve (on a small monitoring split) will occur consistently before the epoch of peak validation AP, and duplicate rate will predict the peak within a small epoch window.
why_important: A near-free early-warning signal (computable on unlabeled or training data) enables cheaper checkpoint selection and adaptive schedules.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: overfitting indicators are typically loss- or accuracy-based; duplicate statistics as a leading indicator for detection appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument several training runs across two architectures; log pre-NMS duplicate statistics each epoch on a fixed monitoring set; test temporal precedence against validation AP peaks.
main_risk: Duplicate rate may be dominated by assignment/schedule artifacts (e.g., LR drops) unrelated to generalization, producing false alarms.
community_default_belief: Overfitting monitoring requires labeled validation evaluation; internal prediction statistics are not reliable proxies.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Duplicate coherence is a self-consistency property that degrades when the model fits noise, and self-consistency losses of this kind often track generalization.
fastest_falsification: Piggyback logging on any planned training runs; no extra training required beyond instrumentation.

one_line: NMS-free detectors wrongly self-suppress genuinely overlapping objects at a rate predictable from training-set co-occlusion statistics.
problem: End-to-end detectors avoid NMS's crowded-scene failure in principle, yet still miss overlapping instances, and the residual failure is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: The learned inter-query inhibition in one-to-one-trained detectors generalizes the statistics of its training data: pairs of objects with overlap patterns rare in training are inhibited as if they were duplicates, so the miss rate for overlapping instance pairs is predictable from the training-set frequency of that overlap geometry and class pair.
falsifiable_prediction: Binning test-set object pairs by (IoU, class-pair) and computing pair-recall will show a monotone relationship with training-set frequency of the same bin, and this relationship will be significantly stronger for end-to-end detectors than for NMS-based detectors evaluated identically.
why_important: Identifies a distribution-inherited ceiling on crowded-scene performance for end-to-end detectors and gives a formula for where to add targeted training data.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: crowded-scene weaknesses of set-prediction detectors are documented, but tying pairwise miss rates quantitatively to training co-occlusion statistics appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute training-set overlap-geometry histograms; evaluate pair-recall by bin for one end-to-end and one NMS-based public checkpoint on the same test data; compare correlation strengths.
main_risk: Pair-recall estimates in rare bins will be noisy; needs careful binning and confidence intervals to avoid overinterpreting.
community_default_belief: End-to-end detectors handle overlapping objects fundamentally better because they lack a hard-coded overlap-suppression heuristic.
why_that_may_be_wrong: They replace the heuristic with a learned prior fit to training co-occurrence; where the prior lacks support, learned suppression can behave worse than geometry-blind NMS.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only on public checkpoints plus training-set statistics; no training runs needed.

one_line: IoU-based losses induce systematic box shrinkage under extent ambiguity, measurable on occluded objects.
problem: Detectors systematically mis-size boxes for occluded and fuzzy-boundary objects, and it is unclear whether the bias comes from data or from the loss.
core_hypothesis: When the true extent is ambiguous, the expected IoU-style loss is minimized by a box smaller than the mean annotation (asymmetric penalty for over- vs under-coverage under label noise), so IoU-loss-trained models exhibit a shrinkage bias on ambiguous objects that L1-trained models do not, holding data fixed.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched architectures differing only in regression loss, the mean signed size error on occluded objects will be significantly negative (shrunk) for IoU-family losses and near zero for L1, while both are near zero on unoccluded objects.
why_important: Shrinkage bias corrupts downstream measurements (distance estimation, grasping, tracking gates) in exactly the hard cases; knowing the cause enables loss-side correction.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: IoU-loss asymmetry under label noise seems analyzable but a controlled shrinkage-bias measurement conditioned on occlusion appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train two small detectors identical except for regression loss; compute signed width/height error stratified by occlusion level; additionally verify the asymmetry analytically or by simulation with synthetic label jitter.
main_risk: Occlusion correlates with annotation convention differences (modal vs amodal), which could produce the same signature without the loss being causal.
community_default_belief: IoU-family losses are strictly better regression objectives because they directly optimize the evaluation overlap.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Optimizing expected overlap under noisy targets is not the same as unbiased extent estimation; the loss can be optimal for AP yet biased for size.
fastest_falsification: The synthetic-jitter simulation (no real training) can establish or refute the asymmetry mechanism in hours.

one_line: Corner and center-size box parameterizations produce decorrelated errors, so cross-parameterization ensembling beats same-parameterization seed ensembling.
problem: Ensembling detectors is expensive and its localization benefit per added model is small, because seeds share systematic errors.
core_hypothesis: Center-size parameterization couples edge errors (an error in width moves two edges), while corner parameterization decouples them; the two parameterizations therefore make systematically different localization errors, and a two-model ensemble across parameterizations reduces box error more than a two-seed ensemble within one parameterization.
falsifiable_prediction: The per-edge error correlation between a corner-trained and a center-size-trained model will be significantly lower than between two seeds of either, and box-averaging the cross pair will yield lower localization error than either same-parameterization pair.
why_important: A free ensembling diversity source that requires no extra data or architecture changes, relevant wherever localization precision matters.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: parameterization choices are treated as interchangeable implementation details; their error-structure consequences for ensembling appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train four small models (2 seeds x 2 parameterizations) on the same data; measure pairwise per-edge error correlations and ensemble localization error for all pairings.
main_risk: Modern heads may mix parameterizations implicitly (e.g., quality-weighted losses), shrinking the achievable decorrelation.
community_default_belief: Box parameterization is a numerically motivated implementation choice with no systematic effect on error structure.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The loss landscape and gradient coupling differ across parameterizations, and gradient coupling is precisely what shapes correlated residual errors.
fastest_falsification: Four short training runs on a small dataset plus error-correlation analysis.

one_line: Localization error has a stride-tied quantization floor that sub-cell offset supervision removes, but only below a predictable object-size threshold.
problem: It is unclear how much residual localization error is attributable to feature-grid quantization versus genuine model uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: Regression targets expressed relative to feature-cell coordinates carry an irreducible error floor proportional to the effective stride; explicitly supervising sub-cell offsets with a higher-resolution target encoding eliminates the floor, and the improvement is significant only for objects smaller than a multiple of the stride.
falsifiable_prediction: Plotting localization error against object size will show a plateau at small sizes matching a stride-proportional constant; the sub-cell supervised variant will remove the plateau for small objects and match baseline for large objects, with the crossover size predictable from stride alone.
why_important: Separates decoding-limited from information-limited localization error, telling the field whether higher-resolution features or better decoders are needed for precise small-object boxes.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: sub-pixel tricks exist in keypoint estimation; a quantitative stride-floor law for box regression and its removal test appear absent in detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with standard vs sub-cell-refined target encodings at two strides; fit error-vs-size curves; check plateau presence, removal, and crossover-scaling with stride.
main_risk: Annotation noise for small objects may sit above the quantization floor, hiding the effect entirely.
community_default_belief: Regression heads interpolate freely below the stride, so grid quantization is not a meaningful error source.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interpolation capacity exists in principle, but the target normalization and the receptive-field alignment both tie gradients to cell geometry, which can hold the error floor in practice.
fastest_falsification: The error-vs-size plateau check on existing checkpoints (inference-only) can refute the floor's existence before any training.

one_line: The classification-regression loss weight sets an operating point on a Pareto surface: the AP50-optimal weight measurably differs from the AP75-optimal weight.
problem: Detection recipes fix one cls-reg loss weighting tuned on aggregate AP, hiding a tradeoff that different applications would resolve differently.
core_hypothesis: Classification and localization capacity compete through the shared backbone; sweeping the loss weight traces a smooth Pareto front between recognition-heavy (AP50) and localization-heavy (AP75/AP90) performance, with distinct optima, so single-weight training is provably suboptimal for at least one of the two metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: A weight sweep will show the argmax weights for AP50 and AP75 separated beyond seed noise, with a monotone trade region between them, consistent across two architectures.
why_important: Applications differ (search wants recall/recognition; robotics wants tight boxes); making the tradeoff explicit lets practitioners choose deliberately and motivates weight-conditioned training.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: loss-weight ablations exist in passing; a systematic Pareto characterization with metric-specific optima as the object of study appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep the cls-reg weight over ~6 values x 2 seeds on a mid-size dataset for two detector families; plot AP50 and AP75 versus weight and test optimum separation against seed variance.
main_risk: The front may be so flat that optima are statistically indistinguishable, making the claim true but practically vacuous.
community_default_belief: There is one 'correct' loss balance per architecture, found by tuning overall mAP, and metric-specific tuning is overfitting to metrics.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Aggregate mAP averages over IoU thresholds precisely to hide this tradeoff; capacity competition makes a genuine front likely rather than a single optimum.
fastest_falsification: A coarse 4-point weight sweep on a small dataset already reveals whether AP50/AP75 curves peak apart.

one_line: Box-edge difficulty is direction-dependent and stable across architectures: ground-contact edges are systematically easier to localize.
problem: Localization error is reported as a scalar (IoU), hiding structured, physically-caused error patterns that could be corrected or exploited.
core_hypothesis: For ground-standing object classes, the bottom edge benefits from a strong ground-plane prior and exhibits systematically lower error than the top edge (which borders variable background); this per-edge asymmetry is a stable property of the data/scene geometry, reproducing across architectures and datasets with ground-standing objects.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-edge error decomposition on multiple public checkpoints will show bottom-edge error significantly below top-edge error for ground-contact classes, with the asymmetry absent for airborne/floating classes; the pattern will replicate across at least three architectures.
why_important: Edge-structured error models improve downstream geometric uses of boxes (height estimation, distance) and motivate edge-weighted losses.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: per-edge error analyses conditioned on physical support relations appear absent from detection literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decompose signed and absolute per-edge errors on validation sets for several checkpoints; group classes by ground-contact status; test the asymmetry and its cross-architecture stability.
main_risk: Annotation conventions (feet vs shadows, occlusion by ground clutter) might drive the asymmetry rather than model priors, though this would itself be a finding.
community_default_belief: Localization error is roughly isotropic per box, so scalar IoU adequately summarizes it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scenes have strong anisotropic structure (gravity, ground plane, camera pose priors), and learned models absorb such structure into direction-dependent accuracy.
fastest_falsification: Entirely inference-plus-analysis on existing checkpoints; a few GPU-hours.

one_line: Regression-gradient conflict at features shared by overlapping objects explains a fixed share of crowded-scene localization error, removable by masked per-instance pooling.
problem: Boxes in crowded scenes are less precise, usually attributed to appearance confusion rather than optimization interference at shared features.
core_hypothesis: When two GT boxes overlap, the shared feature locations receive conflicting regression targets during training, which biases both boxes toward each other; routing regression through instance-masked feature pooling (excluding the overlap region) removes this component, quantifying how much crowded-scene box error is optimization interference versus perceptual difficulty.
falsifiable_prediction: Pairs of overlapping GT boxes will show mutually attracted predictions (signed error pointing toward the neighbor) proportional to overlap; masked-pooling training will reduce this attraction term substantially while leaving isolated-object accuracy unchanged.
why_important: Separates fixable optimization pathology from genuine perceptual limits in crowd localization, guiding architecture and loss design.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: crowd-specific losses exist (repulsion-style ideas), but a gradient-interference quantification with a masking-based causal test appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure neighbor-directed signed error versus pair overlap on an existing checkpoint; train a small model with overlap-masked regression pooling; compare the attraction statistic.
main_risk: Masking may discard genuinely useful context pixels, confounding the interference measurement with information removal.
community_default_belief: Crowded-scene localization error reflects ambiguous appearance evidence, addressed by better features or crowd-specific losses.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Even with perfect features, conflicting targets at shared coordinates provably bias converged regressors; the pathology is in supervision routing, not perception.
fastest_falsification: The attraction-statistic measurement is inference-only; absence of neighbor-directed bias kills the hypothesis immediately.

one_line: Predicted-variance regression heads help mainly through training-time loss attenuation on noisy labels; the variance output is redundant at inference.
problem: Probabilistic box regression (predicting a variance per coordinate) improves AP, but whether the benefit is a training effect or an inference effect is unresolved.
core_hypothesis: The AP gain of variance-predicting regression comes almost entirely from down-weighting the loss on high-noise annotations during training (self-paced attenuation); discarding the variance head at inference and using standard decoding loses almost none of the gain, and the predicted variances correlate more with annotation noise proxies than with actual model error.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating variance-based inference (keeping training identical) will retain the vast majority of the AP gain; predicted variance will correlate more strongly with annotation-ambiguity proxies (occlusion, boundary contrast) than with realized model residuals on clean re-annotated boxes.
why_important: Clarifies that the community is buying a label-noise handling mechanism, not calibrated uncertainty, preventing misuse of the variance output in safety pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: variance heads are popular; the train-vs-inference decomposition combined with the annotation-noise correlation test appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with a variance head; evaluate with and without variance-aware inference; correlate predicted variances against (a) re-annotation disagreement on an audit subset and (b) model residuals.
main_risk: Some architectures may integrate variance into NMS/score fusion in ways that make inference ablation non-trivial to isolate.
community_default_belief: Predicted box variance is an uncertainty estimate whose value lies in better inference-time fusion and downstream use.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Attenuation-style losses are known in other fields to act primarily as robust-loss reweighting; nothing forces the learned variance to track model error rather than label noise.
fastest_falsification: Inference-mode ablation on an existing variance-head checkpoint is immediate; the correlation audit needs only a small re-annotation set.

one_line: Below a predictable size threshold, plain pixel-space L1 beats IoU-family losses for tiny-object regression.
problem: One regression loss is used for all object sizes, though the geometry of IoU degenerates for tiny boxes where one-pixel errors produce huge IoU swings.
core_hypothesis: For boxes below a size threshold set by annotation noise (a few pixels of label jitter), IoU-based losses present a noise-dominated, high-curvature objective that harms optimization, while absolute-pixel L1 remains well-conditioned; a size-switched loss (L1 below threshold, IoU above) outperforms either alone, and the optimal switch point tracks the measured annotation noise scale.
falsifiable_prediction: Size-stratified AP will show L1 superior to IoU-family losses for the smallest size band and inferior for large bands; the crossover size will shift when training on data with artificially increased label jitter, in the direction predicted.
why_important: Tiny-object detection (aerial, medical, surveillance) is a persistent weak spot; a principled loss switch is free to deploy.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: losses are compared globally in the literature; the size-conditional crossover and its predicted dependence on annotation noise appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with L1, IoU-family, and size-switched losses on a dataset rich in small objects; add a jittered-label variant to test crossover shift; compare size-stratified AP.
main_risk: Normalization details (how L1 targets are scaled) could dominate the comparison and need careful matching.
community_default_belief: IoU-aligned losses dominate L1 across the board because they optimize the evaluation metric directly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Metric alignment is worthless when the metric itself is noise-dominated at small scales; loss conditioning then matters more than alignment.
fastest_falsification: A two-loss comparison restricted to a small-object-heavy subset gives a fast directional answer with modest compute.

one_line: Cascade refinement stages mostly correct one systematic scale-dependent bias each; a closed-form per-scale affine correction recovers much of the cascade gain for free.
problem: Cascade/iterative box refinement adds substantial compute, and it is unknown how much of its gain is instance-specific correction versus removal of simple systematic biases.
core_hypothesis: The first-order effect of each refinement stage is to undo a systematic, scale-conditioned affine bias (shrinkage/expansion and center drift) left by the previous stage; fitting that affine correction per size band from validation statistics and applying it post hoc recovers a large fraction of cascade AP gains at zero inference cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Stage-wise output differences of a cascade model will be dominated (in variance-explained terms) by a per-size-band affine map; applying the fitted map to a single-stage detector's outputs will close a large share of the single-vs-cascade AP75 gap.
why_important: If most of the cascade is a bias correction, cheap post-hoc calibration replaces heavy heads in latency-constrained deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: cascade gains are reported holistically; a variance decomposition into systematic-affine versus instance-specific correction appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a cascade checkpoint, regress stage-k outputs on stage-(k-1) outputs per size band; measure variance explained by affine terms; apply fitted affine correction to a single-stage checkpoint and evaluate.
main_risk: The affine story may hold on average but fail on the hard instances that actually drive AP differences at high IoU thresholds.
community_default_belief: Cascade refinement performs instance-adaptive correction requiring learned, feature-conditioned stages.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training-stage IoU-threshold escalation mainly re-centers the target distribution per stage, which is exactly the signature of a distributional (systematic) rather than instance-specific fix.
fastest_falsification: The variance-decomposition on an existing cascade checkpoint is inference-only and immediately diagnostic.

one_line: Extreme-aspect-ratio failure is loss-induced, not representation-induced: features linearly encode the long-axis extent that IoU-loss training fails to extract.
problem: Detectors localize highly elongated objects poorly, and the community cannot tell whether features or objectives are at fault.
core_hypothesis: Backbone/neck features already contain linearly decodable information about elongated objects' long-axis extent, but IoU-family losses provide vanishing gradient along the long axis (IoU is insensitive to long-axis errors relative to short-axis errors), so the head never extracts it; a frozen-feature linear probe will localize the long axis much better than the trained head does.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear probe on frozen features will beat the model's own head at long-axis extent estimation for the top eccentricity decile, while matching it on square objects; retraining the head with an axis-decoupled loss will close most of the head-vs-probe gap.
why_important: Locates the bottleneck precisely, redirecting effort from bigger backbones to loss geometry for elongated-object domains.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: probing is standard in representation analysis but appears unapplied to the loss-vs-feature attribution question for box regression.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze a trained detector's features; fit a linear probe for box extents; compare probe-vs-head error stratified by eccentricity; retrain head only with axis-decoupled loss and re-compare.
main_risk: Probes fit on GT-centered features can cheat via sampling alignment; probe protocol must match the head's actual feature access.
community_default_belief: Elongated-object failure reflects receptive-field and feature limitations, to be fixed with deformable or strip-shaped operators.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the information is probe-recoverable from existing features, operators are not the bottleneck; the gradient geometry of the objective is.
fastest_falsification: Probe fitting on frozen features is cheap (no backbone training); a probe that fails like the head falsifies the claim quickly.

one_line: Tiny-object AP is near the label-noise ceiling: model-vs-annotator disagreement approaches annotator-vs-annotator disagreement below a size threshold.
problem: Small-object AP gaps drive large modeling investments, without knowing how much headroom actually exists above annotation noise.
core_hypothesis: For objects below a certain pixel size, inter-annotator box agreement degrades so much that current detectors already match the human-consistency ceiling; the remaining reported AP gap for tiny objects is largely unwinnable under the existing labels, and per-size headroom can be computed as the gap between model-annotator and annotator-annotator agreement curves.
falsifiable_prediction: On a multi-annotator audit set, the model-annotator IoU distribution for the smallest size band will be statistically indistinguishable from the annotator-annotator distribution, while a clear gap will remain for medium sizes.
why_important: Redirects small-object research toward label-quality and evaluation reform where modeling is already saturated, saving misplaced effort.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: annotation-noise studies exist for detection broadly, but a size-resolved headroom analysis benchmarked against current detectors appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 3-5 independent re-annotations for a stratified sample of small and medium objects; compare agreement distributions (annotator-annotator vs model-annotator) per size band for a strong public checkpoint.
main_risk: Annotator instructions strongly affect agreement; a poorly specified audit protocol could manufacture or hide the ceiling.
community_default_belief: Small-object AP gaps indicate model deficiencies (resolution, features) with substantial headroom for architectural innovation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: AP conflates label noise with model error; at tiny scales a few pixels of annotator jitter destroys IoU-based agreement regardless of model quality.
fastest_falsification: A modest re-annotation audit (hundreds of boxes) plus inference on one checkpoint suffices for the core comparison.

one_line: Small-object detection scores oscillate with sub-stride translation due to aliasing, and anti-aliased downsampling flattens the oscillation.
problem: Small-object detection is unreliable in ways that appear random, but may be a deterministic function of where the object lands relative to the downsampling grid.
core_hypothesis: Strided downsampling aliases high-frequency content that small objects depend on, making detection confidence a periodic function of sub-stride image translation; the oscillation amplitude quantifies aliasing damage, is largest for objects near the stride scale, and is substantially reduced by anti-aliased (low-pass-filtered) downsampling at matched accuracy elsewhere.
falsifiable_prediction: Translating an image in sub-pixel steps will produce near-periodic score oscillations for small objects with amplitude inversely related to object-size/stride ratio; an anti-aliased variant of the same architecture will show significantly lower amplitude and higher small-object AP.
why_important: A deterministic, physics-style account of small-object flakiness that yields both a diagnostic (oscillation amplitude) and a fix direction.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: shift-invariance work exists for classification; a quantitative oscillation analysis tied to object size and stride in detection appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sub-pixel-translate validation images (via high-quality resampling); record per-object score traces for an existing checkpoint; train or obtain an anti-aliased variant and compare amplitudes and small-object AP.
main_risk: Resampling itself introduces blur that disproportionately affects small objects, confounding the translation probe.
community_default_belief: Small-object weakness is a resolution/semantic-capacity problem; shift-variance is a negligible second-order effect.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For objects spanning a handful of pixels, grid phase determines what fraction of their energy survives downsampling, which is first-order, not cosmetic.
fastest_falsification: The translation probe on a public checkpoint is inference-only; absence of size-dependent oscillation falsifies immediately.

one_line: Top-down FPN fusion oversmooths the finest pyramid level, measurably erasing high-frequency discriminability that small objects need.
problem: Feature pyramids are assumed to strictly help all scales, but the top-down pathway adds semantically strong yet spatially smooth content to fine levels, with unquantified costs.
core_hypothesis: After top-down fusion, the finest-level features lose high-spatial-frequency discriminative information present before fusion (measurable by frequency-band-restricted linear probes for small-object presence); gating the fusion by frequency (letting high-frequency content bypass the smoothing) recovers small-object AP without hurting large objects.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes for small-object presence trained on pre-fusion versus post-fusion fine-level features will show higher accuracy pre-fusion in high-frequency bands; a frequency-gated fusion variant will improve small-object AP with unchanged large-object AP.
why_important: Challenges the default 'fusion always helps' assumption and offers a targeted fix for the most stubborn AP category.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: many FPN variants exist, but a frequency-domain information audit of what top-down fusion destroys appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract pre-/post-fusion features from a trained detector; band-pass them; train small-object presence probes per band; then train a frequency-gated fusion model and compare size-stratified AP.
main_risk: Probe accuracy differences may reflect feature-norm or dimensionality artifacts rather than genuine information loss.
community_default_belief: Top-down semantic enrichment strictly benefits fine levels; small-object gains from FPN prove the fusion is helping them.
why_that_may_be_wrong: FPN gains are measured against no-fusion baselines confounded by optimization; fusion can simultaneously add semantics and destroy the fine spatial evidence small objects uniquely depend on.
fastest_falsification: The probe audit needs only forward passes and small probe fits on an existing checkpoint.

one_line: Small objects are recognized mostly from context while large objects are recognized from appearance, and interior-vs-context masking reverses between the two regimes.
problem: The evidence detectors use is assumed uniform across scales, so interventions (augmentation, architecture) are not scale-targeted.
core_hypothesis: Below a size threshold, detection decisions rely mainly on surrounding context (object pixels contribute less than their surround); masking the object interior hurts small-object detection less than masking an equal-area context ring, with the effect reversing for large objects, and the crossover size is a stable architecture property.
falsifiable_prediction: Paired masking interventions will show a context-dominance ratio greater than one for small objects and less than one for large objects, with a measurable crossover size that shifts when training removes context correlations (cut-paste training).
why_important: Scale-conditional evidence use dictates which robustness interventions work at which scales and explains why small-object detection collapses under domain shift when context changes.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: context reliance in detection is studied in aggregate; a size-resolved crossover law with an architectural constant appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For an existing checkpoint, run interior-masking vs context-ring-masking interventions across size bins; compute the dominance ratio curve; repeat for a cut-paste-trained model.
main_risk: Masking artifacts (sharp edges) may themselves trigger or suppress detections, requiring careful blended masking controls.
community_default_belief: Detectors primarily recognize objects from their own appearance at all scales; context is a secondary modulator.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A few dozen pixels often cannot support recognition alone; models plausibly learn that surround statistics are the more reliable evidence channel at small scales.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only masking study on one checkpoint across size bins; a flat dominance ratio falsifies the crossover claim.

one_line: Per-class test-time resolution selection beats any single global resolution because class-wise resolution-AP curves peak at different points.
problem: Deployment picks one inference resolution per model, though classes differ hugely in typical pixel size and texture scale.
core_hypothesis: Class-conditional resolution-AP curves have materially different optima (driven by each class's size distribution and texture frequency); running inference at 2-3 resolutions and reading each class's detections from its best resolution yields an aggregate AP above the best single resolution, and the per-class optima are predictable from class size statistics alone.
falsifiable_prediction: For an existing checkpoint, per-class AP-vs-resolution curves will show optima spread across the tested range, and the oracle-free selection rule (choose resolution by class median object size) will beat the best fixed resolution on held-out data.
why_important: A deployment-level AP gain requiring no retraining, plus a clean characterization of scale sensitivity as a per-class property.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: multi-scale testing is standard as ensembling; per-class resolution routing from size statistics as a principled, predictable rule appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one checkpoint at several resolutions; build per-class curves; apply the size-statistic selection rule on a disjoint split; compare to best fixed resolution and full multi-scale ensembling (for cost reference).
main_risk: Per-class curve estimates are noisy for rare classes, and cross-resolution score calibration differences may confound class-wise reading.
community_default_belief: One well-chosen resolution (or expensive full multi-scale TTA) is the right operating procedure; class-wise routing is over-engineering.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Class size distributions differ by an order of magnitude; a single resolution provably sits far from many class optima if the curves are peaked.
fastest_falsification: Multi-resolution inference on validation data with per-class bookkeeping; entirely inference-time.

consolidation.mutation_note: Keep the falsifiable claim that class-conditional resolution-AP optima diverge and are predictable from class size statistics; drop the per-class selection system as the contribution - multi-scale/selective inference is well-trodden engineering.

one_line: Scale augmentation works by renormalizing objects into a fixed preferred absolute-pixel band, not by teaching scale invariance.
problem: Scale jitter is universally used with an invariance rationale that has never been separated from a competing renormalization account.
core_hypothesis: Detectors have an architecture-determined preferred absolute object-size band (in pixels at the input); scale augmentation helps mainly because it moves more training (and effectively test) objects through that band, not because the model becomes scale-invariant; consequently per-scale AP measured in absolute pixels retains a fixed peak whose location is unchanged by augmentation strength while its width grows only modestly.
falsifiable_prediction: Across augmentation strengths, absolute-pixel-scale AP curves will share a stable peak location (set by architecture, e.g., stride configuration) rather than flattening into scale invariance; test-time rescaling into the band will recover most of the augmentation benefit for weakly augmented models.
why_important: Reframes multi-scale training as distribution matching, predicting when augmentation is wasteful and when test-time rescaling suffices.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: scale-invariance rhetoric is common; an explicit peak-location-stability test across augmentation strengths appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models at several scale-jitter strengths; plot AP versus absolute object pixel size for each; test peak-location stability; run test-time rescaling for the weakest model.
main_risk: Peak location may drift with augmentation via BN statistics or receptive-field adaptation, giving partial support to both accounts.
community_default_belief: Scale augmentation induces approximate scale invariance in the learned representation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Strided architectures are inherently scale-anisotropic; augmentation cannot remove architectural preference, only reshuffle which objects fall inside it.
fastest_falsification: Absolute-pixel-scale AP curves for two existing checkpoints trained with different augmentation (if available) provide an immediate first test without new training.

one_line: Tiling-based small-object gains come substantially from activation-statistics changes, not just effective resolution; matched-statistics full-image inference closes much of the gap.
problem: Tiled/cropped inference is credited entirely to resolution, but tiles also change global activation statistics (normalization context, attention distributions), an unmeasured confound.
core_hypothesis: Part of tiling's small-object improvement arises because tiles present object-denser, background-simpler statistics to normalization layers and global operators; reproducing those statistics on full images (e.g., normalization recalibrated to tile statistics, attention temperature adjusted) recovers a meaningful fraction of tiling's gain without the resolution change or the border-artifact costs.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing the tile-vs-full gap will show a statistics component: full-image inference with tile-matched normalization statistics will close a nontrivial fraction of the gap, and tiling with full-image-matched statistics will lose the same fraction.
why_important: Correctly attributing tiling's gains changes deployment math (tiling is latency-expensive) and reveals statistic-sensitivity as a hidden failure factor for full scenes.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: tiling is treated as a resolution trick; the normalization/attention-statistics pathway appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a checkpoint using normalization layers with input-dependent statistics or global attention, evaluate the 2x2 factorial (tile/full x tile-stats/full-stats) on a small-object dataset and decompose the AP differences.
main_risk: For pure frozen-statistics models (e.g., fully BN-frozen), the statistics pathway may be limited to attention effects and be small.
community_default_belief: Tiling helps purely by increasing pixels-per-object; statistics are irrelevant plumbing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Global operators mix scene-level information into every local decision, so scene composition changes local computations even at fixed pixels-per-object.
fastest_falsification: The factorial evaluation is inference-only with modest engineering to swap statistics sources.

one_line: Small-object skill peaks earlier in training and is forgotten first under continued or fine-tuning updates: a scale-dependent forgetting curve.
problem: Checkpoint selection and fine-tuning schedules ignore that different object scales may have different learning and forgetting dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Small-object accuracy behaves like a fragile, high-frequency skill: it reaches its optimum earlier than large-object accuracy during training, and degrades first when training continues (overfit) or when fine-tuning on a shifted distribution; therefore single-checkpoint selection systematically sacrifices small-object AP, and scale-wise checkpoint blending strictly dominates.
falsifiable_prediction: Size-stratified validation curves will show the small-object AP peak preceding the overall AP peak consistently across runs; merging the small-object-optimal and overall-optimal checkpoints (weight or prediction blending) will beat the best single checkpoint on aggregate AP.
why_important: Free AP from existing training runs and a dynamics-level account of why small objects suffer under transfer and long schedules.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: forgetting curves are studied per class or per task, but per-scale learning/forgetting asymmetry in detection appears uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log size-stratified AP per epoch across several runs and one fine-tuning scenario; test peak-ordering consistency; evaluate scale-wise checkpoint blending against best single checkpoints.
main_risk: Peak ordering may be schedule-dependent (LR drops re-synchronize peaks), weakening generality.
community_default_belief: A single best checkpoint (by overall validation AP) is near-optimal for all object scales; scale-specific dynamics are noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Small-object fits depend on high-frequency features known to be learned late-but-overfit-fast in other settings; there is no reason scale-wise optima should coincide.
fastest_falsification: Re-evaluating already-saved checkpoints from any past run with size-stratified AP answers the peak-ordering question without new training.

one_line: Learned features preserve sub-stride localization information for small objects that standard decoding discards: a readout can beat the stride bound.
problem: It is assumed that once features are downsampled, small-object localization precision is bounded by the feature stride, motivating expensive high-resolution pathways.
core_hypothesis: Distributed activation patterns across neighboring feature cells retain sub-stride positional information (analogous to population coding); a lightweight multi-cell readout trained on frozen stride-8/16 features can localize small objects with error well below the naive stride bound, showing the bottleneck is the decoding head, not the encoded information.
