falsifiable_prediction: A frozen-feature multi-cell readout will achieve small-object center-localization error substantially below half the stride, and below the trained detector head's own error, without any backbone changes.
why_important: If decoding is the bottleneck, cheap head redesigns can replace costly high-resolution feature pyramids for precision-critical small-object tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: sub-pixel decoding exists in keypoint/stereo contexts; a frozen-feature information audit against the stride bound for small-object detection appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze a trained detector backbone; train a small readout (a few layers over 3x3 cell neighborhoods) for center regression of small objects; compare error to stride/2 and to the original head.
main_risk: The readout may exploit dataset-specific context regularities rather than genuine sub-stride evidence; needs shuffled-context controls.
community_default_belief: Localization precision is fundamentally limited by feature-map resolution; higher-resolution features are the only route to precise small-object boxes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Convolutional features are phase-sensitive before pooling, so ensembles of neighboring cells can encode position continuously, like sub-pixel estimation in classical vision.
fastest_falsification: Readout training on frozen features is a small experiment (no detector training); failure to beat the stride bound falsifies directly.

one_line: Detection scores are a range-dependent mixture of three latent factors, and the mixture map predicts where each calibration method works.
problem: Calibration methods for detectors succeed inconsistently because the semantic content of the score is treated as homogeneous across its range.
core_hypothesis: A detection score mixes classification correctness, localization quality, and duplicate-rank information, with mixture weights that vary systematically across score ranges (e.g., top scores dominated by duplicate rank, mid scores by classification); estimating the range-dependent mixture explains and predicts which score ranges each calibration method (temperature, isotonic, IoU-aware rescoring) can and cannot fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing correctness/IoU/duplicate-rank indicators on score per range will reveal significantly non-constant mixture weights; the residual calibration error of each method per range will be predictable from the mixture component it cannot model.
why_important: Turns detector calibration from trial-and-error into a diagnosable problem with per-range method selection.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: detection calibration papers treat score as one signal; a range-resolved semantic decomposition with predictive use appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For existing checkpoints, gather per-detection tuples (score, class-correct, IoU, duplicate rank); fit range-local mixture regressions; apply three calibration methods and test whether per-range residuals match mixture-based predictions.
main_risk: The three factors are correlated, so mixture estimates may be unstable without careful orthogonalization.
community_default_belief: Detector miscalibration is a monolithic property fixable by one good post-hoc method or an IoU-aware head.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scores are produced by heterogeneous mechanisms (softmax, quality weighting, suppression survival), so no single-view calibration can be uniformly correct across ranges.
fastest_falsification: Pure post-processing of existing predictions; the non-constant-mixture test is immediate.

one_line: Per-class calibration error in detectors follows a class-frequency scaling law, so a single frequency-parameterized correction nearly matches per-class tuning.
problem: Per-class calibration for large vocabularies is data-starved for rare classes, and global calibration ignores class differences.
core_hypothesis: The dominant driver of per-class miscalibration is training-set class frequency (through imbalance in positive gradients and background competition); calibration error versus log-frequency follows a smooth monotone law, so a two-parameter frequency-conditioned temperature achieves calibration close to per-class tuning while needing no rare-class validation data.
falsifiable_prediction: Across classes, calibration error will correlate strongly with log training frequency after controlling for size and occlusion; the frequency-parameterized temperature will close most of the gap between global and oracle per-class calibration, including on classes held out from calibration fitting.
why_important: Enables trustworthy scores for rare classes precisely where per-class calibration data cannot exist, critical for long-tail deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: long-tail score adjustment exists for accuracy (logit adjustment), but a calibration-error scaling law and its use as a two-parameter calibrator for detection appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class calibration curves on a long-tail detection validation set; fit the frequency law on half the classes; evaluate calibration on the held-out classes against global and per-class baselines.
main_risk: Rare-class calibration estimates are themselves noisy, potentially masking or inflating the law.
community_default_belief: Per-class calibration requires per-class data; rare classes are simply left miscalibrated or lumped into a global correction.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If miscalibration is caused by a shared mechanism modulated by frequency, the correction is a function of frequency, not of class identity, and generalizes to unseen classes.
fastest_falsification: The correlation and held-out-class test are post-processing on existing predictions from a long-tail checkpoint.

one_line: Cross-domain score-threshold failure is driven by background shift, and label-free recalibration on background-only patches restores threshold validity.
problem: Deployed detectors need re-tuned score thresholds per domain, which requires labeled target-domain data that rarely exists.
core_hypothesis: The score distribution shift that invalidates thresholds across domains originates mostly from changed background statistics (new negatives) rather than changed object appearance; therefore recalibrating the score scale using only target-domain background regions (obtainable without object labels, e.g., from detector-quiet regions or known object-free footage) restores most threshold transferability.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing score shift into FP-score-distribution shift and TP-score-distribution shift will show the FP component dominating threshold miscalibration; background-only recalibration will recover most of the precision-recall operating point without any target labels.
why_important: A label-free domain-adaptation step for the single most common deployment knob (the score threshold) has immediate practical value.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: unsupervised calibration under shift is studied for classifiers; the background-dominance claim and background-only fix for detection thresholds appear specific and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a detector and two domains with labels (for evaluation only); measure TP/FP score-shift components; recalibrate using only object-free target patches; compare restored operating points to full supervised recalibration.
main_risk: Selecting truly object-free target patches without labels may be circular (relies on the miscalibrated detector).
community_default_belief: Domain shift changes everything at once; restoring detector operating points requires labeled target data or full adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Foreground objects are often the most domain-stable content (same physical objects), while backgrounds change wholesale; the miscalibration may live almost entirely in the negatives.
fastest_falsification: The TP/FP shift decomposition on any existing cross-domain evaluation pair is pure analysis of predictions.

one_line: Out-of-distribution false positives have systematically unstable box geometry under input jitter, enabling training-free OOD rejection.
problem: Detectors emit confident false positives on unfamiliar objects, and existing OOD scores rely on classification logits that are precisely what is miscalibrated.
core_hypothesis: For in-distribution objects, the regression head has learned a stable attractor (box estimates are consistent under small input perturbations), whereas confident OOD false positives sit off the learned manifold and their boxes wander under jitter; box-consistency-under-jitter therefore separates OOD FPs from true detections better than any function of the classification logits alone.
falsifiable_prediction: On an evaluation with known OOD objects, AUROC of a jitter-based box-instability score for flagging OOD FPs will exceed that of max-logit/energy-style scores computed from the same detector, across two architectures.
why_important: OOD-robust detection matters for open-world deployment; a signal orthogonal to logits and free of extra training broadens the toolkit.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: perturbation-consistency is used for classifier uncertainty; using regression-branch geometric stability specifically as the OOD channel for detection appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct an OOD evaluation by pasting unseen-category objects into in-domain scenes; compute jitter-instability and logit-based scores per detection; compare AUROC for OOD-FP identification.
main_risk: Small in-distribution objects also show jittery boxes, potentially confounding instability with size.
community_default_belief: OOD detection signals live in the classifier (logits, energies, densities); the box head carries no OOD information.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The regression branch is trained only on in-distribution geometry, making it an implicit density model whose breakdown is informative exactly where the classifier is overconfident.
fastest_falsification: Paste-based OOD evaluation plus jittered inference on an existing checkpoint; no training.

one_line: Box-level and image-level calibration diverge systematically: a detector can be well calibrated per box yet badly calibrated for 'any object present' image queries.
problem: Many applications consume image-level decisions (is any target present?) derived from box scores, but calibration is only ever measured and fixed at box level.
core_hypothesis: Aggregating box scores into image-level probabilities (e.g., via max or noisy-or) inherits correlations between per-box errors within an image, so box-level calibration does not imply image-level calibration; the divergence grows with per-image detection count and error correlation, and direct image-level recalibration beats aggregating box-calibrated scores.
falsifiable_prediction: Detectors calibrated to low box-level error will still show large image-level calibration error for presence queries, increasing with scene density; a simple image-level recalibrator on top of aggregated scores will outperform box-level calibration followed by aggregation.
why_important: Screening applications (medical, security, content moderation) operate at image level; miscalibration there is the operationally relevant kind.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: detection-calibration work focuses on per-box confidence; the aggregation-induced miscalibration mechanism and its density dependence appear unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate a detector at box level; form image-level presence probabilities by standard aggregation; measure image-level calibration stratified by object count; fit and evaluate a direct image-level recalibrator.
main_risk: The result may depend heavily on the chosen aggregation rule, requiring several aggregators to make the claim robust.
community_default_belief: Once box scores are calibrated, any downstream probabilistic use is automatically sound.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Independence assumptions in aggregation are violated by shared-feature errors; correlated box errors provably distort aggregated probabilities even under perfect marginal calibration.
fastest_falsification: All measurements are post-processing over existing validation predictions.

one_line: Detection score rankings are far more seed-stable than score values, so rank-based thresholds transfer better than calibrated-score thresholds.
problem: Operating thresholds tuned on one training run are silently invalidated by retraining, forcing re-tuning with every model refresh.
core_hypothesis: Across random seeds (and minor recipe changes), the induced ranking of detections is substantially more stable than the score values themselves; consequently thresholds expressed as per-image or per-dataset rank/quantile statistics transfer across retrains with less operating-point drift than value thresholds, even after post-hoc calibration of the values.
falsifiable_prediction: Between seed pairs, rank correlation of detection orderings will exceed value agreement by a large margin; quantile-based thresholds will show significantly lower precision/recall drift across seeds than calibrated value thresholds at matched operating points.
why_important: Reduces MLOps churn for every team that retrains detectors regularly, and reframes what part of the score is trustworthy.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: seed variance of AP is documented; the rank-vs-value stability decomposition and its thresholding consequence appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train several seeds of one detector; compare cross-seed rank correlations vs value correlations; simulate deployment by fixing value/quantile thresholds from seed A and measuring operating-point drift on seeds B and C.
main_risk: Quantile thresholds depend on the test-time score distribution, which shifts with content mix, potentially reintroducing drift from another door.
community_default_belief: Calibrated score values are the transferable currency; thresholds should be set on calibrated probabilities.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Calibration maps are themselves seed-dependent, while ranking is determined by relative evidence that may be far more robust to optimization noise.
fastest_falsification: If multiple seeds of any public detector exist, the rank-vs-value comparison is pure inference and analysis.

one_line: Focal loss's calibration damage is temporally separable from its accuracy benefit: a brief final cross-entropy phase restores calibration at no AP cost.
problem: Focal-style losses improve dense-detector accuracy but are known to distort confidence; practitioners accept the tradeoff as inherent.
core_hypothesis: The accuracy benefit of focusing (hard-example emphasis) is realized in representation and localization quality accumulated over training, while the calibration distortion lives in the final classifier layer's output scaling; switching to plain cross-entropy (or reduced focusing) only for the final small fraction of training re-anchors output probabilities without unwinding the learned representations, keeping AP while removing most calibration error.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained focal-then-CE-finish will match focal-only AP within noise while substantially improving calibration error, outperforming post-hoc temperature scaling of the focal-only model especially under distribution shift.
why_important: A free recipe change delivering calibrated dense detectors, removing a standard excuse for uncalibrated deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: loss-schedule fine-tuning exists in other contexts; the specific claim that focal's calibration damage is late-layer and reversible without AP loss appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train baseline focal, focal-then-CE (sweep switch point over 2-3 values), and CE-only models; compare AP and calibration in-domain and under a corruption shift; include temperature-scaled focal baseline.
main_risk: Switching losses may destabilize the score distribution that assignment/NMS thresholds were tuned for, requiring careful re-tuning to make comparisons fair.
community_default_belief: Focal loss's miscalibration is intrinsic to its objective and must be corrected post hoc if at all.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Miscalibration from loss shaping is largely a monotone output distortion; if representations are loss-agnostic late in training, the distortion can be untrained rather than merely patched.
fastest_falsification: One focal-then-CE run against an existing focal baseline on a small dataset gives a quick directional readout.

consolidation.mutation_note: The representation/final-layer separability hypothesis must beat the trivial null: temperature scaling already re-anchors output scaling post hoc (the shard's own protocol includes it). Mutate: surviving claim is advantage over post-hoc recalibration under shift; otherwise dominated.

one_line: IoU-prediction heads mostly re-encode class and size priors; their instance-specific quality signal is small and measurable by a prior-only baseline.
problem: Localization-quality estimation heads are trusted as instance-level quality sensors for downstream fusion, but their information content has never been decomposed.
core_hypothesis: Most of the variance in predicted IoU is explained by class identity and box size (which correlate with typical achievable IoU), not by instance-specific evidence; a baseline predicting quality from (class, size, image-level difficulty) alone will match the head's correlation with true IoU closely, revealing a small residual instance signal.
falsifiable_prediction: The prior-only baseline will achieve a large fraction of the quality head's predictive correlation with realized IoU; the head's advantage will concentrate in a small subset of atypical instances (occlusion, truncation).
why_important: If quality heads are mostly priors, downstream systems can get equivalent signals for free, and research should target the atypical-instance residual specifically.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: quality-estimation heads are widely used; an information decomposition against explicit prior baselines appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For an existing checkpoint with a quality head, fit the prior-only predictor on validation data; compare correlation with realized IoU overall and on atypical-instance strata.
main_risk: The decomposition depends on the richness of the prior feature set; too-rich priors trivially win, too-poor unfairly lose - needs principled feature selection.
community_default_belief: Quality heads perceive instance-specific localization reliability from features and are essential for score-quality fusion gains.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The training signal for quality heads is dominated by easy-to-predict systematic variation (class/size), so gradient pressure to learn hard instance-specific cues is weak.
fastest_falsification: Fitting the prior baseline is a small regression on existing predictions; no training of detectors required.

one_line: False negatives are more predictable than false positives from internal features, enabling a practical 'missed something here' flag.
problem: Detection failure handling focuses on filtering FPs; missed detections are invisible at inference time and considered inherently unpredictable.
core_hypothesis: Images and regions where a detector misses objects have identifiable internal signatures (elevated objectness without box commitment, feature-space proximity to positives, high spatial entropy of low-level saliency vs low detection density); a lightweight predictor on frozen intermediate features flags FN-containing regions with usefully high precision, and FN-predictability exceeds FP-predictability under matched effort.
falsifiable_prediction: A small probe trained on frozen features to predict 'this region contains an unmissed GT' will transfer to held-out data with AUROC meaningfully above chance and above an equivalent FP-region probe, across two datasets.
why_important: An FN flag enables targeted human review and active sensing (zoom, re-scan), addressing the failure mode that filtering can never fix.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: uncertainty literature targets emitted detections; region-level miss prediction from internal features as a first-class task appears rarely if ever formalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using validation data with GT, label regions by FN presence; train probes on frozen detector features for FN and FP region prediction; compare AUROC and precision-at-low-budget on held-out data.
main_risk: FN probes may just learn 'small/occluded objects live here' priors that fail to transfer beyond the training distribution.
community_default_belief: What a detector misses leaves no usable trace; recall improvements must come from better detection itself.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Misses are usually near-threshold events, and near-threshold internal activity is exactly the kind of trace a probe can read even when the pipeline's final outputs are silent.
fastest_falsification: Probe training on frozen features is cheap; failure to beat chance on held-out data falsifies quickly.

one_line: Score-distribution degradation under diverse corruptions collapses onto a single 'effective dose' scalar per model, enabling corruption-agnostic monitoring.
problem: Robustness is characterized per corruption type and severity, producing large matrices that do not transfer to real mixed degradations.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed detector, the changes in its detection-score distribution under many different corruption types lie on a one-dimensional family: each (type, severity) maps to a scalar effective dose, and score-distribution statistics identify the dose regardless of corruption type; consequently, a monitor calibrated on a few synthetic corruptions predicts AP degradation for unseen corruption types from the score distribution alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Embedding corrupted-validation score distributions (e.g., via a few quantile features) will reveal a dominant one-dimensional manifold across corruption types; dose estimated from held-out corruption types will predict their AP drop with small error compared to per-type calibration.
why_important: Label-free performance monitoring under unknown degradations is a core deployment need; a universal dose scalar makes it practical.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: accuracy-prediction-from-confidence exists for classification; the one-dimensional dose structure claim for detection score distributions across corruption families appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Corrupt a validation set with several families and severities; compute score-distribution features and AP per condition; test 1D-manifold structure and cross-family AP prediction from the fitted dose.
main_risk: Corruptions with qualitatively different failure modes (e.g., occlusion-like vs noise-like) may form separate branches, breaking universality.
community_default_belief: Different corruption types damage detectors in fundamentally different ways requiring per-type characterization.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Downstream of diverse input damage, the network funnels degradation through the same score-producing bottleneck, plausibly collapsing type differences into one effective-signal-loss axis.
fastest_falsification: Fully inference-based: corrupt, evaluate, embed, and test the manifold on one checkpoint.

one_line: Detection heads are systematically under-trained relative to backbones: a final frozen-backbone, high-LR head phase yields consistent gains.
problem: One learning-rate schedule serves backbone and heads, though these components differ in initialization (pretrained vs random), gradient scale, and target stationarity.
core_hypothesis: Because head targets keep shifting while assignment and features co-adapt, heads end training away from their optimum for the final feature distribution; freezing the backbone at the end and continuing head-only training at elevated LR (retargeting heads to now-stationary features) adds AP reliably, reversing the usual fine-tuning intuition that heads adapt quickly and backbones need care.
falsifiable_prediction: Appending a short frozen-backbone head-retuning phase to standard recipes will improve AP across two architectures, with gains concentrated in localization quality (AP75) and calibration rather than AP50.
why_important: A recipe-level free lunch applicable to any detector, and evidence about where optimization slack hides in two-component systems.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: head-only fine-tuning exists for transfer settings; as a terminal phase of standard same-distribution training claimed to be systematically beneficial, it appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take completed standard runs; append head-only retuning (sweep LR and length briefly); evaluate AP/AP75/calibration deltas across two detector families and two seeds.
main_risk: Gains may vanish for recipes with long cosine decay where heads are already well-converged to final features.
community_default_belief: End-of-training co-adaptation leaves all components jointly near-optimal; further head-only training just overfits.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Joint training against non-stationary targets is exactly the condition where components lag; the head chases a moving feature distribution and never gets a clean final fit.
fastest_falsification: Head retuning on an existing checkpoint costs a small fraction of a training run and answers directly.

consolidation.mutation_note: Head-only retraining closely resembles decoupled classifier-retraining practice. Mutate: the idea is the measurable head/backbone convergence mismatch under assignment non-stationarity, not the retuning recipe; frame the recipe as the confirmation experiment.

one_line: Classification and localization peak at different training epochs; per-task checkpoint blending beats the best single checkpoint.
problem: Model selection picks one checkpoint by aggregate AP, implicitly assuming all detection subtasks peak together.
core_hypothesis: Classification quality (correct labels, ranking) and localization quality (box accuracy) follow different training trajectories with systematically offset optima; constructing a model whose classification pathway comes from one epoch and regression pathway from another (weight-blend or head-swap) outperforms every single checkpoint of the run.
falsifiable_prediction: Task-decomposed validation curves will show a consistent epoch offset between classification-metric and localization-metric peaks across runs; the cross-epoch head-combined model will exceed best-single-checkpoint AP in the majority of runs.
why_important: Free accuracy from artifacts every run already produces, plus a dynamics insight into multi-task interference within detection.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: checkpoint averaging is standard, but task-asymmetric cross-epoch composition based on distinct task optima appears unexplored for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several saved runs, plot cls-only and loc-only quality per epoch; build cross-epoch composites (swap heads between checkpoints sharing a backbone lineage); evaluate against best single checkpoints and uniform averaging.
main_risk: Heads from different epochs may be incompatible with a single backbone state, making naive swaps degenerate.
community_default_belief: One best checkpoint suffices; subtask temporal structure within a detection run is negligible.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The two objectives have different noise sensitivities and overfitting rates; coincident optima would be the surprising case, not the default.
fastest_falsification: Task-decomposed evaluation of already-saved checkpoints requires no training; peak offset presence/absence is immediately visible.

one_line: 'Longer detection training hurts transfer' is driven by background-logit sharpening, and background-entropy regularization preserves transferability at no in-domain cost.
problem: Detectors trained longer sometimes transfer worse to new domains/datasets, and the mechanism is unattributed, so practitioners guess at early stopping.
core_hypothesis: Extended training primarily sharpens the background decision (negative logits grow confident on dataset-specific background textures), which is the least transferable component; the foreground representations keep improving or plateau. A regularizer keeping background predictive entropy high preserves transfer performance without sacrificing in-domain AP, and background-logit sharpness measured over training predicts transfer degradation.
falsifiable_prediction: Across checkpoints of long runs, transfer AP will correlate negatively with a background-sharpness statistic while in-domain AP still rises; entropy-regularized-background training will flatten the transfer decline with unchanged in-domain AP.
why_important: Explains and fixes a costly tradeoff between in-domain optimization and reusability of detection models.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: overtraining-vs-transfer effects are reported anecdotally; the background-specific attribution and targeted regularizer appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log background-logit statistics across a long run; evaluate multiple checkpoints on a transfer dataset; test the correlation; retrain with background-entropy regularization and compare transfer curves.
main_risk: Foreground class-prototype drift may co-vary with background sharpening, confounding attribution without careful controls.
community_default_belief: Transfer degradation from long training is generic overfitting affecting all components; early stopping is the only remedy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Foreground objects are shared across domains but backgrounds are dataset idiosyncratic; the overfitting pressure is structurally concentrated in the negative space.
fastest_falsification: The correlation study needs only saved checkpoints from one long run plus one transfer evaluation set.

one_line: Assignment adaptivity corrupts the validation loss as a model-selection signal; assignment-frozen validation loss tracks AP better late in training.
problem: Validation loss is the cheap model-selection signal, but for detectors it often disagrees with AP, and the cause is unclear.
core_hypothesis: Because the assignment procedure re-solves per evaluation, a model can lower measured loss by shifting which predictions get matched (gaming the matching) without improving actual detection quality; freezing the assignment (computing loss against a fixed, precomputed matching from a reference checkpoint) removes this degree of freedom and yields a loss that rank-correlates with AP substantially better in mid-to-late training.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank correlation between standard validation loss and AP across late-training checkpoints will be poor, while assignment-frozen loss will correlate strongly, consistently across two detector families.
why_important: Restores a cheap, differentiable model-selection and monitoring signal, reducing dependence on expensive AP evaluation during training.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: loss-AP divergence is folklore; attributing it to assignment re-solving and fixing it by matching freezing appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For saved checkpoint series, compute standard and assignment-frozen validation losses; compare rank correlations with AP over the late-training window.
main_risk: The frozen matching's reference checkpoint choice may bias the measure toward models similar to the reference.
community_default_belief: Detection validation loss is inherently a weak proxy for AP because the loss and metric are structurally different.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Part of the divergence may be an artifact of letting the loss re-match per model - a removable measurement problem, not a structural one.
fastest_falsification: Pure re-evaluation of saved checkpoints with two loss protocols; no training.

one_line: Large-batch detection training should scale LR by positive-instance count, not image count: gradient noise is set by positives per batch.
problem: Large-batch recipes for detection borrow linear-LR-scaling from classification, where each image contributes one supervised example; detection batches vary wildly in supervised positives.
core_hypothesis: The effective gradient noise scale in detection is governed by the number of positive instances per batch (few per image, heavy-tailed across images), not the image count; therefore LR should scale with expected positive count, and batch construction that equalizes positives across batches (instance-balanced batching) improves large-batch stability and final AP over image-count-based scaling.
falsifiable_prediction: At large batch sizes, positive-count-scaled LR with instance-balanced batching will avoid the AP degradation seen with standard linear scaling; measured gradient-noise scale will track positives-per-batch, not images-per-batch.
why_important: Correct scaling rules unlock efficient large-batch/distributed detection training without accuracy tax.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: gradient-noise-scale analysis exists for classification and LM training; a positives-based reformulation for detection with batching consequences appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure gradient-noise scale versus images and versus positives on a mid-size dataset; train at 2-3 large batch sizes under both scaling rules; compare stability and final AP.
main_risk: Background gradients (negatives) may contribute enough signal that positives-only scaling mis-estimates the noise scale.
community_default_belief: Linear LR-batch scaling with warmup, as inherited from classification, is the correct default for detection.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The classification derivation assumes i.i.d. per-image supervision; detection violates this with variable, correlated, sparse positives, changing the noise-scale arithmetic.
fastest_falsification: Gradient-noise-scale measurement (a few hundred iterations of logging) directly tests which count the noise tracks, before any full training.

one_line: Repeating a rare-class instance within one batch is worth less than across batches: shared-feature gradient coupling suppresses same-batch repetition gains.
problem: Rare-class oversampling policies treat 'more copies' as uniform benefit, ignoring where the copies land relative to batching.
core_hypothesis: Multiple copies of the same rare instance in one batch produce highly correlated gradients through shared weights that the optimizer treats as one large step (with clipped/normalized effects), while the same copies spread over consecutive batches interact with different negatives and momentum states, yielding better rare-class learning; thus repeat-factor sampling schedules that spread copies temporally beat within-batch duplication at equal copy budget.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched total repetition counts, across-batch spreading will yield higher rare-class AP than within-batch duplication, with the gap growing as per-batch duplication increases.
why_important: Refines long-tail training recipes at zero cost by specifying not just how much to oversample but how to schedule it.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: repeat-factor sampling is standard; the within-vs-across-batch scheduling variable appears never isolated in detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a long-tail detection dataset, fix the copy budget per rare instance; train variants differing only in copy placement (same batch vs spread); compare rare-class AP over two seeds.
main_risk: Data-augmentation randomness per copy may dominate the placement effect, shrinking the measurable gap.
community_default_belief: Oversampling benefit depends on total exposure count; batch placement is an implementation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Gradient correlation within a batch is a first-order optimizer effect; identical exposures are not identical learning events when their gradient contexts differ.
fastest_falsification: Two matched small-scale runs (placement differing only) on a subsampled long-tail dataset.

one_line: Mosaic-style augmentation gains are mostly a positive-density effect: density-matched conventional sampling closes most of the gap.
problem: Composite-image augmentations are credited with context diversification and scale enrichment, but they also quietly multiply positive instances per iteration, an unseparated confound.
core_hypothesis: The dominant benefit of mosaic-like composition is simply more GT instances per gradient step (higher supervised signal density); a baseline that matches positives-per-iteration by batching more images (or cropping object-dense regions) without composition recovers most of the gain, leaving only a small residual attributable to context/scale mixing.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched positives-per-iteration and matched compute, non-composited training will come within a small margin of mosaic training AP, and the residual gap will shrink further when scale jitter is equalized.
why_important: Correct attribution redirects augmentation research and warns that composition artifacts (fake boundaries, wrong context) are being paid for little unique benefit.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: mosaic ablations exist against no-mosaic baselines, but positives-density-matched controls appear absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train (a) mosaic, (b) plain, (c) plain with density-matched sampling, (d) c plus matched scale jitter; compare AP at equal optimizer steps and equal wall-clock compute separately.
main_risk: Density matching changes image statistics (more crops of dense regions), introducing its own bias that must be reported.
community_default_belief: Mosaic works by exposing objects in novel contexts and scales, teaching context-robust features.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Detection training is signal-starved per iteration (few positives per image); any method that quadruples positives would help regardless of context effects.
fastest_falsification: The four-way comparison on a small dataset with short schedules gives a clear first-order answer.

one_line: EMA's detection benefit concentrates in the regression branch; EMA-ing only neck and box head captures most of the gain.
problem: Weight EMA is applied to whole detectors as a monolith, so nobody knows which components' smoothing actually produces the gain, or what that implies about training noise structure.
core_hypothesis: The regression pathway suffers more from late-training weight oscillation (its loss landscape is more anisotropic due to box-scale heterogeneity), so EMA's benefit is disproportionately a localization-smoothing effect; component-selective EMA (neck + regression head only) achieves most of full-model EMA's AP gain, while cls-head-only EMA is nearly neutral.
falsifiable_prediction: A component-wise EMA ablation will show the reg-pathway-only variant capturing the majority of full EMA's AP75 improvement, with classification-metric improvements from EMA being comparatively small, replicated across two architectures.
why_important: Reveals where training noise damages detectors and enables cheaper or smarter averaging (e.g., different decay rates per component).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: EMA is ubiquitous; a component-resolved decomposition of its benefit in detection appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with checkpointed raw weights; construct post-hoc selective-EMA models (backbone-only, neck+reg-only, cls-only, full); evaluate AP/AP75 for each variant on two detector families.
main_risk: Component interactions may make selective EMA incoherent (mismatched co-adapted weights), understating a component's true contribution.
community_default_belief: EMA is a generic optimizer-noise filter whose benefit is uniformly distributed over the network.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Noise sensitivity is task-geometry dependent; box regression's continuous, scale-heterogeneous targets plausibly make it the dominant beneficiary.
fastest_falsification: If raw (non-EMA) checkpoint trajectories are saved, all variants are post-hoc constructions requiring only evaluation.

one_line: Warmup length in detection is dictated by assignment stabilization, not LR safety: stabilize assignment and warmup can shrink drastically.
problem: Detection recipes carry long warmups inherited as folklore; the actual constraint warmup satisfies has not been identified, so schedules cannot be safely shortened.
core_hypothesis: Early training divergence in detectors is triggered by feedback between fast-changing predictions and cost-based assignment (assignment amplifies prediction noise into label noise); with assignment stabilized early (geometric-prior-based or EMA-smoothed assignment for the first phase), full LR can be applied almost immediately without divergence, showing that warmup was protecting the assignment loop rather than the optimizer.
falsifiable_prediction: With stabilized early assignment, warmup can be cut several-fold with no divergence and no final-AP loss, while the same warmup cut under standard assignment diverges or degrades; divergence onset in standard runs will coincide with assignment-churn spikes rather than gradient-norm spikes.
why_important: Identifies the true constraint behind a universal recipe element, enabling faster training and principled schedule design.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: warmup necessity analyses exist for transformers/optimizers generally; the assignment-feedback attribution specific to detection appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Factorial small-scale study: {standard, stabilized-early assignment} x {full warmup, short warmup}; log assignment churn and gradient norms around any divergence; compare final AP.
main_risk: Optimizer-level instabilities (e.g., attention entropy collapse in transformer necks) may independently require warmup, confounding attribution.
community_default_belief: Warmup protects against large early gradient noise in the optimizer; it is an optimization hygiene requirement independent of detection specifics.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Detection adds a unique self-referential label loop absent in classification; the component that most needs protecting may be that loop, not the optimizer.
fastest_falsification: The 2x2 factorial at small scale (four short runs) directly separates the two accounts.

one_line: Seed-to-seed AP variance is concentrated in an identifiable set of 'swing images', predictable from a single run's internal signals.
problem: Detection results vary across seeds enough to confound comparisons, but variance is treated as unstructured noise requiring many seeds to average away.
core_hypothesis: Cross-seed AP variance is dominated by a small subset of images whose scoring sits near assignment/NMS/threshold decision boundaries (high-ambiguity scenes); these swing images are identifiable from a single trained model via internal ambiguity signals (score margins, duplicate structure, matching cost gaps), enabling variance prediction and variance-adjusted comparisons without training extra seeds.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-image cross-seed outcome variance (measured over several seeds) will be heavy-tailed with a small fraction of images explaining most metric variance; a single-seed ambiguity score will rank images by cross-seed variance with strong correlation.
why_important: Cheap variance estimation makes small AP differences interpretable, improving experimental hygiene field-wide without multi-seed budgets.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: seed variance in detection is documented at the metric level; its per-image concentration and single-run predictability appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 5+ seeds of a small detector; compute per-image outcome variance; test heavy-tailedness; fit and validate the single-seed ambiguity predictor on held-out seeds.
main_risk: Variance may be distributed rather than concentrated for large well-trained models, limiting the finding to small-scale regimes.
community_default_belief: Run-to-run variance is diffuse stochastic noise; only multiple seeds can quantify it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Thresholded pipelines convert continuous weight noise into discrete outcome flips only near decision boundaries, which are image-specific and detectable from one model.
fastest_falsification: Five short-seed runs on a small dataset suffice to measure per-image variance concentration.

one_line: Datasets mix modal and amodal box conventions inconsistently per class, and per-class convention consistency predicts per-class AP75.
problem: Whether occluded objects are boxed by visible extent (modal) or full extent (amodal) is rarely enforced consistently, injecting structured label noise nobody measures.
core_hypothesis: Within standard detection datasets, the modal/amodal choice for occluded instances varies by annotator and by class in measurable proportions; models learn a per-class average convention, and classes with more internally inconsistent conventions have systematically lower AP75 after controlling for size, frequency, and occlusion rate.
falsifiable_prediction: An audit labeling a sample of occluded GT boxes as modal/amodal will find substantial within-class inconsistency; a class-level inconsistency index will negatively predict AP75 residuals across classes and across two datasets.
why_important: Identifies a controllable annotation-protocol variable as a hidden performance cap, guiding dataset construction and relabeling priorities.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: amodal detection is its own subfield, but quantifying convention inconsistency inside standard datasets and linking it to per-class localization performance appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample a few hundred occluded instances per dataset; have annotators judge modal vs amodal style; compute per-class inconsistency; regress per-class AP75 residuals of existing checkpoints on inconsistency.
main_risk: Judging convention from a drawn box is itself ambiguous for mild occlusion, adding noise to the audit variable.
community_default_belief: Annotation guidelines are followed closely enough that convention mixing is a negligible noise source compared to box jitter.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Occlusion forces a discrete style choice where guidelines are weakest; discrete convention flips create bimodal targets, which harm regression far more than small jitter does.
fastest_falsification: The audit itself (a few hundred judgments) immediately establishes whether inconsistency exists at a meaningful rate.

one_line: Ignore-region training creates blind spots that generalize beyond the ignored regions to visually similar non-ignored areas.
problem: Crowd/ignore regions are a standard annotation device assumed to be neutral (no gradient), but their effect on what the model learns to suppress is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Excluding regions from the loss does not make them neutral: because ignored regions share appearance statistics (dense crowds, clutter), the model receives systematically censored supervision for that appearance class and learns reduced detection propensity there; consequently detection recall in non-ignored areas that resemble typical ignore-region appearance is measurably depressed.
falsifiable_prediction: A similarity model mapping image patches to 'ignore-region-likeness' will predict local recall deficits on fully annotated evaluation data; training with ignore regions filled by pseudo-labels (instead of loss masking) will remove the deficit.
why_important: Reveals that a universal annotation shortcut shapes model behavior in unintended, safety-relevant ways (crowded scenes are exactly where misses are costly).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: ignore regions are treated as harmless plumbing; their generalized suppression side effect appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without ignore-region masking on a dataset that has both crowd annotations and exhaustive labels for evaluation subsets; measure recall stratified by ignore-likeness.
main_risk: Datasets with both ignore regions and exhaustively labeled evaluation regions are scarce; may require constructing a semi-synthetic testbed.
community_default_belief: Loss masking is informationally neutral: no gradient means no learned behavior for those regions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Learning is shaped by the distribution of where positives can occur; censoring positives from an appearance class is equivalent to teaching a negative prior over that appearance.
fastest_falsification: The correlational part (ignore-likeness vs recall) can be run on existing checkpoints wherever exhaustive labels exist for crowded scenes.

one_line: Missing annotations concentrate near image borders and small scales, making border 'false positives' disproportionately genuine detections.
problem: FP counts drive both evaluation and hard-negative mining, but if annotation misses are spatially structured, both are systematically biased in specific regions.
core_hypothesis: Annotation misses are not uniform: they cluster at image borders, partial visibility, and small scales; therefore high-confidence detector 'false positives' in those strata are enriched for true objects, and re-reviewing only border/small FPs yields a much higher label-correction rate than reviewing random FPs, with consequences for training (hard-negative mining corrupts exactly there) and evaluation (border-heavy methods are unfairly penalized).
falsifiable_prediction: Human re-review of top-confidence FPs stratified by border distance and size will show the border/small strata containing a several-fold higher proportion of missed-GT than central/large strata, consistently across two datasets.
why_important: Enables targeted label cleaning at a fraction of full re-annotation cost and corrects a structured bias in hard-negative mining and method comparison.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: missing-label robustness is studied generally; the spatial structure of misses and its exploitation for targeted auditing appear uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take an existing checkpoint's top FPs; stratify by border distance and box size; re-review a sample per stratum; compare missed-GT rates across strata.
main_risk: Detector FP placement is itself border-biased (cropped-object artifacts), which must be disentangled from annotation-miss placement.
community_default_belief: Annotation misses are approximately random noise, thin enough to ignore in both training and evaluation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Annotator attention and effort follow image composition; borders and small instances are exactly where labeling effort collapses, making misses structural rather than random.
fastest_falsification: A few hundred stratified re-review judgments on one dataset settle the enrichment question.

one_line: Mid-training checkpoints are better annotation-error detectors than converged models, which have already memorized the errors.
problem: Model-assisted label cleaning uses the best available (converged) model to flag disagreements with GT, but converged models fit label errors, blinding them to exactly what should be flagged.
core_hypothesis: There is a mid-training sweet spot where a detector has learned the true data patterns but not yet memorized annotation errors; model-GT disagreements at this stage have substantially higher precision for genuine label errors than disagreements from the final checkpoint, and the sweet spot is identifiable from training dynamics (before the train-clean/train-noisy loss gap closes).
falsifiable_prediction: On a dataset with synthetically injected, known label errors, error-flagging precision-recall from mid-training checkpoints will dominate that from converged checkpoints; the optimal flagging epoch will coincide with a measurable dynamics marker transferable to real datasets.
why_important: Improves every model-in-the-loop relabeling pipeline at zero extra cost by changing only which checkpoint is used.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: early-learning phenomena are known in noisy-label classification; operationalizing checkpoint choice for detection label auditing with a dynamics-based selection marker appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inject known box/class errors into a training set; train while saving checkpoints; measure per-checkpoint flagging quality against the known errors; validate the dynamics marker; spot-check on real data with human review.
main_risk: Detection's structured errors (misses, box jitter, class swaps) may have different memorization timing, blurring a single sweet spot.
community_default_belief: The most accurate model is the best label auditor; use the final or best-AP checkpoint for cleaning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Accuracy on the noisy benchmark partly measures agreement with the noise itself; the best auditor is the model most faithful to the clean signal, which is an earlier one.
fastest_falsification: The synthetic-injection experiment on a small dataset with saved checkpoints answers the core comparison quickly.

one_line: Fine-grained sibling classes cause score-mass splitting rather than misclassification, and sibling-aware aggregation recovers the lost detections.
problem: Errors on confusable class pairs are assumed to be label swaps (wrong class wins), but the detection pipeline may instead lose such objects entirely below threshold.
core_hypothesis: For visually confusable sibling classes, detectors distribute score mass across the siblings (two medium scores instead of one high score); after thresholding/NMS this manifests as missed detections rather than wrong-class detections, so aggregating scores over sibling groups before thresholding recovers objects that per-class scoring loses, improving group-level recall at no precision cost.
falsifiable_prediction: For confusable pairs (identified by classifier confusion structure), the miss rate will exceed the wrong-class rate; sibling-group score aggregation will convert a measurable share of misses into correct group-level detections across datasets with fine-grained taxonomies.
why_important: Changes the diagnosis of fine-grained detection failure from 'classifier confusion' to 'pipeline score splitting', with an immediate post-hoc fix for applications tolerant of group-level labels.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: hierarchical inference exists, but the specific claim that thresholded pipelines convert confusion into misses (not swaps), with quantification, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify sibling groups from a confusion analysis; compare miss vs swap rates for those groups on existing checkpoints; evaluate group-aggregated scoring against per-class scoring.
main_risk: Softmax-based heads may already concentrate mass (winner-take-all), limiting the effect to sigmoid/multi-label heads.
community_default_belief: Confusable classes produce misclassifications; recall is governed by localization and objectness, not by label granularity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: With independent per-class sigmoid scores, semantic ambiguity directly halves per-class confidence; the ranking/thresholding stage then silently drops the object.
fastest_falsification: Miss-vs-swap accounting for confusable pairs is a pure re-analysis of existing predictions.

one_line: Duplicate ground-truth annotations destabilize one-to-one matching training measurably more than one-to-many, and a duplicate audit predicts which images hurt.
problem: Datasets contain occasional duplicate annotations of the same object; their differential effect across training paradigms is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Under one-to-one bipartite matching, duplicate GTs force the model to produce two distinct predictions for one object, directly contradicting the learned self-suppression objective and injecting persistent gradient conflict; under one-to-many assignment the duplicates largely merge into the same positive set, so the damage is much smaller. Per-image training-loss volatility will therefore flag duplicate-GT images in one-to-one training specifically.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting synthetic duplicate GTs at a controlled rate will degrade one-to-one detectors' AP significantly more than one-to-many detectors' at the same rate; images with real duplicates will show elevated matching-cost volatility in one-to-one training logs.
why_important: Quantifies a paradigm-specific data-quality sensitivity, telling teams which cleaning investments matter for which architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: label-noise studies cover class and box noise; duplicate-annotation noise interacting with matching paradigm appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one-to-one and one-to-many models on data with 0/1/3 percent injected GT duplicates; compare AP degradation slopes; correlate real-duplicate audit findings with per-image loss volatility.
main_risk: Real duplicate rates may be so low that the practical (as opposed to scientific) significance is limited.
community_default_belief: Small amounts of annotation duplication are harmless noise absorbed equally by any training scheme.
why_that_may_be_wrong: One-to-one matching encodes a hard uniqueness constraint; data violating a hard constraint has outsized effect compared to violating soft statistical assumptions.
fastest_falsification: The injection experiment at small scale (two paradigms, three rates) gives clean causal slopes quickly.

one_line: Annotators snap boxes to high-contrast edges rather than true object extents, and models inherit a measurable contrast-seeking localization bias.
problem: Box accuracy is treated as unbiased around true extents, but annotation tooling and human vision both favor visible edges, potentially teaching models a systematic bias.
core_hypothesis: Human-drawn boxes systematically align with strong image gradients even when the object extends beyond them (shadows, low-contrast parts, transparent regions); models trained on such labels reproduce the bias, predicting boxes that snap to contrast edges; the bias is measurable by comparing predicted boxes on objects with deliberately low-contrast extensions (synthetic composites) where the true extent is known.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic composites with controlled low-contrast object extensions, both GT-style human annotations and model predictions will truncate the low-contrast portion at correlated rates; increasing extension contrast will monotonically reduce truncation in model outputs.
why_important: Establishes that some 'localization error' is faithful reproduction of biased labels, affecting applications needing physical extents (measurement, grasping, tracking).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: annotation bias studies exist for class labels and saliency; a contrast-snapping law for box geometry with model inheritance appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build composites with known extents and variable-contrast parts; collect human boxes on a sample; run existing checkpoints; measure truncation vs contrast for both, and their correlation.
main_risk: Synthetic composites may not elicit natural annotator behavior, weakening the human side of the comparison.
community_default_belief: Annotation jitter is symmetric noise around true extents; models average it away.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Perceptual salience is not symmetric: edges attract both annotator attention and cursor placement, producing a directional bias that averaging preserves rather than removes.
fastest_falsification: The model-side contrast-truncation curve on composites is inference-only and already tests inheritance if the bias appears.

one_line: Detectors average synthetic box-label noise for large objects but not below a size threshold, defining a label-quality-dominated regime.
problem: How much annotation precision matters, and for which objects, is unquantified, so labeling budgets are spent uniformly.
core_hypothesis: When box labels carry zero-mean jitter, the learned regressor averages the noise effectively for objects large relative to the jitter scale (many correlated examples, smooth interpolation), but below a size threshold the noise is effectively multiplicative and learning degrades sharply; therefore there exists a measurable size-dependent noise-robustness curve with a knee, and labeling precision only matters below the knee.
falsifiable_prediction: Training with controlled label jitter at several amplitudes will leave large-object AP75 nearly unchanged while small-object AP75 degrades steeply, with the knee position scaling linearly with jitter amplitude.
why_important: Gives dataset builders a quantitative rule for where annotation precision (and hence cost) actually matters, and predicts which applications need re-labeling.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: noisy-box training has been studied for robustness methods; a size-resolved noise-averaging law with a predictable knee appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inject zero-mean jitter at 3 amplitudes into training labels of a clean(er) dataset; train matched models; plot AP75 vs object size per amplitude; test knee scaling.
main_risk: Interaction with assignment (jittered boxes change positive sets) may confound pure regression-noise effects.
community_default_belief: Label jitter degrades performance roughly uniformly; more precise boxes are always proportionally better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Averaging arguments imply noise robustness that is scale-relative, not absolute; uniform-degradation intuition ignores the jitter-to-size ratio that actually governs learning.
fastest_falsification: Three jitter-amplitude runs on a small dataset with size-stratified evaluation reveal the knee (or its absence).

one_line: At the margin, certified object-free regions ('verified negatives') buy more detection quality per annotation dollar than additional positive boxes.
problem: Annotation budgets go almost entirely to drawing more boxes, while the absence of objects is never certified, leaving negative supervision permanently uncertain.
core_hypothesis: Much of the FP rate and score miscalibration of mature detectors stems from uncertainty about whether unlabeled regions are truly negative (missing-label ambiguity); a modest budget spent certifying regions as object-free (cheap per unit area) provides clean negative supervision whose marginal value, in a mature-training regime, exceeds the marginal value of the same budget spent on additional positive boxes.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched incremental annotation cost, adding verified-negative supervision (with a loss that trusts certified negatives more than uncertified ones) will improve FP-rate-at-fixed-recall and calibration more than adding extra positive boxes improves recall, once the base training set exceeds a moderate size.
why_important: Could redirect labeling economics field-wide: certification of absence is fast, unglamorous, and possibly the best marginal spend.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: missing-label-aware losses exist; the budget-matched marginal-value comparison between certified negatives and extra positives appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate both budget allocations on a dataset by hiding labels (extra positives) and certifying regions (using full GT as oracle); train matched models; compare FP-rate/calibration vs recall gains per unit simulated cost.
main_risk: Simulated costs may misrepresent real annotation economics; conclusions need a small real-annotation validation.
community_default_belief: More boxes is always the best use of labeling budget; unlabeled regions are treated as negative anyway, so certifying them adds nothing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Treating unlabeled as negative forces loss down-weighting or noise absorption everywhere; certified negatives permit full-strength negative gradients exactly where they are currently impossible.
fastest_falsification: The oracle-simulated comparison on a fully labeled dataset requires only two matched training runs per budget level.

one_line: Method rankings flip between mAP and fixed-precision recall often enough to change practical conclusions, and the flips are predictable from score-distribution shape.
problem: mAP integrates over all operating points, but deployments run at one point (often high precision); whether mAP-based rankings survive at deployment points is rarely checked.
core_hypothesis: Because mAP rewards long low-confidence tails while deployments never see them, pairs of detectors frequently invert order between mAP and recall-at-fixed-precision; the inversion probability is predictable from the divergence of their score-distribution shapes (tail-heavy vs concentrated), enabling a cheap flag for 'this mAP comparison will not transfer to deployment'.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many public checkpoint pairs evaluated identically, a non-trivial fraction of pairs will invert between mAP and recall-at-90-percent-precision; a score-tail statistic will predict inversions with accuracy well above chance.
why_important: Protects practitioners from choosing the wrong model for deployment based on leaderboard metrics, with a concrete predictive diagnostic.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: criticisms of mAP exist; quantifying inversion rates at scale and predicting them from score-shape appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a pool of public checkpoints on one dataset; compute both metrics; count pairwise inversions; fit and validate the tail-statistic predictor on held-out pairs.
main_risk: Checkpoint pools may cluster into families with similar score shapes, shrinking observable inversion diversity.
community_default_belief: mAP is a faithful single-number summary; better mAP means a better detector for practical purposes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: An integral metric can be dominated by regions of the curve that no application uses; equality of integrals says nothing about ordering at a point.
fastest_falsification: Purely re-evaluating existing checkpoints under both metrics; no training.

one_line: AP can be gamed measurably by score-tail shaping without changing any decision-relevant prediction, exposing a metric integrity flaw.
problem: AP computation details (interpolation, tail handling, per-class normalization) create degrees of freedom that may reward output post-processing having no effect on real detection quality.
core_hypothesis: Manipulating only the low-confidence tail (adding hallucinated near-zero-score boxes in strategic locations, reordering ties, per-class score monotone transforms) changes measured AP by margins comparable to publishable 'improvements', while every fixed-threshold operating point above practical confidence remains identical; the exploit size varies by AP implementation and per-class instance counts.
falsifiable_prediction: A tail-shaping post-processor applied to existing checkpoints will shift mAP by a nontrivial margin (implementation-dependent) while leaving precision/recall at all thresholds above a small score unchanged; rare classes will contribute disproportionately to the shift.
why_important: If method-comparison margins are within reach of semantic-free manipulation, evaluation practice needs guardrails (tail truncation, operating-point reporting).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: individual AP quirks are known piecemeal; a constructive, quantified gaming demonstration across implementations appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement tail-shaping transforms; apply to several checkpoints under two common AP implementations; report mAP deltas and verify operating-point invariance.
main_risk: Well-maintained evaluation servers may already truncate detections per image, capping the exploit; the finding may apply mainly to self-reported evaluations.
community_default_belief: AP differences beyond a small epsilon reflect genuine detection improvements; the metric is not meaningfully manipulable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: AP's integral is estimated from finite, interpolated samples where tail entries shift interpolation anchors; finite-sample estimators are generically exploitable.
fastest_falsification: Pure post-processing plus re-scoring of existing prediction files - hours of work.

one_line: Class-averaged mAP misallocates model capacity relative to downstream utility, and instance-weighted AP reranks models in a utility-aligned way.
problem: mAP weights every class equally regardless of its frequency or downstream importance, silently steering research toward rare-class trickery and away from volume performance.
core_hypothesis: Model rankings under class-equal mAP and instance-frequency-weighted AP diverge materially, and for common downstream aggregate tasks (counting, indexing, alerting on any object) the instance-weighted metric predicts realized utility better; some 'state-of-the-art' differences reflect rare-class score arbitrage rather than broadly better detection.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking a pool of checkpoints by both metrics will produce significant rank divergence; on simulated downstream tasks with instance-proportional utility, the instance-weighted metric's ranking will correlate better with task performance than class-equal mAP's.
why_important: Metrics steer the field; demonstrating a utility misalignment with a concrete alternative could redirect effort toward improvements users actually feel.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: metric critiques exist; a quantified utility-alignment comparison between class-equal and instance-weighted detection metrics appears rare or absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate checkpoints under both weightings; define 2-3 downstream utility simulations (count accuracy, retrieval hit rate); compare metric-to-utility rank correlations.
main_risk: Downstream utility definitions are contestable; results may be dismissed as depending on the chosen simulations.
community_default_belief: Class-equal averaging is the fair default that prevents frequent classes from dominating and serves all users adequately.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fairness across classes is not fairness across use: most deployments consume detections in proportion to their occurrence, which class-equal averaging deliberately distorts.
fastest_falsification: Re-scoring existing evaluation files under the alternative weighting is immediate; rank divergence alone establishes the premise.

consolidation.mutation_note: 'Predicts realized utility better' hinges on contestable utility simulations - conceded in main_risk. Mutate: restrict to the crisp, cheap core (rankings materially diverge between class-equal and instance-weighted AP, driven by rare-class score arbitrage).

one_line: The discrete IoU-threshold ladder in AP misses real localization improvements that a continuous localization metric detects with higher statistical power.
problem: AP averages over a coarse grid of IoU thresholds, quantizing localization quality and possibly hiding genuine model differences within threshold bins.
core_hypothesis: Two models can differ meaningfully in localization (mean matched IoU, tail box errors) while their thresholded AP values are statistically indistinguishable at feasible test-set sizes; a continuous metric (e.g., expected matched IoU or signed-error distributions) detects such differences with substantially higher power, and some published-scale architecture differences are of exactly this hidden kind.
falsifiable_prediction: On checkpoint pairs with near-identical mAP, continuous localization metrics will separate a subset of pairs with high statistical significance, and the separation will be corroborated by downstream box-precision-sensitive task simulations.
why_important: Higher-power evaluation reveals real progress (or its absence) that the standard metric cannot see, changing which methods look promising.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: alternative localization metrics have been proposed; the statistical-power framing with hidden-difference discovery on nominally tied models appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect checkpoint pairs with matched mAP; compute continuous localization statistics with bootstrap confidence intervals; validate meaningfulness via a box-sensitive downstream proxy (e.g., simulated measurement error).
main_risk: Continuous metrics may pick up differences that are real but practically irrelevant, requiring the downstream proxy to establish relevance.
community_default_belief: Averaging AP over many IoU thresholds already captures localization quality adequately; tied mAP means equivalent detectors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Thresholding discards within-bin information by construction; statistical power lost to quantization is a textbook effect, not a detection-specific subtlety.
fastest_falsification: All computations are post-hoc over existing prediction files with bootstrap analysis.

one_line: Cross-dataset detector rankings are unstable under reasonable alternative class-mapping choices, making label-space mapping a hidden researcher degree of freedom.
problem: Cross-dataset evaluation requires mapping class taxonomies between datasets; the mapping is chosen ad hoc per paper and its effect on conclusions is never audited.
core_hypothesis: For typical dataset pairs, multiple defensible class mappings exist (synonym scope, part-whole choices, granularity merges), and detector rankings change across these mappings often enough that some cross-dataset generalization claims are mapping artifacts; the sensitivity is measurable as ranking variance over an enumerated space of defensible mappings.
falsifiable_prediction: Enumerating a set of defensible mappings between two common dataset pairs and re-evaluating a pool of checkpoints will produce ranking inversions in a meaningful fraction of mapping choices, concentrated in classes with taxonomy mismatches.
why_important: Cross-dataset robustness is a headline claim in detection papers; showing its mapping sensitivity forces reporting standards (mapping enumeration or mapping-marginalized metrics).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: mapping choices are acknowledged as messy; a systematic sensitivity analysis with ranking-stability quantification appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 5-10 defensible mappings for one dataset pair (documented rules); evaluate several checkpoints under each; quantify rank instability and identify driver classes.
main_risk: 'Defensible' is subjective; the mapping space must be pre-registered with clear rules to avoid constructing strawmen.
community_default_belief: Any sensible class mapping yields essentially the same cross-dataset conclusions; the mapping is a technicality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rankings between close competitors often hinge on a handful of classes; taxonomy mismatches concentrate exactly there, giving small mapping choices outsized leverage.
fastest_falsification: Re-evaluation under enumerated mappings is pure post-processing of existing predictions.

one_line: A matched error-decomposition shows architectures differ mainly in one error type each, which aggregate AP deltas systematically mis-attribute.
problem: AP differences between detector families are interpreted as generic superiority, though the underlying error-profile differences (misses vs duplicates vs localization vs classification) may be narrow and specific.
core_hypothesis: When errors are decomposed with a consistent matched protocol (each GT and prediction assigned to exactly one error category), major architecture families exhibit signature error profiles (e.g., one family trades duplicates for misses, another trades localization for classification); most pairwise AP gaps are dominated by a single category, so category-targeted fixes could equalize families at far lower cost than adopting new architectures.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing errors for several checkpoint families on one dataset will show, for most pairs, one error category explaining the majority of the AP gap; simulated repair of that single category (oracle substitution) will close most of the gap.
why_important: Changes how architecture results are read and enables cheap targeted interventions instead of wholesale migrations.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: error-analysis toolkits exist; the claim of family-specific single-category dominance with oracle-repair quantification appears untested at systematic scale.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a consistent decomposition over 5-6 public checkpoints from 3 families; compute per-pair category contributions to AP gaps; run oracle-repair simulations per category.
main_risk: Decomposition protocols embed assignment choices that can shift category attribution; results must be shown stable across two protocols.
community_default_belief: Higher-AP architectures are better across the board; the gap reflects accumulated general superiority.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Architectural inductive biases are specific (set prediction vs dense scoring), so their consequences should be specific too; aggregate metrics just launder specificity into a scalar.
fastest_falsification: Fully post-hoc analysis over existing prediction files with an open-source decomposition protocol.

one_line: A cut-paste out-of-context evaluation isolates context reliance as a stable per-architecture scalar that standard AP conflates with recognition ability.
problem: Standard test sets preserve natural object-context correlations, so AP cannot distinguish recognizing objects from recognizing their habitual scenes.
core_hypothesis: Evaluating detectors on a controlled companion set where objects are composited into unfamiliar-but-plausible contexts yields a context-reliance score (in-context AP minus out-of-context AP, artifact-controlled); this score varies widely across architectures at matched standard AP and predicts robustness to natural distribution shifts better than standard AP does.
falsifiable_prediction: Checkpoints with matched standard AP will spread substantially on the context-reliance score; the score will correlate with performance drops on natural-shift evaluations more strongly than standard AP does.
why_important: Adds a second axis to detector evaluation that predicts real-world brittleness, cheap to produce from existing assets.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: out-of-context studies exist for classification and in small detection probes; a standardized reliance scalar validated as a shift-robustness predictor appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the companion set via segmentation-based pasting with artifact controls (matched blending for in-context repastes); evaluate a checkpoint pool; correlate reliance scores with natural-shift performance drops.
main_risk: Pasting artifacts may dominate the measured drop; the in-context repaste control is essential and must be validated.
community_default_belief: Standard AP on held-out natural images adequately captures detection ability; context effects are second-order.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Held-out natural images share the training set's context statistics, so context shortcuts are rewarded identically at train and test - the metric is structurally blind to them.
fastest_falsification: A small pilot companion set (a few hundred composites) and two checkpoints suffice to see whether reliance scores spread at matched AP.
