problem: Distribution-free uncertainty methods are being ported to segmentation by treating pixels as exchangeable units, though errors arrive in large correlated blobs.
core_hypothesis: The spatial correlation length of VLM segmentation errors is large enough that nominal per-pixel guarantees are badly miscovered at the image and region level; correcting with measured effective sample sizes restores advertised coverage at the cost of wider sets.
falsifiable_prediction: Empirical coverage of naive per-pixel conformal sets will fall short of nominal levels on image-level and object-level events, and the shortfall will be predicted by measured error-correlation length.
why_important: Safety cases increasingly cite conformal guarantees; guarantees that quietly assume pixel independence are pseudo-guarantees.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal segmentation papers exist; an autocorrelation-aware audit quantifying the miscoverage and its predictor may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate naive pixel-level conformal masks for one segmenter; measure object-level empirical coverage; correlate shortfall with per-image error correlation length.
main_risk: Defining the practically relevant coverage event (pixel, object, image) involves choices that affect the headline conclusion.
community_default_belief: Conformal methods are assumption-light, so applying them per pixel yields valid uncertainty for segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Exchangeability across pixels within an image is precisely the assumption dense errors violate most flagrantly.
fastest_falsification: Coverage audit on existing predictions with one calibration split, analysis-only, a day.

one_line: Variance across prompt paraphrases is a stronger per-pixel error predictor for VLM dense prediction than standard confidence or MC dropout.
problem: Dense uncertainty estimation reuses vision-only tools (dropout, ensembles) and ignores the text input as a cheap source of controlled perturbation.
core_hypothesis: Because dense errors are often driven by query-embedding fragility, the pixel-wise variance of predictions across meaning-preserving paraphrases identifies error-prone regions better than logit confidence or dropout variance, at a handful of extra inference passes.
falsifiable_prediction: On error-prediction metrics (AUROC of predicting per-pixel mistakes), paraphrase-variance will beat logit confidence and dropout variance for open-vocabulary segmenters, with the advantage concentrated on text-sensitive classes.
why_important: A practical, architecture-agnostic uncertainty signal that directly exploits the multimodal structure everyone else ignores.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ensembling for accuracy is common; using paraphrase variance as a per-pixel uncertainty estimator with head-to-head comparison may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate paraphrase sets for one benchmark's classes; compute the three uncertainty signals for one model; compare error-prediction AUROC pixel-wise.
main_risk: Paraphrase quality control matters: meaning-shifting paraphrases inflate variance for the wrong reason.
community_default_belief: Uncertainty lives in the vision pathway; text input is a fixed conditioning variable, not a perturbation axis.
why_that_may_be_wrong: In open-vocabulary systems the text embedding is half the computation; ignoring its sensitivity discards half the uncertainty.
fastest_falsification: Paraphrase battery of a handful of variants per class on a benchmark subset, inference plus analysis in a day.

one_line: Abstention thresholds for open-vocabulary dense prediction do not transfer across query vocabularies, making per-vocabulary recalibration a hidden deployment requirement.
problem: Practitioners tune a rejection threshold once and reuse it as the vocabulary evolves, assuming score scales are vocabulary-stable.
core_hypothesis: Similarity-score distributions shift with vocabulary size and composition (via normalization and competition effects), so a threshold tuned on one vocabulary yields wildly different precision-recall operating points on another; the shift is predictable from vocabulary statistics, enabling analytic threshold correction.
falsifiable_prediction: A threshold-transfer matrix across vocabularies will show large operating-point drift correlated with vocabulary size and inter-class text similarity, and an analytic correction using those statistics will recover most of the intended operating point.
why_important: Silent operating-point drift is a production incident generator; an analytic correction is a cheap fix nobody currently ships.
why_possibly_novel: Score-distribution shift is known in retrieval; a threshold-transfer characterization with analytic correction for dense prediction may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one segmenter, tune thresholds on several vocabularies; evaluate all thresholds on all vocabularies; regress drift on vocabulary statistics and test the correction.
main_risk: Architectures differ in scoring normalization, so the correction may need per-family forms.
community_default_belief: A confidence threshold is a model property that persists across reasonable vocabulary changes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The score is a competition outcome among queries, so changing the competitors changes the score scale by construction.
fastest_falsification: Threshold-transfer matrix over three vocabularies, inference-only, a day.

one_line: In LLM-based segmenters, verbalized uncertainty and mask confidence are uncorrelated: the model 'says' it is unsure while emitting high-confidence masks, and vice versa.
problem: Systems that both talk and segment have two uncertainty channels, and consumers implicitly assume they agree.
core_hypothesis: Verbalized confidence (elicited via standard prompts) and mask-head confidence are computed by weakly coupled mechanisms, so their correlation across examples is low and neither dominates as an error predictor; their disagreement itself is an informative error flag.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a benchmark, the correlation between the two channels will be weak, and a disagreement-based flag will predict errors better than either channel alone.
why_important: Interactive systems surface verbalized confidence to users while pipelines consume mask confidence; unnoticed divergence misleads one audience or the other.
why_possibly_novel: Verbalized-calibration studies target QA; the dual-channel consistency analysis for dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one talk-and-segment system, elicit verbalized confidence and record mask confidence per example; measure correlation and the disagreement flag's error-prediction power.
main_risk: Verbalized confidence elicitation is prompt-sensitive, requiring multiple elicitation formats to bound the effect.
community_default_belief: A model's stated uncertainty reflects its internal uncertainty, including about its dense outputs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Verbalization is generated by the language head from text-level features, while mask confidence comes from a separate decoder; nothing in training aligns them.
fastest_falsification: Dual-channel logging on a benchmark subset, one inference pass plus analysis.

one_line: Distance of a query embedding from the pretraining caption manifold predicts per-query dense reliability, giving a deployment-time reliability score with no labels.
problem: There is no accepted way to predict, before seeing outcomes, whether an open-vocabulary system will be reliable for a particular query string.
core_hypothesis: Queries embedding far from the density of pretraining-like caption embeddings (approximated by a public caption corpus) receive systematically worse dense performance, and this text-side distance is a stronger reliability predictor than query length, frequency, or visual difficulty proxies.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many queries, rank correlation between manifold distance and per-query dense performance will be strong and will survive controls for frequency and length.
why_important: A pre-deployment query linter ('this vocabulary entry is unreliable') would prevent entire categories of production failure at negligible cost.
why_possibly_novel: Out-of-distribution scoring in text space exists for NLP; using caption-manifold distance as a dense-reliability predictor may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a density model on caption embeddings from a public corpus; score benchmark class names; correlate with per-class dense metrics for two systems, with frequency and length controls.
main_risk: Public caption corpora may mismatch the model's actual pretraining distribution, attenuating the signal.
community_default_belief: Reliability must be estimated empirically per class from labeled data; there is no free predictor.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text tower's training density is the mechanism behind per-class variation, so measuring it directly should predict the variation it causes.
fastest_falsification: Density scoring plus correlation with published per-class numbers, analysis-only, a day.

one_line: Dense finetuning collapses open-vocabulary alignment early and abruptly rather than gradually, and the collapse is detectable within the first fraction of training.
problem: Finetuning VLMs for segmentation is known to hurt open-vocabulary breadth, but the dynamics (when, how fast, which classes first) are uncharacterized, so mitigations are applied blindly.
core_hypothesis: Vocabulary breadth (zero-shot performance on held-out class sets) drops in a sharp early phase tied to large initial gradient norms, not smoothly over training, so cheap interventions targeted at the first phase (warmup, text-tower freezing, gradient clipping) preserve most breadth at no dense-accuracy cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking held-out vocabulary metrics per training step will show most breadth loss within an early fraction of steps, and early-phase-only interventions will retain most breadth while matching final dense accuracy.
why_important: Turns 'finetuning forgets' folklore into a characterized dynamic with a targeted, low-cost fix.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting curves exist for classification continual learning; step-resolved breadth-collapse analysis for dense VLM finetuning may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Finetune one VLM for segmentation while evaluating held-out vocabulary breadth at dense checkpoint intervals; test early-phase interventions against full-course ones.
main_risk: Breadth metrics are noisy at high checkpoint frequency; efficient proxy evaluations are needed.
community_default_belief: Forgetting accumulates gradually with training steps, so mitigation must span the whole run (joint training, replay).
why_that_may_be_wrong: The largest representation displacement happens when gradients first hit a mismatched head; after re-equilibration, drift may be minor.
fastest_falsification: One finetuning run with dense breadth logging, a few GPU-days, curve shape is visible immediately.

one_line: Adapting only the text tower recovers most of dense-adaptation gains, indicating vision features are already dense-sufficient and the mismatch lives on the language side.
problem: Dense adaptation defaults to modifying the vision pathway (adapters, decoders), assuming visual features are the deficient component.
core_hypothesis: At matched trainable-parameter budgets, text-side-only adaptation (query embeddings, text adapters) achieves a large fraction of the improvement of vision-side adaptation for open-vocabulary dense tasks, because the binding constraint is aligning queries to already-present visual structure.
falsifiable_prediction: A three-way comparison (text-only, vision-only, both) at matched budgets will show text-only capturing most of the achievable gain, with the residual concentrated on boundary quality rather than region identity.
why_important: Text-side adaptation is orders of magnitude cheaper and preserves the vision tower for other tasks; if sufficient, it changes the default recipe.
why_possibly_novel: Adapter-placement studies exist for classification; a budget-matched tower-attribution study for dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the three adapter configurations at matched budgets on one dense benchmark from one frozen VLM; decompose gains into region-identity and boundary components.
main_risk: Results may depend on how much the dense domain's imagery differs from pretraining imagery; both near- and far-domain benchmarks are needed.
community_default_belief: Dense tasks need vision-side capacity: features must change to support pixels, so vision adapters are the essential ingredient.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Frozen-feature probing already shows substantial dense information present; what is missing may be queries that address it, a text-side problem.
fastest_falsification: Matched-budget adapter comparison on one benchmark, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Conclusions that VLMs 'lack localization ability' are probe artifacts: nonparametric decoders extract far more spatial information from frozen features than the linear probes used to write off the models.
problem: Claims about what frozen VLM features contain are mediated by probe choice, and the field's default (linear probing) may systematically understate spatially distributed information.
core_hypothesis: Dense information in VLM features is present but non-linearly and non-locally coded, so retrieval-based and attention-readout decoders reveal substantially better localization than linear probes at matched supervision, changing several published capability conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: Across probe families at matched label budgets, the linear-versus-nonparametric gap will be much larger for VLM features than for dense-supervised features, indicating coding format rather than information absence.
why_important: Capability conclusions steer pretraining investments; artifact-driven pessimism about contrastive pretraining would misdirect the field.
why_possibly_novel: Probe-sensitivity is a known caveat; a systematic probe-family comparison targeted at dense VLM capability claims may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate linear, MLP, retrieval, and attention-readout probes on frozen features of one VLM and one dense-supervised baseline at matched supervision on one benchmark.
main_risk: More powerful probes blur the line between reading out and learning anew; supervision-matched controls and probe-capacity accounting are essential.
community_default_belief: Linear probing is the fair standard for measuring what a representation contains.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Linearity is an arbitrary readout convention; information coded in pairwise feature relations is invisible to it yet cheaply available to retrieval decoders.
fastest_falsification: Retrieval-probe versus linear-probe comparison on cached features, a day.

one_line: Weight-space interpolation between a pretrained VLM and its dense-finetuned child traces a better breadth-versus-density tradeoff than joint multi-task training.
problem: Preserving open-vocabulary breadth while gaining dense skill is usually attempted with joint objectives, which are expensive and unstable to tune.
core_hypothesis: The pretrained and dense-finetuned weights are linearly connected with low loss barriers for both objectives, so post-hoc interpolation offers a free family of tradeoff models, some strictly dominating jointly trained baselines on the breadth-density Pareto front.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the interpolation coefficient will produce a smooth tradeoff curve, and at least one interpolated model will match the joint baseline's dense accuracy while exceeding its breadth.
why_important: A zero-training deployment knob for the field's central tradeoff, plus evidence about the loss-landscape geometry of dense finetuning.
why_possibly_novel: Weight interpolation is established for classification robustness; its systematic evaluation for the dense-breadth tradeoff may be less explored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Finetune one VLM densely; sweep interpolation; evaluate breadth and dense metrics; compare the front against one joint-training baseline at matched compute.
main_risk: Interpolation can fail for finetunes involving added modules (decoders), restricting the method to shared-backbone weights.
community_default_belief: Averaging weights between models trained for different tasks produces broken intermediate models; tradeoffs require joint optimization.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Finetuning from a shared initialization typically stays in a connected low-loss basin, making the linear path usable rather than broken.
fastest_falsification: Interpolation sweep needs only existing checkpoints and evaluation passes, a day.

consolidation.solo_drop_note: Weight-space interpolation between a pretrained CLIP-family model and its finetune to trade zero-shot breadth against target accuracy is an established robust-finetuning technique; porting it to dense finetuning is a technique-task permutation, and the Pareto comparison against joint training does not rescue novelty. main_risk also concedes it breaks when decoders are added.

one_line: Dense adaptation has a qualitatively higher LoRA-rank floor than classification adaptation, revealing that dense transfer is not a low-intrinsic-dimension update.
problem: Low-rank adaptation folklore ('tiny rank suffices') comes from classification and text tasks and is applied to dense adaptation without revalidation.
core_hypothesis: The intrinsic dimensionality of the update needed for dense tasks (which must alter spatial feature structure, not just class boundaries) is fundamentally higher, so dense accuracy saturates at much higher ranks and low-rank runs silently sacrifice boundary quality first.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank sweeps on matched backbones will show classification saturating at small ranks while segmentation continues improving to much larger ranks, with the deficit at low rank concentrated in boundary metrics.
why_important: Wrong rank defaults waste either quality (too low) or memory (too high) across thousands of dense finetuning runs; a task-dependent floor changes practice.
why_possibly_novel: Rank studies exist per task in isolation; a controlled cross-task intrinsic-dimensionality comparison with error-anatomy analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: LoRA rank sweep on one VLM for one classification and one segmentation task, matched optimization budgets; record saturation ranks and boundary-versus-interior error anatomy.
main_risk: Saturation rank depends on layer placement of LoRA, requiring the sweep to cover placement as a secondary factor.
community_default_belief: A small LoRA rank captures almost all of finetuning's benefit regardless of the downstream task.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Class-boundary updates are few-directional; reshaping spatial feature geometry across positions plausibly requires many more directions.
fastest_falsification: Two-task rank sweep at three ranks each, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Distilling a VLM into a dense specialist preserves open-vocabulary breadth better than finetuning the VLM itself, at matched dense accuracy.
problem: The standard route to a dense VLM is finetuning the foundation model, accepting breadth loss as inevitable; distillation as the primary adaptation mechanism is under-considered.
core_hypothesis: Keeping the VLM frozen as a teacher and distilling its patch-text affinities into a student dense architecture avoids touching the alignment that finetuning damages, yielding a better breadth-density operating point than direct finetuning at matched compute.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched dense-benchmark accuracy, the distilled student plus frozen teacher pipeline will retain substantially more held-out-vocabulary performance than the finetuned VLM.
why_important: If distillation dominates, the ecosystem's default adaptation recipe is wrong, and foundation-model weights should be treated as read-only assets.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation for open-vocabulary detection exists; the explicit breadth-preservation comparison against finetuning at matched dense accuracy may be underexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build one distilled student and one finetuned VLM from the same teacher at matched compute; evaluate both on dense accuracy and held-out vocabulary breadth.
main_risk: Students inherit teacher errors and add capacity limits; matched-compute bookkeeping across such different pipelines is delicate.
community_default_belief: Finetuning the foundation model is the strongest adaptation route; distillation is a compression afterthought.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Finetuning pays an unpriced cost (alignment damage) that distillation structurally avoids by never writing to the teacher.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale paired comparison on one benchmark with one held-out vocabulary suite, several GPU-days.

consolidation.mutation_note: As written it is a two-recipe bake-off with delicate matched-compute bookkeeping (conceded in main_risk). Mutate: name the mechanism - which alignment structure finetuning damages and distillation preserves - and pre-register the compute protocol; otherwise it is a permutation comparison.

one_line: Paraphrase robustness collapses before seen-prompt accuracy during dense finetuning, providing an early-warning metric for alignment damage.
problem: Practitioners monitor dense accuracy and perhaps seen-class zero-shot performance during finetuning, missing the earliest signs of text-alignment degradation.
core_hypothesis: Finetuning first destroys the text encoder's local semantic smoothness: performance under paraphrased prompts diverges from canonical-prompt performance well before canonical-prompt metrics move, so paraphrase-gap tracking predicts eventual breadth loss early enough to intervene.
falsifiable_prediction: During dense finetuning, the paraphrase gap (canonical minus paraphrase performance) will widen significantly earlier in training than any decline in canonical zero-shot metrics, and its early slope will predict final breadth loss across runs.
why_important: An early-warning signal makes breadth preservation an engineering practice (stop, freeze, or regularize when the alarm fires) instead of a post-mortem discovery.
why_possibly_novel: Paraphrase robustness is studied statically; its use as a leading indicator during dense finetuning may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument one finetuning run with frequent paraphrase-gap and canonical-metric evaluations; test lead-lag structure; replicate across two learning rates.
main_risk: Paraphrase sets must be validated as meaning-preserving, or the gap measures paraphrase quality instead of model smoothness.
community_default_belief: Monitoring canonical zero-shot metrics during finetuning suffices to detect forgetting when it matters.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Canonical prompts are the last thing to break because finetuning data keeps reinforcing their neighborhood; the semantic neighborhood decays first and invisibly.
fastest_falsification: Add paraphrase evaluation to an existing finetuning script and re-run one training, days.

one_line: Attribute-object binding fails at pixel level in predictable directions: dense models swap attributes between instances rather than failing randomly.
problem: Binding failures ('red cup next to blue book' grounding red to the book) are demonstrated for retrieval and generation, but their dense-output structure is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: When multiple attribute-bearing instances are present, dense predictions exhibit structured swaps (attributes migrate to the more salient or larger instance) rather than uniform noise, and swap direction is predicted by a saliency-asymmetry score computable from the image alone.
falsifiable_prediction: On controlled two-object scenes, binding errors will concentrate in the swap configuration far above chance, and a saliency-asymmetry predictor will forecast swap direction significantly better than random.
why_important: Structured errors are exploitable (post-hoc correction, targeted training) while random errors are not; knowing the structure changes the mitigation strategy.
why_possibly_novel: Binding is a known weakness; the dense-level swap-structure characterization with a predictive image-side score may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or render two-object attribute scenes with controlled saliency; evaluate referring queries per attribute-object combination; tabulate error configurations against the predictor.
main_risk: Rendered scenes may understate real-world binding difficulty or introduce distributional artifacts.
community_default_belief: Compositional failures are diffuse noise reflecting general model weakness, without exploitable structure.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Bag-of-words matching plus saliency weighting mechanically produces directional swaps, so structure is expected, not surprising.
fastest_falsification: A few hundred controlled scenes on one model, one day including rendering.

one_line: Attribute information in VLM features is channel-sparse: a few feature directions carry color/material/state, and causal edits to them flip dense predictions.
problem: Whether attributes are encoded diffusely or in localized feature subspaces determines what interventions (editing, debiasing, binding fixes) are possible, and for dense VLM features it is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Linear attribute directions identified on patch features generalize across categories and positions, and intervening on them (projection removal, direction addition) changes attribute-conditioned dense predictions in the predicted direction without disturbing category predictions, demonstrating sparse, manipulable attribute coding.
falsifiable_prediction: Attribute-direction interventions will flip attribute-conditioned mask assignments in a large fraction of cases while leaving category-only queries nearly unchanged, and the same directions will work across object categories.
why_important: Sparse attribute coding would enable surgical fixes for binding and bias problems without retraining, and inform how compositional queries should be executed.
why_possibly_novel: Concept directions are studied for classification interpretability; causal direction-editing evaluated on dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Learn attribute directions from labeled patches; apply interventions on held-out images; measure attribute-query flip rates and category-query stability for one segmenter.
main_risk: Directions may be entangled with correlated attributes (red with warm lighting), making 'surgical' edits leaky.
community_default_belief: Attribute information in deep features is distributed and only manipulable through finetuning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive alignment to compositional text plausibly factorizes attributes into near-linear structure, as it does for word embeddings.
fastest_falsification: Direction fitting and intervention on cached features, one day.

one_line: Part-whole queries fail asymmetrically: 'the wheel of the car' returns whole-car masks, and part grounding quality is predicted by the part's caption-mention rate, not its visual size.
problem: Part segmentation through language is increasingly demanded (robotics affordances, editing), but VLM behavior on part queries is uncharacterized beyond anecdote.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictions for part queries are biased toward the containing whole, with the bias strength inversely related to how often the part is independently captioned in web text; frequently captioned parts (face, wheel) ground well while rarely captioned parts (hinge, cuff) collapse to wholes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a part-query battery, whole-mask leakage will correlate negatively with caption-mention frequency of the part word, controlling for part pixel area.
why_important: Parts are where dense language interfaces meet manipulation and editing; knowing which parts are queryable and why enables vocabulary design and targeted data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Part segmentation datasets exist; the caption-frequency explanation of part-query failure in VLM systems may be untested; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a part-query battery over a part-annotated dataset; measure whole-leakage per part; regress on caption frequency and area.
main_risk: Part annotations vary in granularity conventions across datasets, complicating leakage measurement.
community_default_belief: Part queries are just smaller-object queries; performance tracks visual difficulty of the part.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A part that is never a caption subject has no text anchor of its own, making it invisible to text-driven grounding regardless of visual clarity.
fastest_falsification: Part battery on one part-annotated benchmark, inference plus regression, a day.

one_line: Training with programmatically recombined captions improves pixel-level binding but measurably degrades rare-noun grounding, a compositionality-versus-coverage tradeoff nobody reports.
problem: Compositional augmentation (shuffling attributes and objects into new captions) is a popular fix for binding, evaluated only on binding metrics.
core_hypothesis: Recombined captions inject distributional noise for rare nouns (attaching them to atypical contexts), so binding gains come with a hidden tax on rare-vocabulary dense performance; the tradeoff is tunable by restricting recombination to frequent nouns.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with aggressive recombination will improve on binding batteries while dropping on rare-class dense metrics relative to identically budgeted baselines, and frequency-restricted recombination will recover most of the drop.
why_important: Data-augmentation recipes propagate rapidly; an unreported side effect on the open-vocabulary tail would silently damage exactly what these models are prized for.
why_possibly_novel: Compositional augmentation is studied for binding gains; its interaction with vocabulary-tail performance may be unexamined; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with none/full/frequency-restricted recombination; evaluate binding and frequency-stratified dense metrics.
main_risk: The effect may depend on augmentation ratio, requiring a sweep to characterize rather than a single comparison.
community_default_belief: Compositional augmentation is a free lunch: it fixes binding without costing anything measurable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Any augmentation reshapes the training distribution; for tail nouns whose few examples are their entire signal, reshaping is expensive.
fastest_falsification: Two small matched training runs with the stratified evaluation suite, several GPU-days.

one_line: A dense analogue of minimal-pair compositional benchmarks will show VLM dense systems near chance on composition even when their global image-text matching succeeds.
problem: Minimal-pair compositional evaluation exists for retrieval, but dense prediction lacks an equivalent, so compositional claims about grounded systems rest on unsuitable aggregate metrics.
core_hypothesis: On minimal pairs distinguishable only by composition (same objects and attributes, different binding or relation), dense systems will assign masks at near-chance consistency with the intended reading, and their dense compositional score will be uncorrelated with their retrieval-level compositional score, showing the two abilities dissociate.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense minimal-pair accuracy will hover near chance for most systems, and cross-system correlation between dense and retrieval compositional scores will be weak.
why_important: It gives the field a targeted instrument for measuring grounded compositionality, separating it from image-level matching heuristics.
why_possibly_novel: Retrieval minimal-pair benchmarks are established; a dense-output minimal-pair protocol with the dissociation analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a modest dense minimal-pair suite from staged photos or renders; evaluate several systems on dense and retrieval versions; test the correlation.
main_risk: Constructing truly minimal visual pairs is laborious, and residual low-level differences can leak the answer.
community_default_belief: Grounded systems that pass retrieval compositional tests will also compose correctly at pixel level, since grounding is stricter.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Retrieval success can come from global co-occurrence heuristics that never resolve which pixels bind to which words; strictness is assumed, not demonstrated.
fastest_falsification: A pilot suite of a few dozen pairs on two systems, days including staging.

one_line: Non-English prompts degrade dense prediction disproportionately relative to classification, because pixel-level matching amplifies text-embedding quality differences.
problem: Multilingual capability of VLMs is certified on classification or retrieval, and dense multilingual behavior is assumed to follow, without measurement.
core_hypothesis: Dense tasks compound per-query embedding error across thousands of pixel decisions, so the multilingual performance gap (relative to English) will be systematically larger for segmentation/detection than for classification on matched concepts, and largest for low-resource languages.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring English-relative performance ratios per language, dense tasks will show consistently lower ratios than classification for the same model and concepts, with the deficit ordered by language resource level.
why_important: Global deployments assume multilingual parity certified at image level; a dense-specific multilingual tax would mislead exactly the users least able to debug it.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual VLM audits exist for retrieval/classification; the dense-versus-global degradation comparison may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Translate one benchmark's class names into several languages of varying resource level; evaluate one multilingual VLM on classification and segmentation with matched vocabularies; compare degradation ratios.
main_risk: Translation quality itself varies by language, requiring native-speaker validation of class-name translations.
community_default_belief: A multilingual text tower gives language-independent dense capability; the vision side does the spatial work.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dense outputs are equilibria of many small text-vision comparisons, so small per-comparison embedding degradations accumulate rather than average out.
fastest_falsification: Two-language pilot (one high-resource, one low-resource) on one benchmark, inference-only, a day.

one_line: For non-photographic imagery (thermal, ultrasound, sketches), VLM dense failure is vision-encoder-side, not text-side, and the attribution is measurable by asymmetric substitution.
problem: When VLM dense prediction fails on non-photographic modalities, pipelines cannot tell whether to fix the vision encoder, the text prompts, or both.
core_hypothesis: Substituting a modality-adapted vision encoder (while keeping original text queries) recovers far more dense performance than any text-side intervention (rewriting, ensembling) on the frozen original encoder, establishing that the modality gap lives almost entirely in vision feature extraction.
falsifiable_prediction: In a substitution matrix (original/adapted vision crossed with original/optimized text), the vision axis will explain the large majority of performance variance on non-photographic dense benchmarks.
why_important: It directs scarce adaptation budgets to the right tower and quantifies a decomposition tool reusable across modalities.
why_possibly_novel: Modality-gap studies exist at embedding level; the causal substitution-matrix attribution for dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble the two-by-two substitution matrix for one thermal or sketch dense benchmark; measure variance explained by each axis.
main_risk: Building a fairly 'adapted' vision encoder without leaking dense supervision requires discipline; self-supervised adaptation on unlabeled target imagery is the clean choice.
community_default_belief: Both towers degrade together off-distribution, so full-pipeline finetuning is the necessary response.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Class names for these domains (person, tumor, chair) are ordinary words the text tower handles fine; only the pixels are alien.
fastest_falsification: Text-side-optimization-only versus vision-swap-only comparison on one benchmark, days.

one_line: Open-vocabulary dense performance varies geographically for the same class, tracking the geographic distribution of captioned imagery rather than visual difficulty.
problem: Classes like 'house', 'market', or 'stove' look different across regions, and dense models trained on geographically skewed captions may ground the concept's dominant-region appearance only.
core_hypothesis: Per-region dense performance for common classes correlates with estimated regional representation in caption corpora, after controlling for image quality and scene clutter, revealing a geographic fairness gap specific to the open-vocabulary mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: On geographically annotated imagery, region-stratified dense metrics will show gaps aligned with corpus representation estimates, larger for culturally variable classes than for globally uniform ones (car versus stove).
why_important: Dense systems are deployed globally (mapping, humanitarian response); a geographic performance gradient is a concrete fairness and reliability issue.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic bias is documented for classification; the dense-prediction extension with corpus-representation correlation may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one open-vocabulary segmenter on a geographically diverse annotated set; stratify by region and class cultural-variability; correlate with representation proxies.
main_risk: Region-stratified dense annotations are scarce; may require targeted annotation of an existing geo-diverse image collection.
community_default_belief: A class is a class: open-vocabulary models generalize across appearance variation within a category.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text anchor is shared, but the visual cluster it points to is the caption-weighted average, which is geographically skewed.
fastest_falsification: Region-stratified evaluation on any available geo-tagged annotated subset, analysis within days.

one_line: In unfamiliar visual domains, VLM dense grounding falls back to texture words over shape words, re-expressing the texture bias at the language-grounding level.
problem: When domain shift breaks learned category associations, it is unknown which linguistic cues (shape terms versus texture/material terms) retain grounding power.
core_hypothesis: Out of distribution, queries built from texture and material words will localize regions substantially better than queries built from shape words, mirroring the classic texture bias but now measurable through the language interface, and implying that OOD vocabulary design should prefer material descriptions.
falsifiable_prediction: On cue-conflict and OOD dense probes, texture-word queries will outperform shape-word queries by a margin much larger than their in-domain difference.
why_important: It yields immediately actionable vocabulary-design guidance for OOD deployments and connects the texture-bias literature to the grounding interface.
why_possibly_novel: Texture bias is established for classification; its manifestation in text-query dense grounding may be uncharted; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched shape-word and texture-word query sets for objects in an OOD domain; compare dense localization quality per query type in and out of domain.
main_risk: Shape and texture words differ in frequency and specificity; matching query informativeness across the two sets is the hard part.
community_default_belief: Shape is the more robust cue, so shape-based descriptions should generalize better out of domain.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The vision tower's features may encode texture more transferably than shape, making the text anchor's robustness irrelevant if the visual cluster it addresses dissolves.
fastest_falsification: Matched query battery on one OOD dense dataset, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Code-switched prompts (mixed-language queries) break dense grounding disproportionately, exposing tokenizer-level fragility invisible in single-language evaluations.
problem: Real multilingual users mix languages within queries ('segment the coche on the left'), a regime absent from all dense evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Code-switching fragments tokenization and pushes query embeddings off both languages' manifolds, so dense performance under code-switched prompts falls below the worse of the two single-language conditions, rather than between them as a smooth-interpolation view would predict.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense metrics under code-switched prompts will be significantly below the minimum of the corresponding single-language conditions, and the drop will correlate with tokenization fragmentation measures of the mixed query.
why_important: Sub-minimum behavior means multilingual certification via per-language testing overstates real-world robustness for the many users who code-switch naturally.
why_possibly_novel: Code-switching is studied in NLP; its effect on dense visual grounding may be unexamined; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct code-switched variants of referring expressions in two language pairs; evaluate one multilingual dense system against both single-language baselines; test the sub-minimum prediction.
main_risk: Naturalistic code-switching follows grammatical patterns; artificial mixtures may exaggerate the effect, so templates need native-speaker construction.
community_default_belief: A multilingual model's performance on mixed input interpolates between its single-language performances.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interpolation assumes the mixture stays on the training distribution; code-switched text may be off-manifold for caption-trained encoders, making the mixture worse than its parts.
fastest_falsification: Small code-switched battery for one language pair, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Referring-segmentation benchmarks are largely solvable from the head noun plus saliency, so modifier-ablated evaluation is needed to measure actual referring ability.
problem: High benchmark scores are read as evidence of expression understanding, but most benchmark expressions may be resolvable without reading past the head noun.
core_hypothesis: Ablating all modifiers from referring expressions (keeping only the head noun) preserves the large majority of benchmark accuracy for top systems, meaning the benchmarks mostly test open-vocabulary object detection, and true referring skill is concentrated in (and measurable on) the small expression subset where ablation hurts.
falsifiable_prediction: Head-noun-only accuracy will be a large fraction of full-expression accuracy for several top systems, and cross-model ranking on the ablation-sensitive subset will differ from the full-benchmark ranking.
why_important: If the metric mostly measures detection, progress claims about language understanding in grounding are misdirected, and the sensitive subset becomes the real benchmark.
why_possibly_novel: Ablation analyses exist in pockets; using ablation sensitivity to redefine the effective benchmark and re-rank systems may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three systems on one referring benchmark with full and head-noun-only expressions; compute preservation ratios and subset re-rankings.
main_risk: Automatic head-noun extraction errors could contaminate the ablation; manual verification on a sample is needed.
community_default_belief: Referring benchmarks measure the integration of language constraints with visual grounding.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dataset construction favored unambiguous referents, which mechanically makes modifiers redundant and the language component optional.
fastest_falsification: Head-noun ablation on one system, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Correction turns ('no, the other one') fail in dense VLM systems because nothing represents the rejected hypothesis, and a minimal exclusion memory fixes a large fraction of failures.
problem: Interactive segmentation with language assumes users can repair errors conversationally, but architectures process each turn statelessly at the grounding level.
core_hypothesis: On correction turns, current systems re-predict their first choice at high rates (having no representation of 'not that one'), and augmenting inference with an explicit exclusion constraint (suppress the previously returned instance) recovers most correction-turn failures without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured repeat-error rate on correction turns will be far above chance, and the exclusion-augmented variant will cut it dramatically while leaving first-turn behavior unchanged.
why_important: Correction is the core interaction loop of practical dense tools; a stateless loop that repeats its mistake is unusable regardless of first-shot accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive segmentation studies clicks extensively; language-correction statefulness and the minimal exclusion fix may be unexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a two-turn protocol from existing benchmarks (first query, then a templated correction); measure repeat rates for two systems with and without exclusion augmentation.
main_risk: Templated corrections may not represent natural correction language, though the stateless failure mode should be phrasing-independent.
community_default_belief: Stronger language models in the loop will handle dialog phenomena like corrections without architectural changes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Understanding the correction linguistically does not help if the grounding pathway has no channel to receive and apply an exclusion.
fastest_falsification: Two-turn repeat-rate measurement on one system, one day.

consolidation.mutation_note: The correction-turn statelessness measurement (repeat rate under 'no, the other one') is cheap and genuinely diagnostic; the exclusion-memory fix is the expected trivial intervention. Mutate: lead with the failure law, demote the fix to validation.

one_line: Beyond their information content, longer referring expressions actively hurt dense grounding: added words dilute attention rather than adding constraints.
problem: Users and prompt engineers assume more descriptive expressions help the model; the marginal effect of expression length at fixed information content is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed referent and fixed disambiguating information, padding expressions with redundant true details reduces grounding accuracy monotonically, because pooled or cross-attended text representations dilute the discriminative tokens; the effect is stronger in contrastive-tower systems than LLM-decoder systems.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy versus expression length at matched information content will show a negative slope, steeper for pooled-text architectures, and token-attribution analysis will show discriminative-token weight shrinking as length grows.
why_important: It contradicts universal prompt-writing advice for grounding tasks and gives users a concrete instruction: say less, but say the distinguishing thing.
why_possibly_novel: Length effects are studied for retrieval and LLM prompts; a controlled information-matched length study for dense grounding may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct expression sets per referent sweeping length with verified-constant disambiguating content; evaluate two architecture families; fit the length-accuracy slope.
main_risk: Holding information content truly constant while varying length is linguistically delicate and needs human validation.
community_default_belief: Richer, longer descriptions give grounding models more to work with and can only help disambiguation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fixed-capacity query representations must share mass across tokens, so every redundant word is paid for by the words that mattered.
fastest_falsification: Length-sweep battery for a few dozen referents on one system, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Detection recall for small objects drops as a step function of object size measured in patches, not a smooth function of size in pixels, creating hidden size cliffs set by preprocessing policy.
problem: Small-object failure is reported as a smooth degradation with pixel area, but patch tokenization quantizes the information budget per object, and resize policies silently move objects across integer-patch thresholds.
core_hypothesis: Per-object failure probability in transformer detectors has discontinuities at integer patch-count boundaries (especially below roughly 2x2 patches), so the operative variable is patches-per-object, and resize policy is a hidden failure knob.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-binning recall by patches-per-object instead of pixel area will reveal step-like transitions absent in the pixel-area curve, and changing input resolution will shift the failure cliff in exact proportion to the patch-size change.
why_important: It reframes small-object failure as a controllable preprocessing decision rather than a capability gap, with direct consequences for deployment resolution choices in surveillance, aerial, and medical imaging.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object analyses bin by absolute pixel area (COCO conventions); an explicit patches-per-object failure law across resolutions appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one ViT-backbone detector on COCO at three input resolutions, compute per-object recall binned by patches-per-object, and test for alignment of curves across resolutions versus alignment in pixel-area space.
main_risk: Feature pyramids and multi-scale heads may smear the quantization enough that no sharp step survives aggregation.
community_default_belief: Small-object failure is a smooth resolution/capacity problem best fixed by higher-resolution inputs or specialized small-object modules.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The tokenizer imposes a hard floor on information per object; below one patch, an object contributes no dedicated token, which is a discrete regime change, not a gradual one.
fastest_falsification: Few hours: take an off-the-shelf DETR variant, sweep synthetic images with one object of controlled size, and plot detection probability versus patches-per-object.

one_line: Fixed-square-input models fail disproportionately on objects whose apparent aspect ratio is inverted or extremized by anisotropic resize of extreme-aspect images (panoramas, documents, strips).
problem: Most pipelines squash arbitrary images into fixed squares; for extreme-aspect inputs this deforms objects far outside the shape distribution seen in training crops, but failures are attributed to content rather than the resize geometry.
core_hypothesis: Failure probability on extreme-aspect images is predicted primarily by the per-object deformation factor introduced by the resize, and is largely removed by aspect-preserving tiling, showing the failure is a preprocessing geometry artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: For matched objects, error rate will rise monotonically with resize-induced aspect distortion, and re-evaluating with padded aspect-preserving inputs will recover most of the gap while content-matched controls stay unchanged.
why_important: Panoramic, document, whole-slide, and satellite strip imagery are growing deployment domains where silent squashing may dominate the error budget.
why_possibly_novel: Letterbox-versus-stretch is folklore in detection engineering, but a quantitative failure law linking per-object deformation factor to error in foundation models appears unpublished (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a controlled set by cropping standard images to varying aspect ratios, run a VLM or detector under stretch versus letterbox preprocessing, and regress error on the deformation factor.
main_risk: Letterboxing shrinks objects, trading deformation error for resolution error, so the two conditions must be equated for effective object size.
community_default_belief: Modern models trained with aggressive augmentation are robust to moderate aspect distortion, and preprocessing choice is a minor implementation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Augmentation covers modest distortions, but extreme-aspect inputs create deformations several times larger than any training augmentation, putting objects off the shape manifold.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: run one open detector on the same panoramas under stretch versus letterbox and compare per-object recall.

one_line: When ViTs run at resolutions unseen in training, positional-embedding interpolation concentrates errors in specific spatial zones (borders and corners) independent of image content.
problem: Resolution transfer via positional embedding interpolation is treated as solved plumbing, but interpolation distorts the embedding geometry non-uniformly across the grid, and nobody maps where in the image the resulting errors land.
core_hypothesis: Dense-prediction error at transfer resolutions has a content-independent spatial signature determined by the positional embedding interpolation scheme, with error mass concentrated where interpolation distortion is largest.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaging error maps over many images at a transfer resolution will reveal a stable spatial pattern that (a) disappears at the native resolution, (b) changes shape when the interpolation scheme is swapped, and (c) is uncorrelated with average content statistics at those locations.
why_important: High-resolution inference of pretrained ViTs is standard practice; a systematic spatial error signature would bias any application where object position correlates with image position (driving, retail shelves, radiology).
why_possibly_novel: Resolution transfer accuracy is studied in aggregate, but spatially resolved, content-controlled error maps attributing failure to interpolation geometry appear missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a ViT segmenter at native and 2x resolution on a dataset with uniform spatial label statistics, compute mean per-position error maps, and compare bicubic versus alternative positional interpolation.
main_risk: Spatial label statistics of real datasets are non-uniform (center bias), which can masquerade as a positional error signature unless carefully controlled.
community_default_belief: Positional embedding interpolation degrades performance mildly and uniformly, and fine-tuning at the target resolution fixes it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interpolation error is mathematically non-uniform across the grid (worst where embedding curvature is high), so the degradation should be spatially structured, not uniform.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: mean error maps for one model at two resolutions on a synthetic dataset with objects placed uniformly at random.

one_line: High-norm artifact/register tokens in DINO-family backbones spatially co-locate with a specific class of downstream segmentation leaks into textureless background.
problem: Artifact tokens (high-norm patch tokens repurposed as computation scratchpads) are known to exist in large ViTs, but no one has tied them causally to a characterizable downstream failure mode in dense prediction.
core_hypothesis: Patches hosting artifact tokens carry corrupted local features, so downstream segmentation heads systematically leak masks into (or hallucinate structure within) the textureless regions where artifact tokens preferentially appear.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask leakage events into low-texture background will co-occur with high-norm token locations far above chance, and backbones retrained with register tokens will show a measurable reduction of exactly this leak type while other error types stay flat.
why_important: It would establish a direct mechanistic chain from a known representation pathology to a nameable deployment failure, making the failure predictable from the backbone alone before any head is trained.
why_possibly_novel: Register tokens were motivated by attention map cleanliness and probing accuracy; a causal link to a specific segmentation failure taxonomy appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run DINOv2 with and without registers under identical linear segmentation heads, detect high-norm token positions per image, and measure conditional leak rates given artifact presence in the region.
main_risk: Artifact token positions and textureless regions are correlated by construction, so establishing causality requires the register-token counterfactual, not just co-occurrence.
community_default_belief: Artifact tokens are a representational curiosity that registers already fixed, with no remaining consequence for practical dense prediction.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most deployed checkpoints and derived products still use register-free backbones, and the downstream error attribution was never made, so the practical footprint is unknown rather than absent.
fastest_falsification: One day: overlay high-norm token maps on failure masks for 200 images from a frozen DINOv2 + linear head and compute the conditional error lift.

one_line: Thin-structure segmentation failure is governed by the structure's orientation relative to the sampling grid (aliasing angle), not primarily by its width.
problem: Wires, poles, and cracks are lumped into a 'thin structures are hard' story indexed by width, ignoring that discrete grids alias oblique thin structures far more than axis-aligned ones of the same width.
core_hypothesis: For fixed physical width, per-pixel recall on thin structures is a periodic function of orientation angle modulo 90 degrees, with minima at angles of maximal aliasing, and this angle effect exceeds the width effect over a practically relevant range.
falsifiable_prediction: Rotating the same thin-structure scenes in fine angular steps will produce recall oscillations with extrema at grid-aligned versus maximally-oblique angles, and the oscillation will shrink when inputs are pre-blurred to satisfy sampling limits.
why_important: Powerline detection for drones, crack detection for infrastructure, and catheter/guidewire segmentation in interventional imaging all involve thin oblique structures where an orientation-dependent failure law changes acquisition and augmentation strategy.
why_possibly_novel: Thin-structure difficulty is usually attributed to class imbalance and receptive fields; a grid-aliasing orientation law for modern segmenters appears uncharacterized (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render synthetic scenes with thin structures at controlled widths and angles, evaluate a public segmenter, and fit recall as a function of angle and width to compare effect sizes.
main_risk: Real training data has non-uniform orientation statistics (verticals and horizontals dominate), confounding aliasing effects with orientation frequency effects; synthetic control and frequency-matched analysis are needed to separate them.
community_default_belief: Thin structure failure is a resolution and class-imbalance problem, mitigated by higher input resolution and boundary-aware losses.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Higher resolution does not remove aliasing at fixed width-to-pixel ratios, and the angle dependence predicted by sampling theory is invisible to width-indexed evaluations.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: rotate 20 powerline images in 5-degree steps through a segmenter and plot wire recall versus angle.

one_line: Windowed-attention backbones (Swin-like) localize object boundaries systematically worse when those boundaries coincide with attention-window seams.
problem: Window partitioning creates fixed internal seams where cross-window information flow is delayed by shifted-window mechanics, but boundary-quality evaluations never condition on seam proximity.
core_hypothesis: Boundary localization error is elevated in a band around window seams, and the elevation persists (attenuated) through shifted-window schemes, making window geometry a content-independent predictor of where a model fails.
falsifiable_prediction: Conditioning boundary F-score on distance-to-nearest-window-seam will show a dip at seams for windowed backbones and no such dip for global-attention backbones evaluated on the same images.
why_important: Windowed attention is the default efficiency choice in high-resolution dense prediction; a seam-failure law identifies a silent, spatially structured bias in exactly the deployments that choose windowed models for resolution.
why_possibly_novel: Window artifacts are discussed for generation and restoration models, but a conditioned failure analysis for segmentation/detection boundary quality appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate Swin-based and ViT-based segmenters of comparable mIoU on the same dataset, compute error as a function of pixel distance to seam locations, and compare profiles.
main_risk: Shifted windows alternate seam positions across blocks, potentially averaging the effect below detection threshold at the output.
community_default_belief: Shifted-window designs fully restore cross-window information flow, so window partitioning has no spatially localized accuracy cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shifting restores connectivity but not symmetry: pixels near seams still receive their context with more indirection than window-center pixels, and small asymmetries compound over depth.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: seam-distance-conditioned boundary error for one Swin segmenter versus one ViT segmenter on 500 images.

one_line: Vision models trained on web-scale data treat JPEG compression artifacts as part of natural image statistics, so pristine uncompressed imagery (medical, RAW, professional) is out-of-distribution and fails in characteristic ways.
problem: Robustness work asks how models degrade as compression increases, but almost all training images are already compressed, so the unexamined direction is degradation as compression decreases below the training distribution's floor.
core_hypothesis: Model features partially entrain on block-DCT artifact statistics; on artifact-free images, texture-dependent predictions shift systematically, and lightly re-compressing pristine images toward the training distribution's typical quality improves accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: For models trained on web data, accuracy on never-compressed images will increase when those images are JPEG-compressed to the training corpus's modal quality level, a direction of improvement impossible under the 'compression only hurts' assumption.
why_important: Medical imaging, scientific instruments, and RAW industrial cameras produce exactly the artifact-free inputs where an inverted compression effect would matter and would be invisible to standard corruption benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness is well studied in the degradation direction; the hypothesis that absence of compression is itself a distribution shift appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble RAW-derived never-compressed image sets with labels, evaluate CLIP/DINO-probe classifiers at several added JPEG quality levels, and test for a non-monotic accuracy curve peaking at web-typical quality.
main_risk: Truly never-compressed labeled datasets are scarce, and camera ISP differences between RAW sets and web images confound the compression variable.
community_default_belief: Image quality and model accuracy are monotonically related: cleaner input is always equal or better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models fit the distribution they see, not an idealized clean-image manifold; if the training mode is quality-75 JPEG, that is the in-distribution point, and 'cleaner' is off-distribution.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: take RAW photos, decode without compression, classify with CLIP zero-shot at qualities {100, 95, 85, 75, 60}, and check whether accuracy peaks strictly below 100.

one_line: Silent mismatches between train-time and inference-time resize interpolation kernels (bilinear vs bicubic vs area, antialias flags) cause reproducible small-object and texture failures that get misattributed to domain shift.
problem: Different libraries and even versions of the same library implement resizing differently; deployments routinely mix them, and failure analyses never include the interpolation kernel as a variable.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of reported cross-deployment accuracy variance for the same checkpoint is caused by interpolation-kernel mismatch, with damage concentrated in high-frequency content (small objects, textures, thin edges).
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating one frozen model on one dataset under the matrix of common resize implementations will show accuracy spreads that exceed typical reported domain-shift effects for small-object strata, and matching the training kernel will consistently sit at the top of the spread.
why_important: This is a zero-parameter fix hiding inside the error budget of countless deployments, and it contaminates the failure-mining literature by injecting pipeline failures into content-failure taxonomies.
why_possibly_novel: Antialias-flag discrepancies are known engineering folklore, but a quantified failure attribution study separating kernel mismatch from genuine domain shift appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one checkpoint and dataset; evaluate under PIL/OpenCV/torchvision resize variants with and without antialiasing; stratify deltas by object size and spectral content; compare the spread against a genuine domain-shift baseline.
main_risk: Effect size may be large only for a minority of models (those trained without resize augmentation diversity), limiting the headline claim.
community_default_belief: Resize implementation is a negligible detail; models trained with augmentation are insensitive to interpolation differences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Augmentation diversity in scale does not imply diversity in kernel; most training stacks use exactly one kernel, so kernel signature is a constant of training that inference silently violates.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: run one detector on COCO val with torchvision antialias on versus off and compare small-object AP.

one_line: A measurable share of mined 'model failures' are actually silent metadata mishandling (EXIF rotation, embedded ICC color profiles) upstream of the model, contaminating failure taxonomies.
problem: Failure-mining pipelines collect hard cases from deployment logs without verifying that the pixel array the model saw matches the image a human reviewer sees, so orientation and color-profile bugs masquerade as content failures.
core_hypothesis: Auditing mined failure sets for metadata-handling divergence between the serving pipeline and the review pipeline will reclaim a nontrivial fraction of cases as pipeline artifacts, and this fraction is systematically higher for mobile-captured imagery.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running mined failure cases through a metadata-normalized pipeline will flip a measurable percentage of them to correct predictions, and flipped cases will be enriched in portrait-orientation and wide-gamut captures.
why_important: If failure taxonomies are contaminated with pipeline bugs, downstream investments (targeted data collection, fine-tuning) are aimed at phantom failure modes, wasting the entire remediation budget for those cases.
why_possibly_novel: EXIF bugs are known individually, but quantifying their share of mined failure corpora and their effect on failure taxonomy validity appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a public hard-case collection or generate one from a deployment-like pipeline, diff model-input pixels against correctly decoded pixels for every case, and measure the prediction flip rate after normalization.
main_risk: Well-engineered pipelines may show near-zero contamination, making the finding a statement about pipeline maturity rather than a universal effect.
community_default_belief: Decoding is trivially correct everywhere, so hard-case corpora reflect genuine model limitations.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Orientation and color-management behavior differs across decoding libraries and versions by default, and failure mining pipelines are rarely audited at the pixel level against the serving path.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: for one mined failure set, compare md5 of pixels between the mining decode path and a reference decode path and re-predict any divergent cases.

one_line: Vision models silently assume sRGB; wide-gamut and HDR content gets clipped or misencoded at ingestion, producing hue-specific failures concentrated in highly saturated regions.
problem: Cameras and displays increasingly produce Display-P3/HDR content, but training corpora and preprocessing assume sRGB, and no failure benchmark stratifies performance by color gamut of source content.
core_hypothesis: Predictions on objects whose identity depends on saturated color (produce ripeness, signage, safety markings, skin tones under saturated lighting) degrade systematically for wide-gamut sources, with error concentrated in pixels outside the sRGB gamut.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy on color-critical classes will be lower for wide-gamut captures than for sRGB captures of the same scenes, and correct gamut mapping (instead of naive clipping) at ingestion will recover a measurable share of the gap.
why_important: The installed base of wide-gamut capture devices is growing fast, so this is a failure mode whose prevalence increases over time while remaining invisible to legacy benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Color robustness work uses hue/saturation jitter within sRGB; gamut mismatch as a distribution shift with a spatially localizable failure signature appears unstudied (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture paired P3 and sRGB photos of color-critical scenes, run standard classifiers/detectors under naive versus color-managed ingestion, and compare per-class errors and their spatial overlap with out-of-gamut pixel masks.
main_risk: For most everyday classes, color is not the discriminative feature, so the effect may be confined to a small class subset and easy to dismiss as niche.
community_default_belief: Color space handling is a solved rendering concern irrelevant to recognition robustness.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Clipping is a nonlinear, content-dependent corruption applied exactly where color information is most extreme, which is where color-critical decisions live.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: photograph saturated objects in P3 and sRGB, ingest both naively into CLIP, and compare zero-shot label rankings.

one_line: Legacy ImageNet normalization constants bias modern models at luminance extremes: systematic failure concentration in very dark and very bright images that tracks the mismatch between corpus statistics and hardcoded mean/std.
problem: Nearly every pipeline hardcodes 2012-era ImageNet channel means/stds, though modern web corpora and deployment feeds (night footage, HDR scenes) have different statistics; nobody treats the normalization constants as a failure hypothesis.
core_hypothesis: Error rates conditioned on image luminance percentile rise disproportionately at the tails, and part of that rise is attributable to normalization mismatch rather than information loss, since re-calibrating normalization to the deployment corpus reduces tail error without retraining the backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: Swapping normalization constants to deployment-corpus statistics (a two-parameter-per-channel change) will improve accuracy specifically in the top and bottom luminance deciles with negligible movement in the middle deciles.
why_important: Night-time and backlit scenes are core failure regimes in driving and security; if part of that failure is a six-number configuration issue, it is the cheapest robustness gain available.
why_possibly_novel: Normalization constants are treated as inert boilerplate; a luminance-tail failure attribution study appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a frozen classifier on a luminance-stratified evaluation set under original versus corpus-matched normalization and compare stratified error deltas.
main_risk: Batch-norm-free and layer-norm architectures may be nearly invariant to affine input shifts, nullifying the effect for modern backbones.
community_default_belief: Input normalization constants have no measurable effect as long as they match training; luminance-tail failures are pure information-loss problems.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Matching training is exactly the issue: training-time constants encode a corpus that differs from deployment feeds, and first-layer nonlinearities make the mismatch content-dependent rather than a harmless affine shift.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: stratify ImageNet-val-night-style images by luminance, evaluate a ResNet and a ViT under two normalization settings, compare tail deltas.

one_line: Segmenters trained on composited product/stock imagery learn 'uniform white equals background,' causing systematic failure on genuinely white or high-key objects and scenes.
problem: A large slice of web training imagery is studio compositing on synthetic white; the compositing convention creates a spurious feature (uniform white background) that models can exploit, but its failure footprint on natural white content is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Foreground/background decisions near uniform bright regions are driven partly by the compositing shortcut, so white objects on white scenes (snow, lab equipment, linens, appliances) suffer characteristic mask erosion that vanishes when the same shapes are recolored.
falsifiable_prediction: Recoloring white objects to non-white in controlled scenes will improve their segmentation quality significantly more than the same recoloring applied to non-white objects, and mask erosion will concentrate on the white-to-white contact boundary.
why_important: Medical, laboratory, and winter-outdoor domains are full of white-on-white content, and the shortcut hypothesis predicts precisely where masks silently erode in those domains.
why_possibly_novel: Background shortcuts are studied for classification context bias; a compositing-driven white-background shortcut in segmentation with a targeted counterfactual appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired scenes (white and recolored versions of the same object via physical repaint or controlled relighting/synthesis), run open-vocabulary segmenters, and compare boundary F on contact edges.
main_risk: Recoloring interventions change more than the shortcut variable (contrast, shading cues), so the counterfactual must be constructed carefully to isolate the convention effect.
community_default_belief: Web-scale diversity washes out any single compositing convention; low contrast, not learned convention, explains white-on-white difficulty.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Low contrast alone predicts symmetric difficulty for all iso-contrast pairs, but the hypothesis predicts an asymmetry specific to white, which contrast explanations cannot produce.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: segment white versus gray versions of the same objects at matched contrast against matched backgrounds and test for a white-specific penalty.

one_line: Frames extracted from compressed video (chroma subsampling, deinterlacing, keyframe artifacts) form a distinct sub-domain in training corpora, and models inherit failure modes tied to those artifacts' presence or absence.
problem: Video-sourced frames are a growing share of pretraining data, carrying 4:2:0 chroma resolution and codec-specific texture; the resulting entrainment and its failure footprint on either side (video-artifact vs pristine content) are uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Models learn partially separate processing regimes for video-artifact and photographic content, so color-boundary-critical predictions (small colored objects, chroma-defined edges) degrade on whichever side is rarer in training, and artifact-matched preprocessing shifts accuracy predictably.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying 4:2:0 chroma subsampling to pristine photos will change model predictions on chroma-defined structures in a consistent direction, and the direction will reverse between models pretrained mostly on photos versus mostly on video frames.
why_important: As video becomes the dominant pretraining source, chroma-artifact entrainment could become a first-order silent covariate affecting all downstream color-sensitive tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Codec robustness exists as corruption benchmarks, but the framing of chroma subsampling as a training-corpus covariate with directional failure predictions appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build chroma-critical test cases (small saturated objects on luminance-matched backgrounds), evaluate photo-heavy and video-heavy pretrained models under 4:4:4 versus 4:2:0 inputs, and compare deltas.
main_risk: Pretraining data composition for public models is imperfectly documented, weakening the corpus-composition side of the prediction.
community_default_belief: Chroma subsampling is perceptually negligible and therefore negligible for models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Perceptual negligibility is a human vision statement; models weight chroma differently and small chroma-defined objects lose most of their signal at 4:2:0.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: detect small colored objects on gray backgrounds under 4:4:4 versus 4:2:0 with one open detector and compare recall.

one_line: Most web images carry a downscale-then-upscale resampling signature; models partially key on it, and 'native-resolution' imagery (direct camera capture) is subtly out-of-distribution.
problem: Web images have been through resize chains that imprint spectral signatures; models trained on them may use those signatures as context, but evaluation never separates resample-signature-bearing from native imagery.
core_hypothesis: Model accuracy has a component predicted by the resampling-history signature of the input, so native captures fail at elevated rates on texture- and sharpness-sensitive predictions, and imposing a web-typical resample chain on native captures recovers accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: For frozen models, passing native camera captures through a typical web resize chain (down-up with common kernels) before inference will improve accuracy on a measurable subset of texture-dependent decisions, which is impossible if resampling only destroys information.
