why_important: Every on-device deployment feeds native captures to models trained on web pipelines, so a resample-signature gap would be a universal, correctable domain shift affecting the entire edge-inference ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: Resampling detection is a forensics topic; its role as a covariate that vision models entrain on, with an accuracy-recovery prediction, appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect labeled native captures, evaluate under identity versus web-typical resample chains across several models, and test for consistent recovery on texture-sensitive classes.
main_risk: The effect competes with the JPEG-absence effect (C-009); a factorial design separating compression from resampling is needed to attribute recovery correctly.
community_default_belief: Higher-fidelity input can only help; any processing chain applied before inference is neutral or harmful.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fidelity is defined relative to the scene, but model competence is defined relative to the training distribution, and the training distribution is processed, not pristine.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: classify native smartphone RAW-derived images with and without a down-up resample chain in CLIP zero-shot and compare.

one_line: Segmenters reproduce dataset-specific annotator boundary conventions (systematic inset/outset of polygons), so cross-dataset boundary scores measure convention mismatch rather than localization competence.
problem: Boundary-quality metrics assume ground truth marks the true object edge, but annotation guidelines and tools bias polygons systematically inward or outward per dataset, and models fit that bias.
core_hypothesis: Each training corpus induces a signed, roughly constant boundary offset in model predictions; cross-dataset boundary F-score differences are dominated by offset mismatch, and removing a fitted global offset collapses much of the apparent cross-dataset boundary gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating a single signed dilation parameter per train-test dataset pair and applying it to predicted masks will recover a large share of cross-dataset boundary F degradation while leaving region IoU nearly unchanged.
why_important: Boundary metrics increasingly gate model selection (e.g., high-quality segmentation model comparisons); if they encode convention mismatch, the field is optimizing and ranking models on an artifact.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation inconsistency is acknowledged diffusely, but a quantitative offset-decomposition of cross-dataset boundary scores appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or take models fit on COCO, LVIS, and ADE20K; evaluate boundary F cross-dataset before and after per-pair signed dilation correction; report the fraction of the gap explained.
main_risk: Boundary conventions may vary by class and annotator rather than being a per-dataset constant, requiring a richer offset model and weakening the clean story.
community_default_belief: Boundary F differences across datasets reflect real generalization differences in edge localization ability.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models are trained to minimize loss against convention-biased truth, so faithfully reproducing training convention is optimal behavior that the metric then scores as failure elsewhere.
fastest_falsification: One day: sweep a signed mask dilation from -3 to +3 pixels on cross-dataset predictions and check how much boundary F recovers at the optimum.

one_line: Models trained on mixtures of amodal and modal annotation policies blend the two, producing occlusion-boundary predictions that follow neither policy and fail predictably in proportion to the training mixture.
problem: Datasets differ silently on whether occluded object parts are annotated (amodal) or not (modal); training on mixtures forces one network to fit contradictory targets for the same visual configuration.
core_hypothesis: Under occlusion, predicted mask extent interpolates between modal and amodal conventions with a mixing coefficient determined by training data proportions, so occlusion errors are policy-blend artifacts rather than perception failures, and are predictable without looking at the image content.
falsifiable_prediction: Across occlusion test cases, predicted extents will fall systematically between modal and amodal ground truths, and models trained on re-labeled single-policy versions of the same images will move to the corresponding pole and gain accuracy under the matching metric.
why_important: Occlusion handling is a headline weakness of segmenters; if a major share of it is target inconsistency, the fix is data governance rather than architecture, which changes research resource allocation.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal segmentation exists as a task, but the hypothesis that mixed-policy training causes a quantifiable interpolation failure appears unarticulated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take an occlusion test set with both modal and amodal ground truth, measure where predictions of standard models fall on the modal-amodal axis, and correlate the mixing coefficient with documented training data composition.
main_risk: Estimating training composition for foundation models is approximate, so the correlation part of the test may be weak even if interpolation is confirmed.
community_default_belief: Occlusion failures reflect missing capacity for reasoning about hidden object parts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A model given contradictory supervision for identical inputs must average; averaging looks exactly like 'poor occlusion reasoning' while being purely a label problem.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: for 100 occluded instances with dual ground truth, compute where SAM-style mask extents fall on the modal-amodal axis.

one_line: COCO-style 'crowd/ignore' regions teach detectors to suppress predictions in high-density areas, so recall collapse in dense scenes is partly a trained suppression behavior, not a capacity limit.
problem: Crowd regions are excluded from the loss or labeled as ignore, which from the model's perspective is systematic evidence that dense clusters need no individual detections, but density-dependent failure is always attributed to occlusion and NMS.
core_hypothesis: Detectors trained with crowd-ignore conventions internalize density-conditioned suppression: at matched per-instance visibility, recall drops as local instance density rises, and models trained on fully-instance-annotated dense data of the same scenes do not show the same drop.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic or re-annotated scenes where every instance in dense clusters is labeled, standard-trained detectors will under-detect relative to their own performance on matched-visibility sparse arrangements, and fine-tuning on fully-annotated dense data will recover recall faster than scale alone predicts.
why_important: Crowd counting, retail shelf audit, and aggregation-heavy biology imaging all operate in the dense regime where a trained-in suppression bias would set the effective performance ceiling.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd annotations are known as an evaluation convenience; their causal role as a training signal for suppression appears unquantified (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct visibility-matched sparse versus dense arrangements (synthetic compositing), evaluate standard detectors, then ablate by retraining with crowd regions fully annotated versus ignored, comparing density-conditioned recall curves.
main_risk: Disentangling trained suppression from NMS artifacts requires evaluating pre-NMS outputs, which complicates comparisons across detector families.
community_default_belief: Dense-scene recall failure is caused by occlusion plus NMS, and more data or better NMS is the remedy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The training signal explicitly rewards emitting nothing inside crowd regions; a model that generalizes this signal exhibits density-gated suppression that no NMS fix can undo.
fastest_falsification: One day: compare pre-NMS objectness maps for matched-visibility sparse versus dense composites and test for density-conditioned score depression.

one_line: Stock-photo watermarks and text overlays correlated with specific classes act as hidden features; a measurable slice of class-conditional accuracy evaporates when watermarks are removed or transplanted.
problem: Web corpora contain class-correlated watermarking (stock sites dominate certain content types), creating shortcut features that standard evaluations, which share the same watermark statistics, can never expose.
core_hypothesis: For classes whose training imagery is watermark-enriched, model confidence and accuracy depend partly on watermark presence, so cleaned images lose accuracy and watermark-transplanted negatives gain false positives, with effect size predictable from per-class watermark prevalence in the corpus.
falsifiable_prediction: Inpainting watermarks from test images will reduce accuracy on watermark-enriched classes significantly more than on matched control classes, and pasting typical watermarks onto out-of-class images will raise false-positive rates for those same classes.
why_important: It quantifies a data-governance failure with direct legal and safety resonance and explains anomalous confidence patterns in deployment where watermarks are absent.
why_possibly_novel: Watermark memorization is discussed for generative models; a class-conditional shortcut analysis for discriminative FMs with transplant counterfactuals appears rare (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-class watermark prevalence in an open corpus (LAION-like) via a watermark detector, pick enriched and control classes, run inpainting and transplant counterfactuals through CLIP zero-shot and a detector, and regress accuracy shifts on prevalence.
main_risk: Inpainting introduces its own artifacts, so a clean-capture control set is needed to separate inpainting damage from shortcut loss.
community_default_belief: Watermarks are low-level nuisance patterns that large models learn to ignore.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models ignore features uncorrelated with targets; watermark presence is class-correlated by the economics of stock photography, which makes it signal, not nuisance.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: measure CLIP zero-shot score shifts for a suspect class with and without a synthetic stock-style watermark overlay on matched images.

one_line: Detector and VLM object hallucination rates follow a quantitative law driven by class co-occurrence statistics of training corpora: hallucinated objects are those whose contextual partners are present.
problem: Hallucination is reported as per-class anecdotes; there is no predictive model of which object will be hallucinated in which scene, though co-occurrence priors offer an obvious candidate mechanism.
core_hypothesis: The probability that a model hallucinates class B in an image containing class A is an increasing, approximately monotone function of the corpus co-occurrence P(B|A), so hallucination is predictable scene-by-scene from corpus statistics alone, before running the model.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank-ordering candidate hallucinations by corpus co-occurrence will predict observed hallucination frequencies with high rank correlation, and scenes constructed to contain strong context objects with the partner absent will elicit hallucinations at rates matching the co-occurrence curve.
why_important: A predictive hallucination law converts an unpredictable safety concern into a computable per-scene risk score usable for deployment gating without any model access.
why_possibly_novel: Contextual bias is known qualitatively; a fitted, transferable quantitative law linking corpus co-occurrence to hallucination probability appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute co-occurrence from an open corpus, build context-present/partner-absent test scenes by compositing or curation, measure hallucination rates for several detectors and VLMs, and fit the rate versus co-occurrence curve.
main_risk: Hallucination also depends on visual ambiguity of local textures, so the co-occurrence law may explain only part of the variance and require a two-factor model.
community_default_belief: Hallucination is a stochastic decoding or miscalibration problem, mitigated by better training rather than predictable from data statistics.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If hallucinations were decoding noise, they would be class-uniform given confidence; their strong contextual patterning suggests they are learned priors firing without evidence, which is exactly what co-occurrence statistics would predict.
fastest_falsification: One day: composite 50 kitchen scenes without any bottle, query a VLM for bottles, and compare the hallucination rate against a co-occurrence-mismatched control object.

one_line: Photographer framing bias makes object-position-in-frame a learned prior: recognition and detection degrade with distance from typical framing positions, and each corpus leaves a measurable positional fingerprint in its models.
problem: Web imagery is intentionally framed, so object position is not uniform; models inherit that prior, but positional failure profiles are never used to characterize or compare models, nor controlled in evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Per-object failure probability as a function of normalized image position forms a stable, model-specific surface (the positional fingerprint) that (a) mirrors the training corpus's object-position density and (b) transfers across content categories, so peripheral placements fail at rates unexplained by resolution or lens distortion.
falsifiable_prediction: Sliding the same object crop across positions in a fixed background will produce a smooth accuracy surface peaked where the training corpus places objects, and different pretraining corpora will yield distinguishable surfaces under the same test.
why_important: Robotics and egocentric video present objects at atypical positions constantly; a positional fingerprint quantifies an entire silent failure axis and provides a corpus-attribution tool for auditing model provenance.
why_possibly_novel: Center bias is folklore in saliency research; systematic positional failure fingerprints of FMs, and their use for corpus attribution, appear unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite objects at a grid of positions in neutral scenes, evaluate several detectors and CLIP-style models, estimate accuracy-versus-position surfaces, and compare against corpus position densities estimated from open datasets.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts could interact with position (e.g., lighting mismatch more visible on plain regions), requiring careful rendering or real captured position sweeps.
community_default_belief: Convolutional and windowed architectures plus random-crop augmentation make position effects negligible in practice.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Random cropping reshapes but does not equalize positional statistics, and learned positional embeddings in ViTs give models explicit machinery to encode positional priors.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: slide one object crop over a 5x5 position grid in 20 backgrounds through an open detector and check for a center-peaked recall surface.

one_line: Vertex-budget limits of polygon annotation tools cap the boundary curvature present in ground truth, so segmenters inherit a curvature ceiling: they cannot produce high-curvature boundaries even when image evidence supports them.
problem: Annotation tools and guidelines implicitly limit polygon vertices per instance; ground-truth boundaries are therefore low-pass filtered versions of true shapes, and this instrument effect on learned boundary statistics is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: The curvature spectrum of model-predicted boundaries is bounded by the curvature spectrum of training annotations rather than by image evidence, so models systematically round corners and serrations, and training on curvature-rich synthetic supervision lifts the ceiling without architecture changes.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted boundary curvature distributions will be truncated near the training annotation curvature limit across content types, and evaluation on objects with true high-curvature boundaries (gears, leaves, fabric edges) will show error concentrated exactly in high-curvature segments.
why_important: Industrial inspection and biology depend on fine boundary geometry; a supervision-induced curvature ceiling implies benchmark scores overstate achievable geometric fidelity and points to a data-side fix.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation coarseness is acknowledged, but the framing as a measurable curvature transfer function from tool to model, with a spectrum-truncation prediction, appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate curvature spectra of COCO/LVIS polygons and of model predictions on curvature-rich test shapes; fine-tune the same model on synthetic data with exact high-curvature masks and test whether the predicted spectrum extends.
main_risk: Decoder output resolution independently limits curvature, so architecture ceilings and supervision ceilings must be separated by the synthetic fine-tune control.
community_default_belief: Boundary roundness is a resolution and loss-function problem (soft masks, downsampled decoders), not a property inherited from annotation instruments.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models trained to match low-pass targets are penalized for producing sharp corners even when visible, so the optimum under the training loss is rounded regardless of decoder capacity.
fastest_falsification: One day: compare curvature histograms of SAM outputs versus true shapes on 100 gear/leaf images and check for truncation at the annotation-typical curvature.

one_line: Ground-truth false negatives (unannotated real objects) train detectors into category-specific under-detection, so part of what benchmarks call 'hard categories' is annotation incompleteness echoed by the model.
problem: Detection training treats unannotated regions as negatives; categories with high annotation miss rates therefore receive systematic negative supervision on true positives, but per-category miss rates and their downstream effect are rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: Per-category deployed recall is depressed in proportion to the category's ground-truth miss rate in training data, and re-scoring benchmarks with exhaustively re-annotated ground truth reorders both category difficulty rankings and model rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: Categories with higher measured annotation miss rates will show recall depression beyond what visual difficulty metrics predict, and models fine-tuned on miss-corrected labels will gain recall specifically on those categories with little movement elsewhere.
why_important: It redirects effort from modeling to label auditing for a predictable subset of categories and warns that failure mining against incomplete ground truth manufactures fake failure cases (correct detections scored as false positives).
why_possibly_novel: Missing-label noise in detection is studied as a training robustness topic; using measured per-category miss rates to explain deployed failure structure and re-rank benchmarks appears less explored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Exhaustively re-annotate a sample of a standard benchmark for a dozen categories spanning suspected miss rates, quantify miss rates, and regress model recall depression against them across several detectors.
main_risk: Re-annotation is expensive and itself imperfect; miss-rate estimates need multiple annotators to be credible.
community_default_belief: Benchmark ground truth is complete enough that residual annotation misses are noise, not a systematic force shaping model behavior.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training explicitly punishes detections in unlabeled regions, so even moderate miss rates are not noise but consistent anti-supervision concentrated on specific categories.
fastest_falsification: One day: for two suspect categories, re-annotate 200 images, compute miss rate, and check whether detector 'false positives' cluster on missed ground truth.

one_line: Near-duplicate leakage between web-scale pretraining data and evaluation sets deflates measured failure rates: deduplicated evaluations reveal a hidden mass of failures and change robustness conclusions.
problem: Foundation models are evaluated on benchmarks whose images (or near-duplicates) partially exist in pretraining corpora; failure mining on such benchmarks samples from a contaminated distribution and understates true failure prevalence.
core_hypothesis: Stratifying evaluation by pretraining-similarity (embedding-space nearest-neighbor distance to the training corpus) will show failure rates rising steeply in the far-from-corpus stratum, and headline robustness claims shrink materially when only the uncontaminated stratum is scored.
falsifiable_prediction: For open-corpus models, error rate as a function of nearest-neighbor distance to the corpus will be strongly increasing, and model rankings on the far stratum will differ from full-benchmark rankings for at least some model pairs.
why_important: If failure mining and robustness evaluation are run on partially memorized data, the field's map of failure modes is drawn on the easiest terrain, and deployment surprise is guaranteed.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination is studied for LLM benchmarks; distance-stratified failure analysis for vision FMs with ranking-reversal tests appears less developed (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute nearest-neighbor distances from benchmark images to an open corpus (LAION-scale index), stratify error rates for CLIP-family models, and test ranking stability across strata.
main_risk: Embedding-based duplicate detection conflates semantic similarity with true duplication, so distance strata need visual audit to confirm the contamination interpretation.
community_default_belief: Benchmark contamination is an LLM problem; vision benchmarks predate the corpora or differ enough that leakage effects are minor.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Web-scale scrapes ingest benchmark mirrors and derivative reposts wholesale, and vision near-duplicates (recrops, recompressions) evade exact-match filters routinely.
fastest_falsification: One day: for one benchmark and one open-corpus model, plot error versus corpus nearest-neighbor similarity and check for a steep slope.

one_line: VLM failure on visual concepts tracks the linguistic provenance of training captions: concepts described mostly in particular languages or caption styles fail when queried outside that provenance.
problem: Alt-text quality and vocabulary vary enormously by website language and region; a concept's visual grounding can be strong under one linguistic framing and absent under another, but failure analyses treat concepts as language-neutral.
core_hypothesis: Per-concept VLM accuracy is predicted by the caption-language and phrasing distribution under which that concept appears in training, so translating the query toward the dominant training phrasing recovers accuracy, revealing that many 'visual' failures are provenance mismatches.
falsifiable_prediction: For concepts with skewed caption provenance, querying in the dominant training language or phrasing will outperform semantically equivalent alternate phrasings by margins far exceeding those for provenance-balanced concepts.
why_important: Multilingual deployment of VLMs is expanding; a provenance-mismatch failure law identifies which concept-language pairs will fail before deployment and separates language-side from vision-side failures in mining.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual gaps in CLIP are documented at the language level; per-concept provenance-conditioned failure prediction and its use in failure attribution appear underexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using an open captioned corpus, estimate per-concept caption-language and phrasing distributions, select skewed and balanced concepts, evaluate retrieval/classification under matched multilingual queries, and regress accuracy gaps on provenance skew.
main_risk: Text-encoder multilingual quality varies independently, so the analysis must control for general translation competence of the text tower.
community_default_belief: Once a concept is visually learned, query language only matters through the text encoder's general multilingual strength.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive training aligns images with specific caption distributions, not with concepts in the abstract; alignment mass follows phrasing, so grounding can be phrasing-local.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: pick 20 culture-specific concepts, query CLIP retrieval in the origin language versus English, and compare against 20 provenance-balanced controls.

one_line: Failures of independently developed vision FMs are highly correlated because of shared web data, imposing a hard ceiling on ensemble and cross-check safety architectures.
problem: Safety designs assume disagreement between independent models catches errors, but 'independent' models share crawled data, curation heuristics, and augmentation culture, so their failure sets may overlap far beyond chance.
core_hypothesis: Across model families with different architectures and training recipes, per-image failure indicators exhibit correlation well above what accuracy levels alone imply, and the shared-failure core is enriched in data-borne causes (rare compositions, convention conflicts) rather than architecture-specific ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring pairwise failure correlation across many public FMs at matched accuracy will show excess correlation over an independence baseline, the excess will shrink for model pairs with disjoint training corpora, and the shared-failure set will be stable across architecture swaps.
why_important: Every redundancy-based safety argument (two-model gating, ensemble uncertainty) is quantitatively wrong if failure correlation is high, and the correlation number itself is the missing constant in those designs.
why_possibly_novel: Error correlation of classifier ensembles is classical; a systematic corpus-attribution study of failure correlation across modern FMs, isolating data overlap as the driver, appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a matrix of public models (different labs, architectures, corpora) on a common evaluation set, compute excess failure correlation versus corpus overlap estimates, and test the corpus-overlap regression.
main_risk: Corpus overlap between public models is hard to quantify precisely, weakening the attribution even if excess correlation is confirmed.
community_default_belief: Different architectures and labs produce sufficiently decorrelated errors for ensembling and cross-checking to provide strong safety multipliers.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The dominant common factor is the web itself: if failure causes live in data (missing coverage, convention conflicts), architecture diversity cannot decorrelate them.
fastest_falsification: One day: score five public detectors on one hard set, compute pairwise agreement on failures, and compare with the independence prediction from marginal error rates.

one_line: Distillation and fine-tuning transmit failure sets nearly intact along model lineages, making failure provenance traceable like a phylogeny across the model ecosystem.
problem: Most deployed models descend from a few teachers via distillation or fine-tuning, but nobody measures how much of a teacher's failure set survives in descendants or uses failure overlap to map lineage.
core_hypothesis: Per-instance failure overlap between teacher and student is far higher than accuracy-matched unrelated pairs, persists through multiple derivation generations with a measurable decay rate, and is strong enough that failure fingerprints alone can identify a model's ancestor among candidates.
falsifiable_prediction: Given a set of models with known lineage, failure-set similarity will cluster them into the true family tree with high accuracy, and blind lineage identification from failure fingerprints will beat chance by a wide margin.
why_important: It implies monoculture risk assessments can be run empirically (audit descendants of a compromised teacher), and that fixing a failure in a widely-distilled teacher has quantifiable ecosystem-wide value.
why_possibly_novel: Model fingerprinting exists for IP protection via weights or outputs; using persistent failure sets as heritable fingerprints and measuring their generational decay appears novel (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble public model families (e.g., a teacher and its distilled/fine-tuned descendants plus unrelated controls), evaluate all on a common hard set, and test lineage recovery from failure-overlap matrices.
main_risk: Fine-tunes on divergent data may overwrite enough failures to blur lineage signals beyond one generation.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning and distillation substantially reshape model behavior, so descendant models are effectively new models with fresh error profiles.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Distillation objectives explicitly copy the teacher's function including its errors, and fine-tuning moves weights locally, so failures outside the fine-tuning distribution have no gradient pressure to change.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: compare failure overlap of one open teacher and its official distilled student against an accuracy-matched unrelated model on 1000 hard examples.

one_line: Per-image failure persistence across model generations is bimodal: transient failures that any scale increase fixes, and permanent failures immune to generation changes, with different causal signatures.
problem: Progress is reported as aggregate deltas between model generations, hiding the instance-level dynamics of which failures get fixed and which persist across every generation of a family.
core_hypothesis: Tracking fixed evaluation instances across a model lineage will show failure lifetimes clustering into two modes (fixed at the next generation versus never fixed), the permanent mode being enriched in label-convention conflicts, adjudication-ambiguous content, and information-theoretically limited inputs rather than capability gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: Instance-level failure survival curves across at least three generations will fit a two-population mixture significantly better than a single-population model, and human audit of the permanent population will find a majority of non-capability causes.
why_important: The permanent-failure population defines the true asymptote of scaling for a task; identifying and sizing it tells the field which failures need non-scaling interventions (label reform, sensor change, task redefinition).
why_possibly_novel: Longitudinal instance-level failure tracking across FM generations with survival analysis framing appears rare (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three or more generations of one model family on a frozen benchmark, build per-instance failure trajectories, fit mixture survival models, and audit a sample of never-fixed instances for cause categories.
main_risk: Generation changes bundle data, architecture, and recipe changes, so attributing persistence to intrinsic instance properties requires care with confounds.
community_default_belief: Scaling steadily fixes failures roughly uniformly; today's errors are tomorrow's solved cases.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Aggregate improvement is compatible with a frozen hard core: if generation N+1 fixes many transient failures while permanent ones persist, averages rise while the asymptote stays hidden.
fastest_falsification: One day: take two generations of one open model family, list common versus fixed failures on a benchmark, and audit 50 persistent failures for cause type.

one_line: Test-time augmentation agreement is higher on failures than successes for shortcut-driven errors: models are consistently wrong under augmentation exactly where TTA-disagreement detectors are trusted to fire.
problem: TTA disagreement is widely used as a cheap failure detector on the assumption that errors are unstable under input perturbation, but shortcut-driven errors should be stable because the shortcut feature survives augmentation.
core_hypothesis: Failure cases split by augmentation-consistency: ambiguity failures show low TTA agreement while shortcut and prior-driven failures show TTA agreement as high as correct predictions, so TTA-based failure detection has a structural blind spot covering the most dangerous (confident, systematic) errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Partitioning errors by an independent shortcut criterion (e.g., context-swap sensitivity) will show the shortcut partition matching correct-prediction TTA agreement levels, and TTA-based detectors will exhibit near-zero recall on that partition while performing well on the ambiguity partition.
why_important: Deployed monitoring stacks lean on TTA and perturbation consistency; a proven blind spot for systematic errors would force redesign of failure detection in safety-critical vision systems.
why_possibly_novel: TTA uncertainty is popular; a causal partition of errors by augmentation-stability with the blind-spot conclusion appears unformalized (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a benchmark with known shortcut structure (context-dependent classes), compute TTA agreement distributions for correct, shortcut-error, and ambiguity-error groups, and measure TTA-detector recall per group.
main_risk: Constructing the independent shortcut-error criterion without circularity (not itself using augmentation) requires careful design, e.g., counterfactual context edits.
community_default_belief: Prediction instability under augmentation is a reliable general-purpose proxy for error likelihood.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Instability tracks sensitivity to nuisance variation, but systematic errors are by definition insensitive to nuisance variation; the proxy conflates two error mechanisms with opposite signatures.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: on a context-bias dataset, compare TTA agreement for correct versus contextually-induced wrong predictions of one classifier.

one_line: Naturally-occurring failure images and adversarial perturbation directions share low-dimensional subspace structure, so mining natural failures can substitute for expensive adversarial search and vice versa.
problem: Natural failure mining and adversarial robustness research run as separate programs with separate tooling, though both probe the same decision boundary; whether their findings coincide geometrically is untested.
core_hypothesis: Feature-space directions that separate natural failure cases from matched successes align significantly with locally-computed adversarial gradient directions, implying a shared vulnerability subspace, so hardening against mined natural failures transfers to adversarial robustness within that subspace and vice versa.
falsifiable_prediction: Principal directions of natural-failure displacement in feature space will show cosine alignment with adversarial perturbation subspaces far above random-subspace baselines, and fine-tuning on either failure source will measurably reduce the other's failure rate within the shared subspace.
why_important: If confirmed, cheap natural-failure telemetry from deployments becomes a proxy for adversarial audit, and robustness budgets can be unified rather than split across two communities.
why_possibly_novel: Connections between natural and adversarial robustness exist at the accuracy-correlation level; explicit subspace-alignment tests and bidirectional-transfer predictions appear unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect natural failures for one classifier, compute failure displacement subspaces in penultimate features, compute adversarial subspaces on matched successes, measure principal angle statistics, and run the bidirectional fine-tune transfer test.
main_risk: Feature-space displacement of natural failures conflates content differences with vulnerability directions, so matched-pair construction (same class, similar content) is critical.
community_default_belief: Adversarial vulnerability is a worst-case, gradient-specific phenomenon geometrically unrelated to average-case natural failures.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Both phenomena are shaped by the same under-constrained decision boundary in regions of sparse training data; sparsity creates both natural error and adversarial fragility at the same locations.
fastest_falsification: One day: for 200 natural failures of one model, test whether small steps along the local adversarial gradient from matched correct images reproduce the same wrong labels.

one_line: Ecosystem-wide reliance on a few frozen backbones (CLIP, DINO) creates feature-level correlated blind spots: inputs poorly separated in backbone feature space fail across all downstream heads simultaneously.
problem: Thousands of products build different heads on identical frozen features; if some input pairs are unresolvable in feature space, every downstream system fails on them together, but no one measures this systemic layer of failure.
core_hypothesis: There exist characterizable input regions where backbone feature geometry collapses distinctions (feature-space confusability), and downstream failure across independent heads is predicted by that confusability score computed from the backbone alone, defining a systemic-risk map independent of any head.
falsifiable_prediction: A confusability score (local feature-space margin between relevant distinctions) will predict simultaneous multi-head failure with high precision, and heads trained on different tasks and data will nonetheless share failures exactly where the score is low.
why_important: Regulators and platform owners need monoculture risk metrics; a backbone-level confusability audit provides one, and it prioritizes which backbone deficiencies matter across the whole dependent ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: Monoculture concerns are discussed qualitatively for foundation models; an operational feature-geometry risk score validated against multi-head failure coincidence appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train several diverse heads (classification, retrieval, detection-lite) on one frozen backbone, compute per-input confusability from feature margins, and test whether low-margin inputs show coincident failure across heads at rates predicted by the score.
main_risk: Defining task-relevant distinctions for the margin computation requires labels, partially circularizing the score unless proxy distinctions generalize.
community_default_belief: Downstream fine-tuning and head diversity provide enough behavioral variety that shared-backbone systems fail mostly independently.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Heads cannot recover information the frozen features destroyed; feature-space collapse is a hard information bottleneck that no downstream diversity can undo.
fastest_falsification: One day: train three linear heads on frozen CLIP features for different label sets, and test whether their failure sets coincide on inputs with the lowest feature-space margins.

one_line: The natural failure set of a vision FM concentrates in a low-rank feature subspace: a handful of 'failure directions' explains most failure mass, making failures compressible and monitorable.
problem: Failure sets are treated as unstructured collections of hard cases; if they concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace of representation space, mining, monitoring, and repair could all exploit that structure, but dimensionality of failure sets is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Displacements between failures and matched successes in FM feature space are low-rank: a small number of directions captures a large share of failure variance, the directions are semantically interpretable (e.g., lighting regimes, style axes), and distance along them predicts failure probability on fresh data.
falsifiable_prediction: Spectral analysis of failure displacement matrices will show variance concentration far exceeding matched-success-pair baselines, and a logistic model on the top few directions will predict held-out failures substantially above chance across content categories.
why_important: Low-rank failure structure means deployment monitors can watch a few projections instead of everything, and data collection can target directions instead of enumerating cases, changing the economics of robustness.
why_possibly_novel: Error-mode clustering exists; a rank-deficiency claim about failure geometry with a predictive projection test appears unformalized (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine several thousand failures for one FM-based classifier, construct matched success pairs, compute displacement spectra, compare with control spectra, and evaluate top-direction failure predictors on held-out data.
main_risk: Low-rank structure may reflect the mining method's biases rather than the model's failure geometry; multiple independent mining sources are needed.
community_default_belief: Failures are heterogeneous long-tail phenomena without exploitable global geometry.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Failures are generated by a small set of systematic causes (priors, conventions, coverage gaps), and a small causal basis should manifest as low-rank geometry in a good representation.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: PCA on failure-minus-success feature displacements for 1000 mined pairs and compare the eigenvalue decay against shuffled-pair controls.

one_line: Model errors form two mechanistically distinct populations, confidently-wrong (shortcut/prior-driven) and diffidently-wrong (ambiguity-driven), and every mitigation helps one while leaving or harming the other.
problem: Calibration and failure-detection research pools all errors, but errors near the decision boundary and errors far on the wrong side have different causes, signatures, and remedies; the pooled treatment produces mitigation methods that look better than they behave.
core_hypothesis: The error population of vision FMs is bimodal in confidence and in cause: high-confidence errors trace to shortcuts and priors while low-confidence errors trace to genuine ambiguity, and standard mitigations (temperature scaling, selective prediction, TTA) exclusively address the low-confidence mode, leaving the high-confidence mode as an invariant residual.
falsifiable_prediction: Cause-audited error sets will show confidence bimodality with cause enrichment per mode, and applying standard mitigations will reduce diffident errors substantially while the confident-error rate stays statistically unchanged across mitigation families.
why_important: The confident-error mode is the dangerous one in deployment; if standard tooling structurally cannot touch it, safety cases built on calibration and abstention are systematically overstated.
why_possibly_novel: Overconfidence is well known in aggregate; a two-population causal decomposition with a mitigation-invariance claim appears uncrystallized (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect errors for several classifiers/detectors, audit causes via counterfactual probes (context swap, texture randomization), test bimodality, apply mitigation families, and measure per-mode reduction.
main_risk: The confidence boundary between modes may be blurry and dataset-dependent, requiring the causal audit rather than a simple threshold to define populations.
community_default_belief: Better calibration plus selective prediction handles the practical error problem; error confidence is a continuum, not a mixture of mechanisms.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shortcut activations produce evidence-like internal signals, so no recalibration of the same signal can flag them; the continuum view hides a mechanism boundary that mitigation cannot cross.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: histogram error confidences for one model on a shortcut-rich dataset, test for bimodality, and check temperature scaling's effect on the high-confidence lobe.

one_line: Per-pixel segmentation confidence is spatially anti-aligned with error severity: lowest at tolerable boundary zones, highest inside regions where errors are catastrophic whole-instance mistakes.
problem: Downstream systems consume segmentation confidence maps as risk maps, but confidence is trained per-pixel and concentrates uncertainty at boundaries, while the costly failures (mislabeling an entire region or instance) occur in high-confidence interiors.
core_hypothesis: The spatial distribution of segmentation confidence is dominated by boundary proximity rather than semantic risk, so severity-weighted risk (probability times cost of the error at that pixel) is anti-correlated with the confidence map's implied risk over a large fraction of images, making confidence maps actively misleading for downstream risk consumers.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets where errors can be classified by severity (boundary-offset versus wrong-region), the confidence map will rank boundary pixels as riskiest while realized severe errors concentrate in interior pixels ranked safe, yielding negative rank correlation between confidence-implied and severity-weighted realized risk.
why_important: Autonomous systems and medical pipelines gate decisions on segmentation confidence; a demonstrated anti-alignment would show that gating logic is pointed at the wrong pixels.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-concentrated uncertainty is a known descriptive fact; the severity-weighted anti-alignment claim and its consequence for downstream gating appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several segmenters, decompose errors into boundary-offset and region-level classes with severity weights, compute realized-risk maps, and correlate with model confidence maps across images.
main_risk: Severity weighting is application-specific; results need at least two distinct downstream cost models to show robustness of the conclusion.
community_default_belief: Segmentation confidence maps are imperfect but directionally useful risk signals across the image.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-pixel cross-entropy training makes confidence a proxy for local label ambiguity, and label ambiguity is structurally highest at exactly the pixels where errors matter least.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on a driving dataset, check whether whole-instance segmentation errors occur predominantly in the top confidence quartile of pixels.

one_line: Classification confidence and localization quality of detections are nearly statistically independent, so score-threshold failure mining systematically misses the well-scored badly-localized failure stratum.
problem: Failure mining and deployment gating both use the classification score as the master quality signal, implicitly assuming it also reflects localization quality, an assumption that decoupled training losses give no reason to support.
core_hypothesis: Across detector families, the mutual information between classification score and localization error (IoU with truth) is low, so a distinct failure stratum exists (high score, poor box) that score-based mining never samples, and this stratum is enriched in downstream-harmful cases (truncated boxes on pedestrians, merged boxes on adjacent objects).
falsifiable_prediction: Joint distributions of score and IoU will show near-independence beyond a weak trend, and audits of high-score detections will find localization failures at rates far exceeding what score-based failure models predict, with family-specific structure (set-prediction versus anchor-based differing in stratum shape).
why_important: If the miner cannot see a whole failure stratum, targeted improvement loops (mine, retrain, redeploy) converge to models that are precisely wrong: confident, plausible, badly localized.
why_possibly_novel: Localization-aware scoring papers exist as fixes; the failure-mining blind-spot framing with stratum enrichment analysis appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public detectors, compute score-IoU joint statistics on standard benchmarks, quantify the high-score/low-IoU stratum, and audit its content composition against downstream harm categories.
main_risk: IoU-aware heads (already present in some detectors) may partially couple the variables, requiring family-stratified conclusions rather than a universal claim.
community_default_belief: Detection score is an adequate single quality signal; low-quality boxes mostly come with low scores.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Classification and regression branches optimize different losses on different targets, and nothing in standard training forces their errors to correlate; independence is the default outcome, not the exception.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: scatter-plot score versus IoU for one detector's true-positive-matched detections on COCO val and compute their correlation.

one_line: Calibration transfers across class-prior shift in a predictable direction: models calibrated on balanced sets become overconfident on majority classes and underconfident on minority classes in deployment, with error computable from the prior ratio alone.
problem: Calibration is fit on curated evaluation distributions and shipped into deployments with different class priors; the resulting miscalibration is treated as unpredictable drift rather than a computable, correctable quantity.
core_hypothesis: For softmax classifiers, deployment miscalibration under pure prior shift follows the analytic Bayes correction determined by the train-to-deploy prior ratio, so measured deployment calibration error will match the closed-form prediction, and applying the correction restores calibration without new labeled data beyond prior estimates.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing deployment sets with controlled prior shifts will produce calibration error curves matching the analytic prediction across shift magnitudes, and prior-corrected models will show near-baseline calibration while uncorrected temperature scaling fails in the predicted direction.
why_important: Prior shift is the most common deployment shift and prior estimates are often available operationally; a validated closed-form fix would replace expensive recalibration cycles for a large class of deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Prior correction is classical for accuracy; its systematic validation as the dominant, predictable component of deployed FM miscalibration appears under-documented (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample a benchmark into several prior-shifted deployment sets, measure calibration error of frozen models with and without analytic prior correction, and compare against the closed-form curve.
main_risk: Real deployment shifts mix prior shift with covariate shift, so the clean predictability claim applies to the prior component and needs a decomposition method in the wild.
community_default_belief: Deployment miscalibration is a symptom of general distribution shift requiring learned recalibration on deployment data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The prior-shift component of miscalibration is mathematically determined and needs no learning; treating it as unpredictable conflates the correctable part with the genuinely hard covariate part.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: resample CIFAR/ImageNet val to a skewed prior, measure a frozen model's calibration error, and compare against the analytic prediction.

consolidation.solo_drop_note: prior_art_risk drop (unverified but high confidence): analytic prior-shift/Bayes-correction recalibration is classical statistics; the residual claim is a validation study rather than a new hypothesis. Consolidator may reinstate if a novelty check disagrees.

one_line: Under style shift (paintings, sketches, renders), model confidence does not degrade smoothly but bifurcates toward extremes, invalidating threshold-based OOD triggers precisely on stylized inputs.
problem: OOD monitoring assumes confidence decreases with distribution distance, but style-shifted inputs may resolve to either strong-but-wrong prior matches or total feature mismatch, producing a bimodal rather than shifted confidence distribution.
core_hypothesis: As inputs move along a photo-to-abstract style continuum, per-input confidence distributions transition from unimodal to bimodal (near-one and near-zero lobes) rather than shifting downward, so any single confidence threshold either floods alerts or misses the confident-wrong lobe entirely.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence histograms along a controlled stylization continuum will show growing bimodality (dip statistic increasing), and threshold-based OOD detectors will exhibit a characteristic precision-recall collapse at intermediate stylization that density-based detectors on features do not show.
why_important: Stylized and rendered content is ubiquitous in user-generated and synthetic-media streams; monitoring that structurally fails on this slice leaves a large deployment surface unguarded.
why_possibly_novel: Style robustness is measured in accuracy; the confidence-distribution-shape analysis and its consequence for threshold monitors appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate a stylization continuum for a fixed image set (style transfer at graded strengths), record confidence distributions for several classifiers, test for bimodality trends, and benchmark threshold versus density OOD detectors along the continuum.
main_risk: Stylization methods introduce content distortion correlated with strength, so content must be verified stable (human check) to attribute effects to style alone.
community_default_belief: Confidence declines roughly monotonically as inputs leave the training distribution, so thresholds trade sensitivity against alert volume smoothly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Style shift does not move inputs uniformly away from all classes; it moves them toward whatever class's training data contained similar styles, creating confident capture rather than graceful decay.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: stylize 200 photos at five strengths, histogram a classifier's max-softmax per strength, and test for bimodality.

one_line: SAM-style mask quality scores inherit the prompt distribution of training: quality prediction fails specifically for atypical prompts (boundary-adjacent, off-center, multi-point), mis-ranking masks exactly when users prompt unusually.
problem: Promptable segmenters ship a learned quality head used to select among candidate masks, but that head was trained under a synthetic prompt distribution, and its reliability conditioned on prompt typicality is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Quality-score reliability (correlation with true IoU) degrades sharply as prompts depart from the training prompt distribution, so for boundary-adjacent or unusually-placed prompts the model both segments worse and mis-scores its candidates, compounding failure at selection time.
falsifiable_prediction: Binning interactions by prompt typicality (distance from object center, proximity to boundary, prompt count) will show quality-score-to-true-IoU correlation collapsing in atypical bins while remaining high in typical bins, and oracle selection among candidates will beat score-based selection by the largest margins exactly in the atypical bins.
why_important: Interactive segmentation workflows trust the score to auto-select masks at scale (dataset labeling, medical contouring); a prompt-conditional reliability hole silently corrupts downstream datasets where prompting is naturally atypical.
why_possibly_novel: SAM failure analyses focus on mask quality; conditional reliability analysis of the quality head under prompt-distribution shift appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample prompts across a typicality grid on a labeled dataset, record SAM candidate masks with scores and true IoUs, and estimate score-IoU correlation per bin plus oracle-versus-score selection gaps.
main_risk: Prompt typicality must be estimated relative to SAM's actual training prompt synthesis, which is only partially documented, so a proxy typicality model is needed.
community_default_belief: The predicted-IoU head is a reliable, roughly uniform quality signal across reasonable user prompts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Learned quality heads are regressors valid on their training input distribution; prompt placement is an input to that regressor, and users explore regions synthetic prompt generation never covered.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: for 300 objects, compare score-IoU correlation between center-point prompts and near-boundary prompts.

one_line: A single temperature calibrated in-domain moves calibration in a predictable harmful direction under covariate shift (overconfidence grows with feature-space shift distance), making shift distance a sufficient statistic for recalibration.
problem: Temperature scaling is the default calibration fix, but its transfer behavior under shift is treated as unpredictable, though the direction (shifted inputs get relatively overconfident) may be systematic and quantifiable.
core_hypothesis: Calibration error under covariate shift grows monotonically with feature-space distance from the calibration set, always in the overconfident direction for in-domain-calibrated models, so a distance-conditioned temperature (one scalar function, no shift labels) restores most calibration across shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Across shift benchmarks, plotting calibration error against mean feature distance will show a monotone overconfident trend for temperature-scaled models, and a distance-conditioned temperature fit on one shift family will transfer to unseen shift families with large calibration recovery.
why_important: It would replace per-domain recalibration with a single deployable rule, and provide a falsifiable structural law about how confidence degrades, useful for monitoring design.
why_possibly_novel: Accuracy-on-the-line style regularities exist for accuracy; a corresponding distance-law for calibration direction with a transferable conditional temperature appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate temperature-scaled classifiers across corruption and natural-shift suites, regress signed calibration error on feature distance, fit the conditional temperature on half the shifts, and test transfer on the rest.
main_risk: Some shifts (label-correlated or adversarially structured) may break monotonicity, restricting the law to covariate-only shifts and requiring a shift-type detector.
community_default_belief: Calibration transfer under shift is idiosyncratic; each deployment domain needs its own recalibration data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shift-induced overconfidence has a common mechanism (softmax saturation on off-manifold features), and common mechanisms produce lawful, not idiosyncratic, behavior.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: for one model on a corruption suite, plot signed calibration error versus corruption severity and check the monotone overconfident trend.

one_line: VLMs switch from vision to language-prior answering at a measurable visual-evidence threshold: a psychometric 'blindness point' that is a stable model constant across content.
problem: Language-prior bias in VLMs is documented anecdotally, but there is no quantitative model of when the switch happens, so failures look random rather than governed by an evidence-strength threshold.
core_hypothesis: For questions with prior-consistent and prior-violating answers, VLM accuracy as a function of visual evidence strength (contrast, size, occlusion of the deciding cue) follows a psychometric curve whose inflection (the blindness point) is stable across content domains for a given model, making prior-override behavior predictable from one calibration set.
falsifiable_prediction: Psychometric curves measured on one content domain will predict the evidence threshold at which the same model abandons visual evidence in other domains, and models ranked by blindness point on synthetic stimuli will retain that ranking on natural counterexample benchmarks.
why_important: A single-number characterization of prior dominance enables model selection and risk assessment for applications where images routinely contradict priors (defect detection, medical anomalies).
why_possibly_novel: Counterintuitive-image benchmarks exist; extracting a transferable psychometric constant for prior override appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build stimulus ladders degrading the visual cue that contradicts a strong prior (e.g., a green stop sign at graded visibility), fit psychometric curves per model per domain, and test cross-domain threshold stability.
main_risk: Evidence strength is multidimensional (size, contrast, blur), so the threshold may be cue-specific rather than a single constant, complicating but not invalidating the framework.
community_default_belief: Prior-driven errors are qualitative quirks to be trained away, not lawful threshold phenomena that can be measured and compared.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The switch reflects a quantitative competition between evidence and prior inside a fixed computation; fixed computations produce reproducible tradeoff curves, which is exactly what psychometrics measures.
fastest_falsification: One day: create one cue-degradation ladder for one counterintuitive scene family, query two VLMs, and check whether accuracy follows a sigmoid with model-specific thresholds.

one_line: VLM counting errors mirror human numerosity psychophysics (exact subitizing up to about four, logarithmic error growth beyond) because caption statistics encode human number usage, not because models perceive numerosity.
problem: Counting failures are reported as accuracy tables; the structure of the errors (which counts get confused with which) is unanalyzed, leaving the mechanism (perceptual limits versus linguistic priors) unresolved.
core_hypothesis: VLM count-response distributions will show human-like signatures: near-perfect small-number performance, scalar variability (error proportional to magnitude), and round-number attraction, and these signatures will track caption corpus number-word frequencies rather than image encoder capacity, implying counting is linguistic prior readout above the subitizing range.
falsifiable_prediction: Error distributions will show variance growing with true count and mass concentrated on round numbers matching corpus frequency, and interventions that change visual encoding capacity (resolution, crops) will not move the large-count error structure, while prompt phrasing that shifts linguistic framing will.
why_important: If counting is prior readout, applications needing counts (inventory, biology, crowd estimates) require structured decomposition tools rather than better VLM scaling, redirecting engineering effort.
why_possibly_novel: Counting weakness is well documented; the psychophysical signature analysis tied to caption statistics as the mechanism appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Query VLMs on controlled dot/object arrays across counts, fit variance-versus-magnitude and round-number attraction models, and compare against number-word frequencies from open caption corpora and against resolution-intervention controls.
main_risk: Tokenizer representation of numbers introduces its own artifacts that must be separated from corpus frequency effects.
community_default_belief: Counting failure is a visual grounding limitation that scale and resolution will progressively fix.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If failure were visual, error structure would track visual variables; the hypothesis predicts it tracks linguistic variables instead, which resolution cannot fix.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: query one VLM on arrays of 3 to 60 dots, histogram responses, and check for round-number spikes and scalar variance growth.

one_line: Left/right spatial-relation failures in VLMs are chiral: systematically asymmetric in a direction matching reading-order statistics of training captions, so mirroring images flips the error asymmetry.
problem: Spatial relation benchmarks report symmetric-looking accuracy numbers, but if errors are directionally biased by language statistics, the aggregate hides a chiral structure that mirroring would expose.
core_hypothesis: VLMs answer 'A left of B' questions with an asymmetric error profile (one direction systematically overreported), the asymmetry sign matches subject-first/reading-order biases in caption corpora, and horizontally mirroring the entire evaluation flips the model's error asymmetry, proving the bias is representational rather than stimulus-driven.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed error asymmetry will be significantly nonzero and consistent across content, will flip sign under global image mirroring, and will correlate across models with the reading-order statistics of their (documented) caption sources.
why_important: Chiral failure is invisible to standard accuracy but decisive for robotics and AR instructions where left/right correctness is the whole task; the mirroring test also provides a cheap audit tool for any deployed VLM.
why_possibly_novel: Spatial reasoning weakness is documented in aggregate; the chirality signature, mirror-flip causal test, and corpus-statistics linkage appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build balanced left/right scenes, measure signed asymmetry per model, rerun with mirrored images, and verify sign flip plus magnitude preservation.
main_risk: Object-category confounds (some objects appear more often on one side in photos) must be controlled by synthetic balance and per-pair counterbalancing.
community_default_belief: Spatial relation errors are symmetric noise from weak spatial grounding, equally likely in both directions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text decoder generates relations with language-model priors that are directionally biased by reading order and phrase frequency; symmetric noise is the least likely outcome for a language-mediated readout.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 100 two-object scenes, ask left/right, mirror all images, re-ask, and compare signed error asymmetries.

one_line: Open-vocabulary detectors and VLMs match negated queries ('a cup without a handle') to the negated concept itself, and the failure is diagnosable entirely from the text encoder's geometry before any image is seen.
problem: Negation failures are typically evaluated end-to-end, mixing vision and language causes; if the text embedding of a negated phrase lands near the affirmative embedding, the system fails for a purely textual reason predictable offline.
core_hypothesis: For contrastive text encoders, embeddings of negated attribute phrases are dominated by the negated content word, so text-side similarity structure alone (negated phrase near affirmative phrase) predicts image-side failure rates per concept, and text-encoder-only audits can forecast which negation queries a deployment will get wrong without any image evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Cosine similarity between negated and affirmative phrase embeddings will predict per-concept negation failure rates on image benchmarks with strong correlation, and interventions purely on the text side (compositional re-encoding) will recover image-task accuracy in proportion to the text-geometry fix.
why_important: Negation is common in safety-relevant queries (find products without safety caps); an offline text-side audit that forecasts failures cheaply changes how such systems are validated.
why_possibly_novel: Negation weakness in CLIP-like models is documented; the quantitative text-geometry-to-image-failure forecasting claim appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute negated-affirmative embedding similarities for a concept battery, evaluate open-vocab detection with negated queries on a labeled set, and regress failure rates on text-side similarity.
main_risk: Some negation failures may be genuinely visual (attribute absence is hard to verify), which the regression residual should expose but could also muddy the headline correlation.
community_default_belief: Negation failure is a joint vision-language reasoning gap requiring multimodal fixes and training data with negated captions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the text tower collapses the negation before fusion, no visual improvement can matter; the failure is inherited upstream and its size is measurable without images.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: embed 50 negated/affirmative phrase pairs in CLIP text space, then check retrieval behavior for the five most and least collapsed pairs.

one_line: Attribute-object binding errors in VLMs grow superlinearly with the number of attributed objects in the scene, following a capacity law of cross-attention rather than a per-object constant error rate.
problem: Binding failures (assigning the red color to the wrong object) are demonstrated with two-object scenes, but how failure scales with scene complexity is unmeasured, leaving deployments without a load limit for attribute-critical tasks.
core_hypothesis: Binding error per object rises with object count following a superlinear curve with a model-specific capacity knee, because attention resources for maintaining object-attribute association are shared and contended, so scene complexity is a quantitative predictor of binding failure and the knee is a comparable model constant.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled scenes with n attributed objects will show per-object binding error flat up to a knee then rising steeply, knee position will vary across models but be stable across content within a model, and shrinking attention capacity (token pruning) will move the knee left predictably.
why_important: It converts binding from a qualitative flaw into a measurable capacity spec (max reliable attributed objects), directly usable in application design and model comparison.
why_possibly_novel: Binding benchmarks exist for small scenes; scaling-law characterization with a capacity-knee constant appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic scenes with 2 to 16 uniquely attributed objects, query attribute-object pairs, fit per-object error versus n curves per model, and test knee stability across two content families.
main_risk: Synthetic scenes may underestimate real-scene binding difficulty; a natural-image validation subset is needed to anchor the law.
community_default_belief: Binding is a fixed per-model weakness with roughly constant error probability per object pair regardless of scene load.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Association maintenance consumes shared attention capacity, and shared-resource systems degrade nonlinearly at load, not at a constant per-item rate.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: colored-shapes scenes at n in {2,4,8,12}, one VLM, plot binding accuracy versus n and look for the knee.

one_line: Increasing input resolution without increasing visual token budget raises VLM hallucination on fine details: per-token information compression, not resolution, is the operative variable for detail fidelity.
problem: Higher resolution is assumed to reduce hallucination by providing more detail, but if the visual token budget is fixed, each token must compress more content, and the effect of compression ratio on hallucination is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Hallucination rate on detail-level questions is governed by pixels-per-visual-token rather than raw resolution, so raising resolution at fixed tokens increases detail hallucination in describable-but-compressed regions, while raising tokens at fixed resolution decreases it, making the compression ratio a design law for VLM configuration.
falsifiable_prediction: Factorial evaluation over resolution and token budget will show hallucination tracking the ratio (iso-ratio configurations matching), with the paradoxical cell (higher resolution, same tokens) showing more detail hallucination than the lower-resolution baseline.
why_important: Teams tune resolution as a quality dial assuming monotone benefit; a compression law would correct configuration practice across every deployed VLM and explain contradictory anecdotes about resolution scaling.
why_possibly_novel: Token-budget ablations exist for accuracy; the compression-ratio law for hallucination specifically, with the paradoxical prediction, appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one open VLM across a resolution-by-token grid on a detail-question benchmark with hallucination scoring, and test iso-ratio matching plus the paradoxical cell.
main_risk: Token merging strategies inside the vision tower differ across models, so the law's form may be architecture-conditional.
community_default_belief: More input resolution monotonically improves VLM detail fidelity and reduces hallucination.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The language model reads tokens, not pixels; if tokens are overloaded, the decoder fills gaps with priors, and higher resolution at fixed tokens increases overload by definition.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: one VLM with configurable input size, fixed token count, detail-QA on 200 images at two resolutions, compare hallucination rates.

one_line: VLMs lean on embedded text as a crutch for perception questions: removing or altering incidental text in images collapses accuracy on questions that ostensibly require only visual understanding.
problem: Benchmark images are full of incidental text (signs, labels, packaging) that leaks answers; reported visual understanding may partly be OCR-plus-reasoning, but text-reliance is never quantified per capability.
core_hypothesis: For a substantial fraction of benchmark items labeled as visual perception, model accuracy drops sharply when embedded text is inpainted away or adversarially altered, and the text-reliance fraction varies by capability category, being highest for fine-grained recognition and scene understanding, revealing inflated capability estimates.
falsifiable_prediction: Text-removed benchmark variants will show accuracy drops far exceeding human drops on the same variants, altered-text variants (wrong labels painted in) will pull answers toward the painted text, and capability rankings between models will reorder once text-reliance is subtracted.
why_important: Capability inflation misleads model selection for text-free deployment domains (nature, industrial interiors, medical), where the OCR crutch is unavailable and true performance is unknown.
why_possibly_novel: Text-shortcut effects appear in isolated probes; a systematic text-reliance decomposition of standard perception benchmarks appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inpaint incidental text from a sample of a standard VLM benchmark, verify content preservation with human checks, re-evaluate several VLMs, and compute per-capability text-reliance fractions.
main_risk: Inpainting quality issues could depress accuracy for non-text reasons; the altered-text (rather than removed-text) condition controls for this.
community_default_belief: OCR ability is a bonus capability layered on top of genuine visual understanding, not a substitute for it in benchmark performance.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Text is the highest-signal-to-noise feature in any image containing it, and training rewards using it; substitution rather than addition is the efficient learned solution.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: pick 100 benchmark items containing text, paint over the text, re-query one VLM, and compare accuracy drop against a no-text control set.

one_line: VLM performance on an image is predicted by how likely that image's natural description is under web caption style: content whose honest description diverges from alt-text conventions fails regardless of visual difficulty.
problem: Failure analysis focuses on visual attributes of hard images, ignoring that VLM training aligns images to a narrow stylistic register of text, so images whose accurate descriptions are stylistically improbable (geometric, procedural, relational) may fail for text-distribution reasons.
core_hypothesis: The likelihood of an image's ground-truth description under a caption-style language model predicts VLM task accuracy on that image beyond visual difficulty measures, so style-improbable content (dashcam geometry, instrument panels, tables of objects) forms a coherent failure stratum invisible to visual-attribute mining.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-image VLM accuracy on caption-style likelihood will show a significant effect after controlling for visual complexity metrics, and rewriting task prompts toward caption-register phrasing will recover accuracy on the style-improbable stratum but not the control stratum.
why_important: It reframes part of failure mining from image space to text-distribution space, giving a cheap corpus-side predictor of failure and a prompt-side mitigation, both testable without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is well known; using caption-style likelihood of the scene description as a failure predictor appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score benchmark images' reference descriptions with a caption-corpus language model, evaluate VLMs, and fit accuracy models with and without the style-likelihood covariate; run the phrasing-mitigation arm on the extreme strata.
main_risk: Caption-style likelihood correlates with content rarity, so visual-difficulty controls must be strong to isolate the text-side effect.
community_default_belief: VLM failure on unusual content reflects visual rarity; the text side is a neutral output channel.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive and captioning objectives only bind images to text that plausibly occurs; content that occurs visually but is rarely captioned faithfully is trained to align with whatever text does occur, which is systematically off-task.
fastest_falsification: One day: rank 500 benchmark images by description likelihood under a caption LM and compare VLM accuracy of the bottom versus top deciles at matched visual complexity.

one_line: VLM visual verification has a phrasing-dependent yes-bias: agreement rates track question-form frequency in training text, so the same visual fact gets different answers under logically equivalent phrasings.
problem: Verification benchmarks use one phrasing per fact, so the measured accuracy confounds visual grounding with the model's phrasing-conditioned response prior, and the size and structure of that prior is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: For fixed visual evidence, the yes/no response distribution shifts systematically across logically equivalent phrasings (positive, negative, tag-question, existential forms), the shift direction follows form-frequency statistics of instruction corpora, and phrasing-marginalized evaluation changes both absolute scores and model rankings on standard verification suites.
falsifiable_prediction: A phrasing battery over identical visual facts will yield response shifts far exceeding sampling noise with a stable direction per form, and ensemble-over-phrasings scoring will reorder some model pairs relative to single-phrasing benchmarks.
