main_risk: Some instability is benign relabeling of the same structure; agreement metrics must operate on case memberships, not names, to avoid overstating the problem.
community_default_belief: Automated slice discovery reveals real, reproducible failure structure that teams can safely build remediation plans on.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Clustering high-dimensional weak signals is notoriously initialization- and metric-dependent, and failure sets are small samples of rare events, the worst case for stable clustering; stability was assumed, never audited.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run one slice-discovery tool five times with different seeds on one model-dataset pair and compute pairwise slice-membership overlap.

one_line: Fixing mined failures by fine-tuning damages a predictable collateral set of previously-correct cases, and the repair-damage exchange follows a measurable locality law in feature space, defining a conservation-like constraint on cheap fixes.
problem: Targeted fine-tuning on failures is standard practice with regression testing as the only safeguard; whether collateral damage is random or lawfully concentrated near repairs in representation space is unknown, so damage cannot be predicted or budgeted.
core_hypothesis: Post-repair regressions concentrate in feature-space neighborhoods of the repaired cases with damage probability decaying with representational distance, the decay profile is stable per architecture and fine-tuning method (defining a repair kernel), and total repair-minus-damage is approximately invariant across fine-tuning hyperparameters for fixed data, implying a budget that can be estimated before committing to a fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Regression cases will be strongly enriched within measured feature radii of repair targets versus matched controls, the estimated repair kernel will predict held-out collateral damage counts, and hyperparameter sweeps will trade repair against damage along an approximately fixed frontier rather than beating it.
why_important: Continuous-deployment vision systems ship weekly fixes; a validated damage-prediction kernel would replace blind regression testing with pre-hoc risk budgeting and reveal when a fix is net-negative before shipping.
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting is studied for tasks and domains; a per-case spatial damage law with kernel estimation for failure-repair workflows appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune models on controlled failure batches, log flips on large evaluation pools, fit damage-versus-distance profiles, validate kernel predictions on new batches, and map the repair-damage frontier across hyperparameters.
main_risk: Feature-space distance may be the wrong metric for damage locality; several representation layers and metrics should be compared before rejecting the law.
community_default_belief: With small learning rates and replay data, targeted fixes are essentially free; regressions are rare accidents rather than lawful consequences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Weight updates that change one decision necessarily move a region of the function, not a point; locality of that region in representation space is the mathematically expected form, making 'rare accidents' the surprising claim, not the law.
fastest_falsification: One day: fine-tune on 50 failures, identify all flipped cases in a 50k pool, and test whether flips concentrate within the nearest-neighbor radii of the 50 targets.

one_line: Which instances a model will fail on at convergence is largely determined early in training: learning-event signatures (forgetting counts, late first-learn epochs) forecast final failure sets long before training ends.
problem: Failure mining happens after deployment, at maximal cost; if final failure membership is legible from early training dynamics, mining could move upstream, but the forecast horizon and accuracy are unmeasured for modern vision training.
core_hypothesis: Per-instance training dynamics in the first fraction of training (forgetting events, first-learn time, loss oscillation) predict final-model failure membership substantially above chance, prediction transfers to held-out data via a dynamics-trained probe on input features, and the early-determined failure fraction is enriched in data-borne causes (label conflict, rare compositions) versus late-emerging failures that track optimization noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Probes on early-training dynamics will forecast converged-model failures with strong precision at moderate recall, forecast quality will saturate well before mid-training, and the early-predictable stratum will show the predicted cause enrichment under audit.
why_important: Moving failure discovery from post-deployment to early training collapses the cost of the mine-fix loop and gives data teams a triage signal (fix labels, add coverage) while training is still running.
why_possibly_novel: Example difficulty and forgetting statistics exist for curriculum research; their use as converged-failure forecasters with transfer probes in vision FMs appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument training runs of mid-scale vision models to log per-instance dynamics, train forecast probes at several checkpoints, evaluate against converged failure sets on train-distribution and shifted evaluations, and audit the early-predictable stratum.
main_risk: Requires training instrumentation access, so the claim cannot be tested on API-only foundation models, limiting scope to reproducible-training settings.
community_default_belief: Final failure sets depend on the whole training trajectory and data order; early dynamics are too noisy to forecast them usefully.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Failures caused by data conflicts and coverage gaps exist independent of trajectory details; training dynamics merely reveal them early, and such causes may dominate mined failure sets.
fastest_falsification: One day with a small model: train on CIFAR-scale data logging per-example dynamics, and test whether epoch-10 forgetting statistics predict epoch-200 errors.

one_line: Frame-to-frame prediction flicker in video segmentation spikes seconds before catastrophic tracking losses: instability is a leading indicator with a usable warning horizon, not just a cosmetic artifact.
problem: Temporal instability of video model outputs is treated as an aesthetic smoothness problem to be filtered away, and catastrophic failures (identity switches, mask collapse) are treated as sudden; whether instability temporally precedes catastrophe is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Catastrophic failure events in video segmentation and tracking are preceded by statistically elevated output instability (mask boundary churn, score oscillation) over a horizon of many frames, the precursor holds after controlling for scene difficulty dynamics, and thresholding the instability signal yields early warnings with operationally useful precision, while temporal smoothing (the standard remedy) destroys the warning signal without reducing catastrophe rates.
falsifiable_prediction: Aligned event studies will show instability rising before failures at rates far above matched non-failure windows, warning precision-recall will beat confidence-based baselines at equal lead time, and smoothed pipelines will show unchanged catastrophe rates with eliminated precursor visibility.
why_important: Video perception failures in robotics and driving are dangerous precisely because they arrive unannounced; a validated free precursor signal converts sudden failures into anticipated ones, and indicts the ubiquitous smoothing practice as safety-negative.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal consistency is optimized as a quality target; its role as a catastrophe precursor with event-study validation appears unstudied (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run video segmenters and trackers on datasets with failure annotations, extract instability time series, perform event-study alignment with difficulty controls, and evaluate warning systems against confidence baselines plus the smoothing ablation.
main_risk: Instability and difficulty co-rise with scene changes; the difficulty-controlled analysis is essential and hard to get right.
community_default_belief: Flicker is cosmetic noise to be smoothed; catastrophic failures stem from discrete events (occlusions, cuts) without accessible precursors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Catastrophes in dynamical prediction systems typically follow loss of stable tracking equilibria, and oscillation is the canonical signature of equilibrium loss; treating it as cosmetics discards the system's own distress signal.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on one video-object-segmentation benchmark, compare mask-churn statistics in the three seconds before failure events versus random control windows.

one_line: Motion-blur failure depends on blur direction relative to object contours and text orientation, not just magnitude: benchmarks using uniform-direction blur systematically mis-estimate real-world blur robustness.
problem: Blur robustness is benchmarked with scalar severity levels, ignoring that motion blur is a vector; real blur directions correlate with motion geometry (camera shake versus subject motion), and directional interaction with content structure is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: At fixed blur magnitude, failure rates vary strongly with the angle between blur direction and dominant object contours (blur parallel to critical edges preserves them, perpendicular destroys them), so real-world blur robustness depends on the joint geometry of motion and content, and scalar-severity benchmarks misrank models whose directional profiles differ.
falsifiable_prediction: Directional blur sweeps at fixed magnitude will produce failure-rate variation comparable to a full severity step, per-class directional profiles will follow contour statistics (text and thin structures showing the strongest anisotropy), and two models tied on scalar benchmarks will separate under direction-resolved evaluation.
why_important: Handheld, vehicular, and drone imagery have strongly non-uniform blur direction distributions; robustness certification that ignores direction certifies against the wrong distribution and hides model differences that matter in the field.
why_possibly_novel: Motion blur augmentation and deblurring are mature; direction-content interaction as a failure law with benchmark-validity consequences appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply parameterized directional blur to detection and OCR-bearing datasets at controlled magnitudes, evaluate model panels direction-resolved, and quantify direction-content interaction terms plus ranking changes versus scalar protocols.
main_risk: Synthetic linear blur under-represents real blur trajectories (curved shake paths); a real handheld-capture validation subset is needed.
community_default_belief: Blur severity is the operative variable; direction averages out and can be ignored in robustness evaluation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Blur is a directional low-pass filter and image structures are directional; the interaction is dictated by signal processing, and real motion directions are far from uniformly distributed, so nothing averages out.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: fixed-magnitude blur at 0, 45, 90 degrees on scene-text images through an OCR-capable VLM and compare accuracy across directions.

one_line: A large share of claimed temporal understanding in video models fails the shuffle test: predictions are invariant to frame order or time reversal, exposing single-frame shortcuts behind temporal benchmarks.
problem: Video benchmarks credit models with temporal reasoning when answers are correct, without testing whether the temporal dimension was used; the fraction of benchmark performance attributable to genuinely order-sensitive computation is unknown for modern video FMs.
core_hypothesis: For current video models, a substantial fraction of correct answers on temporal-sounding tasks survives frame shuffling and time reversal, the surviving fraction varies strongly by task category (high for appearance-answerable, low for causal-order questions), and benchmark-level temporal capability scores shrink dramatically under order-sensitivity normalization, reordering model comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Shuffle and reversal invariance rates will be high on tasks marketed as temporal, invariance will predict which items scale poorly with more frames, and order-sensitivity-normalized scores will change model rankings relative to raw benchmarks.
why_important: Temporal understanding claims drive deployment into monitoring and safety applications where order matters (fall detection, procedure verification); capability inflation from single-frame shortcuts is a direct deployment risk and a benchmark-design indictment.
why_possibly_novel: Shuffle controls appear in individual papers historically; a systematic order-sensitivity audit of modern video FMs with normalized scoring appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate video models on standard temporal benchmarks under original, shuffled, and reversed frame orders, compute per-item and per-category invariance, and publish order-sensitivity-normalized capability scores.
main_risk: Shuffling can break tokenization assumptions in some architectures; implementation must distinguish computational breakage from informational insensitivity.
community_default_belief: Strong scores on temporal benchmarks demonstrate temporal reasoning; frame order sensitivity is implied by task design.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Benchmark questions are constructed by humans who see the temporal structure, but answer keys are often recoverable from appearance priors; models exploit whatever suffices, and nothing in the scoring verifies order usage.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: run one video model on 200 temporal-benchmark items with shuffled frames and report the score retention fraction.

one_line: Tracker failures at occlusions are governed by a model-specific memory horizon: failure probability transitions sharply when occlusion duration exceeds a constant that is independent of object appearance, making occlusion risk computable from geometry alone.
problem: Occlusion robustness of trackers is reported as aggregate scores on datasets with uncontrolled occlusion statistics, so no one knows whether failure is governed by a duration threshold, appearance similarity, or scene complexity, preventing any predictive risk model.
core_hypothesis: Per-event tracking failure probability as a function of occlusion duration is sigmoid with a sharp model-specific midpoint (the memory horizon), the horizon is stable across object categories and appearance at matched re-detection difficulty, and horizon length measured on synthetic occlusions predicts real-world failure rates given deployment occlusion-duration distributions.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled occlusion-duration sweeps will produce sigmoid failure curves with tight midpoint estimates per model, midpoints will vary across architectures (memory-based versus detection-based) but not across content at matched conditions, and convolving measured horizons with deployment occlusion statistics will predict field failure rates.
why_important: A single-constant risk model turns occlusion robustness from a leaderboard number into an engineering quantity: deployments can measure their occlusion-duration distribution and compute expected failure rates before installation.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion handling is a core tracking topic; the duration-threshold constant framing with content-independence and field-prediction validation appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate controlled occlusion events (synthetic compositing and staged captures) sweeping duration, fit per-model sigmoid curves, test content independence, and validate field prediction on an annotated real dataset.
main_risk: Re-appearance context (position predictability during occlusion) matters alongside duration; the design must stratify by motion predictability to keep the horizon interpretable.
community_default_belief: Occlusion failure is a complex function of appearance similarity, distractors, and scene clutter, too entangled for a single-parameter law.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Memory mechanisms decay or drift at rates set by architecture, not content; if memory decay is the binding constraint, duration dominates and the entanglement story confuses secondary modulators with the primary variable.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: composite occluders of controlled duration over tracked objects in existing sequences and plot one tracker's failure rate versus duration.

one_line: Video models fail on high-frame-rate and timelapse footage because the operative variable is motion magnitude per frame, not content: frame-rate mismatch is a hidden distribution shift misdiagnosed as content difficulty.
problem: Web training video clusters near standard frame rates, fixing a narrow distribution of inter-frame motion magnitudes; deployment footage (high-speed, timelapse, variable-rate streams) violates it, but evaluations never condition on effective motion-per-frame.
core_hypothesis: Video model accuracy is a function of inter-frame motion magnitude with a tuned optimum near web-typical values, degrading on both sides (too-small motion starves temporal signals, too-large motion breaks correspondence assumptions), so resampling deployment footage to web-typical motion-per-frame recovers accuracy without any model change, proving the failure is rate mismatch rather than content.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy versus motion-per-frame curves will be non-monotone with an interior optimum consistent across content types, temporally resampling high-fps and timelapse footage toward the optimum will recover a large share of the deficit, and the optimum will track the training corpus's motion statistics across models trained on different corpora.
why_important: Industrial inspection, sports analytics, and surveillance increasingly use non-standard frame rates; a resampling fix and a corpus-statistics predictor would immediately improve deployments and re-attribute a class of mined failures from content to acquisition.
why_possibly_novel: Frame-rate augmentation exists as a trick; the motion-per-frame distribution-shift framing with the interior-optimum prediction and corpus-tracking test appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate video models on fixed content captured or resampled across a wide motion-per-frame range, fit accuracy curves, run the resampling-recovery arm, and compare optima across models with documented training corpora.
main_risk: Resampling introduces its own artifacts (frame interpolation errors, temporal aliasing) that must be bounded with capture-native high-fps ground truth.
community_default_belief: Video models generalize across frame rates since content is unchanged; failures on unusual footage reflect unusual content.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Temporal architectures learn correspondence and motion priors calibrated to the training inter-frame displacement scale; content identity is irrelevant to whether those priors match the input's temporal sampling.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: take one action-recognition model, evaluate the same clips at native rate and subsampled by factors of 2 to 16, and plot accuracy versus effective motion-per-frame.

one_line: Deployed vision failures arrive in temporal bursts because consecutive inputs share failure-inducing conditions: per-image metrics understate operational risk, and the failure autocorrelation function is the missing deployment statistic.
problem: Evaluation treats inputs as exchangeable and reports marginal failure rates, but deployments consume correlated streams where one failure predicts more; burst structure determines real-world harm (consecutive missed detections) yet is never measured or modeled.
core_hypothesis: Failure indicator time series from deployed streams exhibit strong positive autocorrelation over condition-persistence timescales, burst-adjusted risk metrics (probability of k consecutive failures) exceed IID predictions by orders of magnitude, and the autocorrelation function is predictable from environmental persistence statistics, enabling stream-level risk certification that per-image metrics cannot provide.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured failure autocorrelation on dashcam and surveillance streams will greatly exceed shuffled-baseline levels, k-consecutive-failure frequencies will match a fitted correlated model and violate IID extrapolations, and cross-deployment ACF differences will track condition-persistence differences.
why_important: Safety cases quantify harm via consecutive-failure probabilities (missed pedestrian across n frames); computing them from marginal rates under IID assumptions is the current practice and may be wrong by orders of magnitude in the dangerous direction.
why_possibly_novel: Correlated errors are acknowledged qualitatively in safety engineering; measured failure ACFs for modern vision systems and their integration into evaluation practice appear absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run detectors on continuous annotated streams, extract failure time series, estimate ACFs against shuffled controls, fit burst models, and compare k-failure predictions against IID baselines and against held-out stream measurements.
main_risk: Continuous ground truth is expensive; semi-automatic annotation with human audit of failure windows makes it tractable.
community_default_belief: Per-frame or per-image failure rates, possibly stratified by condition, adequately characterize deployment risk.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Stratification by known conditions captures only the modeled covariates; residual correlation from unmodeled persistent factors (sensor state, scene geometry, weather microstructure) remains and is exactly what bursts are made of.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run one detector over a labeled driving sequence set, compute failure-run-length distributions, and compare against the shuffled-order distribution.

one_line: Failure mining only sees failures humans can adjudicate: models are never evaluated on inputs where human ground truth is unattainable, and the adjudication boundary silently shapes both training data and claimed capabilities.
problem: Every benchmark and mined failure set requires human-verifiable labels, so inputs where humans cannot agree or cannot know (extreme conditions, ambiguous scenes, beyond-human acuity regimes) are excluded from evaluation entirely, leaving model behavior there unmeasured and unmineable by construction.
core_hypothesis: Model behavior degrades or becomes pathological beyond the human adjudication boundary in ways detectable without full ground truth (via physical consistency checks, instrument cross-validation, or downstream outcome verification), and the excluded regime constitutes a substantial share of deployment inputs for real systems, so capability claims certified inside the boundary systematically overstate deployed reliability.
falsifiable_prediction: Using instrument-verified ground truth that bypasses human labeling (physical measurements, multi-sensor consensus), model performance in the beyond-adjudication regime will fall significantly below extrapolations from the adjudicable regime, and the deployment share of such inputs will be measurable and non-negligible for several application domains.
why_important: The field's entire evidence base has a selection filter nobody accounts for; quantifying behavior past the filter, and the filter's deployment share, would recalibrate reliability claims for every high-stakes vision application.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation ambiguity is studied within labeled data; the systematic exclusion of unadjudicable inputs and instrument-based measurement of model behavior beyond the boundary appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: In one domain with independent instrumentation (e.g., distance measurement versus monocular estimates, laboratory assays versus visual inspection), assemble input sets spanning the adjudication boundary, measure model performance against instrument truth on both sides, and estimate the deployment frequency of beyond-boundary inputs.
main_risk: Instrument ground truth is domain-specific and expensive, restricting initial evidence to a few domains from which generalization must be argued carefully.
community_default_belief: Benchmark distributions cover deployment adequately; inputs humans cannot label are rare edge cases irrelevant to capability measurement.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Deployment samples nature, not what annotators can label; fog, glare, distance, and ambiguity are common in the world, and their systematic exclusion is an artifact of the labeling economy, not of deployment statistics.
fastest_falsification: One day: compare monocular depth model errors against lidar truth stratified by whether human annotators could confidently order the depths, and check for a performance discontinuity at the adjudication boundary.

one_line: Benchmark-targeted training conserves failure mass rather than destroying it: as benchmarks saturate, failures migrate to input regions outside benchmark support, measurable as unchanged failure rates on independently sampled wild distributions.
problem: Benchmark scores improve steadily, and the community reads this as failure reduction; whether total failure probability under natural input distributions declines correspondingly, or merely relocates outside benchmark support, is untested because nobody maintains benchmark-independent evaluation streams.
core_hypothesis: For successive model generations optimized against saturated benchmarks, failure rates measured on continually refreshed, benchmark-disjoint wild samples decline far slower than benchmark gains imply, the divergence grows with benchmark age (a Goodhart drift law), and failure composition on wild samples shifts toward input types structurally absent from benchmark support, demonstrating migration rather than elimination.
falsifiable_prediction: Longitudinal evaluation of model generations on frozen benchmarks versus freshly-sampled wild sets will show diverging trend lines, wild-set failure composition will shift toward benchmark-unrepresented strata over generations, and the divergence will be largest for the most heavily targeted benchmarks.
why_important: If failure mass is conserved under benchmark optimization, the field's progress metrics systematically overstate reliability gains, and deployment surprise is a predictable consequence of the evaluation economy rather than bad luck.
why_possibly_novel: Goodhart effects and benchmark overfitting are discussed; a quantitative conservation-versus-elimination test with refreshed wild sampling across model generations appears unexecuted (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble model generations spanning several years, evaluate all on their era benchmarks plus a protocol-fixed refreshed wild sample (random web and sensor captures with post-hoc labeling), and compare improvement slopes and failure composition drift.
main_risk: Wild sampling must avoid its own drift and leakage into training corpora of newer models; capture-after-training-cutoff protocols mitigate but complicate comparisons.
community_default_belief: Benchmark gains, especially on diverse modern suites, reflect genuine broad reliability improvement that transfers to deployment distributions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Optimization pressure concentrates improvement exactly on measured support; without pressure elsewhere, error mass has no reason to shrink there, and high-dimensional input spaces have unbounded unmeasured regions for it to occupy.
fastest_falsification: One day: evaluate three model generations on one saturated benchmark and on 500 freshly captured never-online photos of matched content, comparing the two improvement slopes.

one_line: Human-assigned failure categories (occlusion, blur, clutter) misidentify causal mechanisms: ablation-based causal attribution disagrees with human failure labels in a large fraction of cases, invalidating remediation plans built on human taxonomies.
problem: Failure review processes have humans tag error causes by looking at images, assuming visible difficulty equals operative cause; the agreement between these intuitive attributions and intervention-based causal tests has never been measured.
core_hypothesis: For a substantial fraction of mined failures, counterfactual interventions (removing the occlusion, deblurring, decluttering via editing) do not flip the prediction, revealing the human-assigned cause was incidental, the true causes being invisible factors (context priors, convention conflicts, pipeline artifacts) that humans cannot see, so remediation targeted by human taxonomy fixes the wrong variable at scale.
falsifiable_prediction: Intervention audits will show low flip rates for human-attributed causes on a large case fraction, flip-rate-validated taxonomies will differ structurally from human taxonomies, and retraining targeted by validated causes will outperform retraining targeted by human labels at matched budget.
why_important: Industrial failure review is built on human cause-tagging; measuring its causal validity, and finding it poor, would redirect failure analysis toward intervention-based tooling and explain why cause-targeted data collection often underdelivers.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual editing exists as a technique; using it to audit the causal validity of human failure taxonomies at scale appears novel (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample mined failures with human cause tags, construct intervention edits per tag with modern editing tools plus quality control, measure prediction flip rates, and run the remediation comparison arm on the largest cause categories.
main_risk: Editing artifacts can flip predictions for spurious reasons; edit-quality controls and placebo edits (matched edits on non-attributed factors) are essential.
community_default_belief: Experienced reviewers can identify why a model failed from inspection; human cause taxonomies are reliable inputs to remediation planning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Humans see the image's salient difficulty, but models fail for model reasons (features, priors, pipeline state) that are invisible in the image; the visible-difficulty heuristic is a category error about where causes live.
fastest_falsification: One day: for 50 failures tagged occlusion, inpaint the occluder away and count how many predictions actually flip to correct.

one_line: A measurable share of benchmark failures are cases where ground truth is contested among annotators: model-truth disagreement and annotator-annotator disagreement overlap heavily, and separating them changes model rankings and failure-rate estimates.
problem: Benchmarks ship single-truth labels, so evaluation cannot distinguish model errors on clear cases from disagreements on inherently contested cases; the contested fraction of reported failures, and its effect on rankings, is unquantified for modern vision benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: Re-annotating benchmark samples with multiple independent annotators will show mined model failures strongly enriched in high-disagreement items, scoring only consensus items will change absolute failure rates substantially and reorder some model pairs, and the contested stratum will have distinct visual characteristics allowing cheap contestedness prediction for un-re-annotated benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Failure enrichment in high-disagreement strata will be several-fold, consensus-only scoring will move model rankings for measurable pairs, and a contestedness predictor trained on re-annotated subsets will transfer across benchmarks with useful accuracy.
why_important: Failure rates drive both research claims and deployment sign-offs; conflating contested-truth cases with genuine errors inflates failure counts, punishes models that disagree with an arbitrary annotator, and pollutes mined sets with unfixable cases.
why_possibly_novel: Label noise and annotator disagreement are studied per-dataset; the systematic decomposition of mined failure sets into contested versus clear strata with ranking-impact analysis appears missing for modern FMs (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-annotate stratified samples of standard benchmarks, measure failure enrichment by disagreement level, recompute leaderboard rankings on consensus subsets, and train the contestedness predictor.
main_risk: Multi-annotation cost limits scale; stratified designs and existing multi-annotator datasets partially substitute.
community_default_belief: Benchmark labels are correct enough that failure rates measure model deficiency; annotator disagreement is second-order noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models converge toward annotator-average behavior, so their residual disagreements with single annotators concentrate precisely on items where annotators disagree with each other; enrichment is the expected geometry, not an anomaly.
fastest_falsification: One day: triple-annotate 300 items from one benchmark, and compare model failure rates on unanimous versus split items.

one_line: Specific systematic failures are fossils of training objectives, not data or architecture: loss-function swaps transplant characteristic failure signatures (boundary smoothing, dominant-mode collapse) across architectures and datasets.
problem: Failure modes are habitually attributed to data gaps or architecture limits, while the loss function's shaping of error structure is unexamined as a first-class causal factor with a testable transplantation signature.
core_hypothesis: Holding data and architecture fixed while swapping objectives (cross-entropy versus Dice versus boundary losses; softmax versus contrastive heads) will move characteristic failure signatures with the objective, the signatures will be recognizable across architectures trained with the same objective on different data, and a classifier can identify the training objective of a black-box model from its error structure alone, establishing objectives as dominant failure determinants.
falsifiable_prediction: Objective-swap experiments will show failure-signature transfer exceeding architecture-swap and data-swap effects for a defined signature set, and blind objective identification from error statistics will succeed well above chance across model families.
why_important: If objectives dominate failure structure, remediation via data collection is misdirected for objective-fossil failures, and objective design becomes a failure-engineering tool with predictable consequences, changing how systematic failures are diagnosed and fixed.
why_possibly_novel: Loss effects on metrics are studied per-task; the transplantation test and black-box objective identification from failure signatures appear new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train factorial grids (objective by architecture by dataset) at moderate scale for segmentation and classification, extract failure-signature statistics, quantify variance attribution across factors, and run the blind identification protocol.
main_risk: Factorial training is compute-heavy; signature definitions must be pre-registered to avoid post-hoc pattern hunting.
community_default_belief: Failure modes primarily reflect what the model saw (data) and what it can compute (architecture); the loss is an optimization detail once converged.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The loss defines which errors were cheap during training; converged models sit at loss-specific tradeoff points, and different tradeoff points are different failure structures by definition.
fastest_falsification: One day: train two small identical segmenters with cross-entropy versus Dice on one dataset and compare their error-type histograms for the predicted signature shift.

one_line: Auto-labeling feedback loops amplify initial failure modes at a rate governed by the acceptance threshold: model-curated training data converts small biases into entrenched blind spots across iterations, with a measurable amplification law.
problem: Production pipelines increasingly train on model-accepted or model-generated labels; the dynamics of failure-mode amplification under this feedback (which errors compound, how fast, and what the threshold dependence is) are unmeasured though the loop is now standard practice.
core_hypothesis: Iterated auto-label training amplifies precisely the confident systematic failures (which pass acceptance thresholds) while suppressing diffident errors, amplification rate per iteration is an increasing function of the acceptance threshold's confidence cutoff, and content strata initially failed confidently disappear progressively from effective training data, producing measurable coverage collapse invisible to aggregate metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled auto-label loops will show per-stratum error growth for initially confident-failed strata against flat or improving aggregate metrics, amplification rate will vary with threshold as predicted, and injecting a small human-audited counter-stratum will arrest amplification, isolating the feedback mechanism.
why_important: The industry is scaling exactly this loop to cut labeling costs; an amplification law with threshold dependence would provide the missing safety parameterization and predict which deployment biases will worsen autonomously over time.
why_possibly_novel: Self-training degeneration is known in theory and for language model collapse; a quantitative amplification law for vision failure strata with threshold dependence appears unmeasured (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate multi-iteration auto-label pipelines on detection or segmentation with planted systematic biases, sweep acceptance thresholds, track per-stratum error trajectories, and validate the arrest intervention.
main_risk: Simulation realism (planted biases versus organic ones) limits external validity; one arm should replicate the effect starting from a real model's organic confident failures.
community_default_belief: Confidence-thresholded auto-labels are conservative and safe; quality control on accepted labels prevents error compounding.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Thresholds filter by confidence, not correctness; systematically confident errors pass by definition, and each iteration increases their training share, which is the compounding mechanism quality control never samples.
fastest_falsification: One day: two iterations of self-training for a detector with a known confident failure mode, tracking that mode's error rate against aggregate mAP.

one_line: Published failure analyses over-represent photogenic, interpretable failure types while deployed error budgets are dominated by unglamorous causes (pipeline mismatches, threshold drift, metadata bugs): the literature's failure map is aesthetically curated.
problem: The community's collective understanding of how vision systems fail is assembled from published analyses, which are subject to selection pressure toward visually compelling and intellectually interesting failure types; whether this literature distribution matches deployed failure-cause distributions is an open empirical question.
core_hypothesis: Coding failure types reported in published analyses against failure-cause distributions from systematic deployment audits will reveal large, directional divergence: interpretable perceptual causes (adversarial patterns, unusual objects, occlusions) over-represented by large factors, and operational causes (preprocessing mismatch, calibration drift, version skew, metadata handling) under-represented, so research effort allocation tracks the aesthetic distribution rather than the harm distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: A structured comparison of literature-reported failure taxonomies against audited deployment incident taxonomies will show statistically significant composition divergence in the predicted direction, and the divergence will be larger in venues with stronger visual-presentation norms.
why_important: If the field studies the failures that photograph well rather than those that cause harm, the research-to-reliability pipeline is broken at the agenda-setting stage, and quantifying the mismatch is the first step to correcting resource allocation.
why_possibly_novel: Publication bias is studied for effect sizes; failure-type selection bias in the vision failure-analysis literature, measured against deployment audits, appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Systematically code failure types from a defined corpus of published failure analyses, obtain or construct deployment incident taxonomies from available industrial postmortems and audits, and compare compositions with agreement-controlled coding.
main_risk: Deployment incident data is scarce and itself selectively reported; multiple independent sources and sensitivity analysis are required for a defensible comparison.
community_default_belief: The published failure literature, in aggregate, reflects the practically important failure landscape of deployed vision systems.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Publication requires novelty and compelling figures, while deployed failures skew toward mundane engineering causes that are neither; the selection filters are strong, independent, and both point the same direction, away from representativeness.
fastest_falsification: One day: code failure types in 50 recent failure-analysis papers and compare against failure categories in publicly available autonomous-vehicle disengagement and incident reports.
